Why Mamdani opposes RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's NYC event
articles.content: Zohran Mamdani called the Hindu nationalist group's ideology "exclusionary" ahead of Mohan Bhagwat's New York event. But can the mayor do anything to stop it? New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he does not support an upcoming event featuring Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Hindu nationalist group Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), though he acknowledged the city likely has no power to stop it. Bhagwat is scheduled to speak Saturday at Madison Square Garden as part of what organizers are calling the "Universal Oneness Celebration," an event expected to draw around 5,000 attendees, local media reported. It is part of a broader global outreach tour tied to the RSS's centenary year, wherein Bhagwat is visiting the United States, Canada and the UK. When asked whether the event should be canceled at a press conference, Mamdani said: "I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on canceling a private event." Mamdani is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor in New York City's history. He added that his opposition to the visit reflected his role leading a city that believes in "the belonging of each and every person, no matter their color, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from." His mother is acclaimed Indian filmmaker Mira Nair. He added that he grew up with an understanding of India as "a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India." "It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision." The event is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, which says it has backing from over 135 Hindu American organizations and is meant to promote shared heritage and interfaith unity. However, several interfaith and civil rights groups – including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York – have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history. They held a news conference outside New York City Hall calling for the event to be canceled. "Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus. He leads an extremist Hindu nationalist movement that has fueled violence, exclusion and fear for minority communities," said Sravya Tadepalli, Deputy Executive Director of Hindus for Human Rights, in a statement. "New York should not provide the RSS with a stage on which religious nationalism can be repackaged as unity." The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS, is a right-wing Hindu organization founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in 1925. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for National Volunteer Organization. The group describes itself as a "Hindu-centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus and disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance. The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization. In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities. The US government advisory body called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims." United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more. India's BJP-led government denies any discriminatory intent, pointing to programs such as food subsidies and electrification initiatives, which it says benefit all communities. The organization has been banned in India on multiple occasions, including in 1948 after a Hindu nationalist who had ties with the RSS assassinated independence leader Mahatma Gandhi. articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Navy has quietly fired or removed several top officers in recent months but broke with its usual practice of announcing those changes, drawing pushback from Congress. Two Democratic lawmakers said Thursday that the Navy failed to inform Congress that it fired the entire leadership team of a nuclear-powered attack submarine last month after an underwater collision. Separately, the sea service in September fired the commander of a destroyer deployed to the Middle East, according to a defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe sensitive personnel matters. Michigan sues Mackinac Island ferry operator, claims it’s a monopoly
articles.description: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said the ferry companies have raised prices and ‘leveraged their power in alarming ways.’
articles.content: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has sued the ferry operators serving Mackinac Island Nessel accuses the ferry operators of acting like a monopoly and raising prices while limiting services The owner of the ferry companies notes a federal court has already rejected antitrust claims against the company Michigan is suing the company that owns and operates ferry services on Mackinac Island, alleging they have monopolized the market. Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said in a press conference Thursday that Hoffmann Marine violated Michigan’s anti-trust laws when it bought out all ferry lines to the island and long-term parking options. Nessel said the company has “leveraged massive power” by threatening to suspend ferry services to the island if officials did not comply with pricing. “We’ve seen Hoffmann do exactly what you’d expect a monopoly to do,” Nessel said. ”They’ve raised prices, limited services, and leveraged their massive power in alarming ways.” Hoffmann Marine told WCMU that they’re disappointed by the lawsuit and believe they are not violating state or federal anti-trust laws. RELATED: Mackinac Island ferry fight to continue despite legislation Appeals court allows Mackinac Island authority over ferry rates — for now Lawmakers give Mackinac Island control of ferry rates. Neighbors aren’t happy Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel at Central Michigan University on Tuesday, Oct. 3, 2023. (Rick Brewer/WCMU News) “As a reminder, the federal court has already twice rejected the City of Mackinac Island’s antitrust claims in its federal litigation against us,” said Hoffman Marine in an emailed statement to WCMU. In April, Nessel issued a statement encouraging the island and ferry company to resolve disputes. Hoffmann Marine told WCMU they agreed with that statement and believe this lawsuit “threatens to derail those efforts.” Nessel filed the lawsuit as she approaches the end of her time as Michigan’s attorney general due to term limits. She said attorney general-elect Eli Savit is aware of the lawsuit and supports it. “He’s in full-throated support of continuing this and making sure that we are, again, protecting the businesses and the people of Mackinac Island, as well as people all over the state and our country who wish to enjoy it,” Nessel said.Donate Nessel said a judge should force Hoffmann Marine to sell their ferry lines to restore competition. The suit comes shortly after voters passed an amendment to the island’s charter on Nov. 3, giving Mackinac Island officials the final say over ferry ticket and parking rates. articles.title: US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then see Zelenskyy in Dublin
articles.description: US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then see Zelenskyy in Dublin AP News Kushner says Europe to join next Ukraine talks, but Putin stands firm on territorial demands CNN Russia, Ukraine reach deal on prisoner swap as US says lack of trust holds back talks Reuters Putin’s chief negotiator vows to return ‘every inch of Russian land’ in Ukraine Atlantic Council In Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner Ask Putin
articles.content: DUBLIN (AP) — U.S. envoys met Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin before heading to Ireland for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as Washington sought new momentum for its peace efforts. Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, brokered talks this week between delegations from Moscow and Kyiv. The session in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, brought the first direct discussions between Ukrainian and Russian representatives in nine months as the push for a settlement stalled. The talks produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced. Plans for another round of talks were announced as well, with Witkoff and Zelenskyy saying Europe will join, though they gave no details about which countries or how many. Kushner and Witkoff met with Putin for about two hours before going to Dublin, where they met with Zelenskyy for more than an hour as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark. Kushner said one goal of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader’s blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent’s broader security arrangements. In Abu Dhabi, several European security advisers were involved on the sidelines but not in the main three-way talk. Speaking to reporters before boarding a plane to leave Moscow, Witkoff said the next round of talks has been agreed upon. Russian state TV showed Witkoff saying that “the Europeans will join at the next meeting,” but he did not elaborate. Zelenskyy in Dublin indicated the Europeans would not be on the sidelines. “Next meeting, Europe will be during negotiations, will be a negotiation team – not some way, not separately. They will have a voice,” he said. The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow. Russia, meanwhile, doesn’t want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine’s military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent. But Washington and European capitals have sometimes seemed at odds in their diplomatic efforts. Trump has repeatedly sided with Putin, last month waiving sanctions and striking a deal to import Russian diesel, in moves that dismayed Ukraine and European leaders. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov argued that for Europe to join peace talks, it first must name a representative. “The Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar. If someone takes the initiative to establish contact with the Russian side, such people are facing ostracism.” Many in Europe also see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO’s eastward expansion as a main security threat and has demanded the alliance’s troops be pulled back from Russia’s borders. Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO’s strategy in return for peace in Ukraine — a possibility that alarms European leaders. Thursday’s talks were “substantive, constructive, frank and useful,” Putin’s aide Yuri Ushakov said. He added that the Kremlin leader reminded Witkoff and Kushner about Moscow’s proposals from 2021 -- before it sent troops into Ukraine -- demanding that NATO roll back the alliance’s military deployments in Central and Eastern Europe. Russia will update those with “fresh considerations,” Ushakov said. Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire — an idea long floated by Europe to prevent a new attack by Moscow — would be “absolutely unacceptable” and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate target. “In other words, the war would resume immediately,” the Russian president said. He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled. Zelenskyy is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte. Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are “very much aligned” on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January. “But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire,” Rutte said. Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line. Russia’s bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow’s drone and missile strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a “weaponization of winter.” Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-manufacturing plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said. Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said. Ukraine is experiencing another slowdown in the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that the country needs to defend itself against Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said Thursday on social media. Military units have recorded “significant disruptions,” including speed restrictions limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph), Zelenskyy said, adding that a military investigation established that the restrictions weren’t random errors. Ukraine uses Starlink and Starshield for intercepting Russian drones and launching its own strikes. Last month, limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations and alarmed Kyiv officials who fear U.S. support could drop off. Elon Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn’t be used for offensive strikes against Russia. Zelenskyy said the speed limits cover operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and that Kyiv is trying to find out from U.S. officials what is going on. A Russian serviceman was killed in St. Petersburg early Thursday when his vehicle exploded, according to the Investigative Committee, the country’s main criminal investigation agency. It didn’t identify the victim or say who was behind the bombing. The Fontanka news outlet said the victim was a colonel and that a bomb in his car exploded as he drove off. Several senior Russian military officers have died in bombings and other attacks that Moscow blames on Ukraine. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some attacks on Russian soil. Susie Blann and Samya Kullab in Kyiv, Ukraine, Lorne Cook in Brussels and Barry Hatton in Lisbon, Portugal, contributed. Mike Myers Says He “Might” Be in ‘Shrek’ Spinoff ‘Donkey,’ Calls Film “Long Overdue”

articles.content: The veteran actor also confirmed to The Hollywood Reporter that a fourth 'Austin Powers' movie is in the works: "I'm writing it right now; I'm having a great time." As Mike Myers prepares to return to the swamp with Shrek 5 next summer, the actor is already looking ahead to the franchise’s future — and sharing his excitement about Donkey finally getting a movie of his own. “I’d love to,” Myers told The Hollywood Reporter Wednesday night at the Focker-in-Law premiere in New York when asked about continuing the Shrek films beyond their fifth installment. “It’s so much fun. It’s so well written. The filmmakers are so lovely and they’re so nice to me and I love playing the character. I love the messages in there and Cameron [Diaz]’s fantastic and Eddie [Murphy]’s a genius.” Related Stories Movies Skyler Gisondo Reacts to James Gunn, Peter Safran's DC Exits: "There's a Lot I Still Don't Know" TV 'Yellowjackets' Stars on Finally Escaping the Wilderness in Final Season: "Feels Like a Completely Different Show" In addition to Shrek 5, which will welcome Focker-in-Law star Skyler Gisondo into the mix as Farkle, one of Shrek (Myers) and Fiona’s (Diaz) teenage triplet sons, the franchise is also expanding with a standalone Donkey movie. Murphy is set to return to voice the beloved character in the DreamWorks Animation feature with a release date set for June 30, 2028. While the Donkey movie has been described as a prequel exploring the character’s origin story, Myers isn’t entirely ruling out the possibility that Shrek could make an appearance. Regardless, he’s looking forward to seeing his longtime co-star get the spotlight. “I wish Donkey lived in my house! I love that character so much,” he said. “I don’t think I’m in it. I might be. I’m not sure, but it’s long overdue. That character is one of my favorite characters of all time, and Eddie’s so great in it. I’m surprised it hasn’t come sooner, but I’ll be the first in line to see it. I love that guy.” Myers even joked about just how much he loves the character, adding, “Honest to God, I have a cat named Pickles, and I love that cat as much as I love Donkey.” Another long-awaited project Myers addressed was a fourth Austin Powers movie. Myers and filmmaker Jay Roach, who directed the 1997 original Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery and its two sequels, have previously teased the possibility of another installment in the James Bond-spoofing franchise. The last film, Austin Powers in Goldmember, hit theaters in 2002. Though Myers was tight-lipped about revealing too much, he confirmed to THR that he is currently writing the screenplay for a fourth film. “Yes, we are. I’m writing it right now; I’m having a great time,” he said. “I’m very, very secretive. articles.content: In 2025, more than 360,000 abortions — about a third of all U.S. abortions last year — were provided by advanced practice clinicians rather than physicians, according to new data released by the Guttmacher Institute. (Photo by Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent)In 2025, more than 360,000 abortions — about a third of all U.S. abortions last year — were provided by advanced practice clinicians rather than physicians, according to new data released by the Guttmacher Institute, a think tank that researches and advocates for abortion access. Twenty-five states and the District of Columbia allow abortions to be provided by health providers who are advanced practice clinicians, a category that includes physician associates, advanced practice registered nurses, nurse practitioners, certified midwives and certified nurse midwives. The new findings show that abortions provided by advanced practice clinicians – which included both procedures and those by pill – accounted for nearly a third of all abortions nationwide last year, not counting self-managed abortions or those obtained outside the formal medical system. The organization says these types of providers fill a crucial access need at a time of OB-GYN shortages and more than a dozen state abortion bans. Arizona nurses say Prop. 139 should give them the right to perform abortions “These data help to illustrate the critical role that (advanced-practice clinicians) play in providing abortions across the country, including in many underserved communities,” said Isaac Maddow-Zimet, Guttmacher data scientist and study lead, in a written statement. He added that such providers also provide counseling and follow-up care “even in states where they are not permitted to provide direct abortion services.” Whether advanced practice clinicians can provide abortions varies by state laws and regulations, with many states limiting the types they can provide to aspiration procedures in the first trimester or pills. Twenty-five states and the District of Columbia allow at least some non-physician occupations to provide abortions. The states include: Alaska, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Washington. Arizona, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin could also consider allowing those providers to offer abortions after Democrats won trifectas in this month’s midterm elections and promised to expand abortion access. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends allowing advanced practice clinicians to provide abortions, saying in an issue brief that restricting abortion care provision to only physicians or board-certified OB-GYNs “are not based in science; improperly regulate medical practice; and impede patients’ access to quality, evidence-based health care.” In 2016, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration changed the guidelines around the abortion drug mifepristone, permitting advanced practice clinicians such as midwives to prescribe mifepristone. In the years since Roe v. Wade was overturned, several states, including Alaska, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio, have struck down physician-only abortion laws. An ongoing lawsuit brought by nurses and midwives in Arizona challenges laws barring them from providing abortion, saying they violate the state’s constitutional amendment enshrining abortion rights passed in 2024. After striking down many of Missouri’s abortion restrictions earlier this year, a judge upheld that state’s physician-only law, noting the difference in training for different types of abortions. articles.content: Jensen Huang resigned this morning as Nvidia’s CEO following reports of affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Right now, the company is being led by its CFO on an interim basis. But President Donald Trump is already throwing around one person he thinks should take over the chipmaking giant: former Apple CEO Tim Cook, who stepped down from leading the company on September 1st and moved into an executive chairman role. Shortly after Huang’s resignation was announced today, Trump posted his idea about Cook on Truth Social: “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump said. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” In a new episode of Stephen A. Smith’s Straight Shooter podcast published today, Trump made his pitch for Cook again, saying that Apple “would never be what it is today” if Steve Jobs was still “around”: > Can [Huang] be replaced? > Well, you know, the expression, Anybody can be replaced? So it’s very hard to replace him, but I had an idea this morning that I sort of just released: Tim Cook. He just sort of semi-retired from Apple. He’s done one of the greatest jobs in the history of business. > I think if Tim Cook, who built Apple… If Steve Jobs were around, Apple would never be what it is today. Tim Cook took a lot of these brilliant ideas and designs and everything else from Jobs and others, and he made it into one of the great companies of the world in a fairly short period. I think Tim Cook would be a great candidate to run Nvidia. Apple and Nvidia didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. Cook is well-known for his ongoing relationship with President Trump, including gifting the president a 24k gold and glass statue last year. (Trump, after Cook announced his transition plan earlier this year, posted a story about having “the head of Apple calling to ‘kiss my ass.’”) During the podcast, Trump said he spoke to Huang yesterday and that Huang is “going through hell”: > Should [Huang] have stepped down? > Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy, and I don’t know if that’s been determined yet, but if the woman was a spy, yes, if the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different. > But I can tell you this. Somehow, he’ll end up on his feet. I mean, I know him, I know him pretty well. I always thought of him as a fine man. > I spoke to him yesterday. He’s going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That’s what he is, really… that’s what he told me. I’m president, and he called me. And he said, What I’ve done to my wife and family is... That’s what he talked about. Trump, on the podcast, called Huang a “tremendous talent.” Other tech leaders have also publicly supported Huang following his resignation.

articles.title: Are Audiences Ready for a Johnny Depp Career Comeback?
articles.description: After years away from studio features, the star returns to the box office fray with Paramount's 'Ebenezer.' Analysts are taking note of his lack of introspective press moments on the tour: "It's a clever — if obvious — strategy."
articles.content: After years away from studio features, the star returns to the box office fray with Paramount's 'Ebenezer.' Analysts are taking note of his lack of introspective press moments on the tour: "It's a clever — if obvious — strategy." For many onlookers, it likely seems fitting that Johnny Depp returns to the big screen this weekend to play a man haunted by past mistakes. Depp has largely disappeared from public life for nearly a decade following allegations of domestic abuse, along with negative headlines surrounding his and ex-wife Amber Heard‘s messy 2022 defamation trial. Depp won the case and has denied any abuse allegations, but his professional path has seen its share of setbacks, including Warner Bros. dropping him from the Fantastic Beasts franchise in 2018 on the heels of the actor losing a libel suit against the publisher of The Sun. He has yet to hit the big screen for a studio project in the ensuing years. Related Stories Movies 'Ebenezer' Reviews Roundup: Johnny Depp's Comeback Gets a Chilly Reception Movies 'Ebenezer' Review: Johnny Depp Gets a Creepily Effective Comeback Vehicle in Ti West's Horror-Tinged Take on Dickens' Yuletide Classic That is set to change with Ebenezer, as director Ti West‘s feature adaptation of Charles Dickens’ classic A Christmas Carol hits theaters Friday. Paramount Pictures, which greenlit the film shortly after David Ellison’s Skydance Media acquired the studio two years ago, releases Ebenezer in more than 3,500 North American locations and projects an opening of $20 million domestically, along with another $20 million internationally. Such a turnout is likely to place it No. 1 at the North American box office, as the other major release for the frame is David Leitch’s How to Rob a Bank, eyeing a domestic launch in the high single digits against a $40 million budget. Adrian Daub, who serves as director of the Clayman Institute for Gender Research at Stanford University, closely analyzed social media reactions to Depp and Heard’s legal battle. He tells THR that many individuals’ viewpoints were based on feeling connected to Depp’s roles during his stretch as a major Hollywood star, and indeed, plenty of YouTubers were rewarded with a bounty of clicks from posts defending Depp and blasting Heard. Many Depp fans likely feel nostalgic for the era in the 2000s when the actor, initially known as a reluctant heartthrob and rebellious Hollywood outsider with Edward Scissorhands and What’s Eating Gilbert Grape, rocketed up the A-list with the 2003 smash Pirates of the Caribbean, which became the first of his three Oscar nominations in that decade. “When my team and I analyzed millions of YouTube comments around Depp v. Heard, we found that a lot of commenters seemed less swayed by the specific facts in the case and more by a general nostalgia for Depp roles of the early aughts that they felt were meaningful,” says Daub. “Lots of invocations of Jack Sparrow — that sort of thing. It also seems like non-North American audiences seem much readier to move on — so the studio is likely banking on nostalgia, and on the fact that non-English speaking audiences like Depp and didn’t track #MeToo in Hollywood all that closely.” In his heyday, Depp was among the industry’s highest-paid stars, collecting a reported $50 million and beyond, including backend, for his Pirates sequels and 2010’s live-action Alice in Wonderland. But his track record included box office hiccups even before his relationship with Heard began generating unflattering press, as he suffered critical and financial disappointments with 2014’s Transcendence and 2015’s Mortdecai. Heard’s first allegations of abuse against Depp came in court documents filed just days before Disney released the sequel film Alice Through the Looking Glass, which became a money loser for the studio in 2016. Notably, a number of Depp’s press opportunities were done while in character as Scrooge, including an unannounced appearance at an unrelated San Diego Comic-Con panel that saw the actor riffing for much longer than expected. As himself, Depp participated in the film’s recent junket and spoke to such outlets as Collider, CBS Mornings, Entertainment Tonight, On Film With Kevin McCarthy and Heart Radio U.K. Paramount has been pleased with data suggesting that audiences want Depp back and that he still holds universal appeal, with the in-character appearances having been intended to remind fans of the way that he has previously immersed himself to portray memorable roles like Jack Sparrow and Willy Wonka. Earlier this month at the film’s London premiere, Depp hinted at his involuntary hiatus from studio work. When the Associated Press asked him about not having booked a Hollywood film in years, he quibbled about the question’s wording before replying, “There was a bit of a vacation, which is fine,” and then a publicist quickly whisked him away from the reporter. “Refusing to come out of character in promotional events feels like a form of protection for Depp,” Brian J. Robb, author of the 1996 biography Johnny Depp: A Modern Rebel, tells THR. “It both gives audiences a flavor of what the film might be like and very helpfully protects the star from any searching questions about the recent past. He clearly wants to disappear into the role of Ebenezer, hoping that if audiences respond well to the character and the film, then he will have a chance to secure a more long-term comeback. It’s a clever — if obvious — strategy.” It doesn’t take a detective, the likes of which Depp has played in such projects as 1999’s Sleepy Hollow, to unearth that his real-life trajectory bears similarities to that of Ebenezer Scrooge, a public figure with PR issues until he gets a chance at redemption. Indeed, Ebenezer’s marketing itself has leaned into this connection, with the first trailer featuring Depp delivering the line, “It’s good to be back.” The film appears to have divided critics, as it holds a 50 percent approval from critics on Rotten Tomatoes, although THR’s favorable review declares that it “fulfills its ostensible goal of restoring the actor to A-list status.” Depp is set to follow Ebenezer with Lionsgate’s Day Drinker, director Marc Webb’s thriller that is slated for a March 2027 release and also stars Madelyn Cline and Penélope Cruz. If the comeback works, Depp would look to follow the paths of such embattled stars as Robert Downey Jr., who bounced back from his addiction-related controversies to lead the MCU and earn an Oscar, and Mel Gibson, whose headlines for antisemitic, racist and anti-gay remarks preceded his best director Oscar nomination for Hacksaw Ridge, not to mention his work helming the forthcoming high-profile follow-up to The Passion of the Christ. Other ostensibly “canceled” public figures have found ways to pivot, whether shifting to lower-profile work or catering directly to a right-wing crowd. Ernest Owens, author of the book The Case for Cancel Culture and the forthcoming release Divided We Stan, sees a missed opportunity in Depp’s decision to avoid acknowledging his challenging past. “I thought it would be a cool narrative that he could say, ‘Look, I was a Scrooge. I was a very misguided person and reflected on it, and I’m a new person, like he becomes in the end of A Christmas Carol,‘” the journalist says. “That would have been an interesting, metaphorical way of talking about the movie and his journey. But you have to actually feel that way. And I think Depp is not someone who actually thinks he did anything wrong.” Sign up for THR news straight to your inbox every day Subscribe for full access to The Hollywood Reporter

articles.title: In reversal, American Cancer Society urges routine prostate cancer screening
articles.description: Men aged 50–69 and at average risk should get PSA screening every two years.
articles.content: In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test. Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday. Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Feeding deer and elk could once again be banned in parts of Lower Peninsula
articles.description: The Michigan Department of Natural Resources recommends the state’s hunting and fishing regulator prohibit feeding deer and elk in 11 counties to try to prevent the spread of disease.
articles.content: Parts of the Lower Peninsula could once again see prohibitions on feeding deer and elk for recreational purposes. The Natural Resources Commission banned deer and elk feeding in the Lower Peninsula starting in 2019 Those restrictions were lifted this year when new state legislation passed Deer and elk feeding restrictions lifted in July in Michigan’s Lower Peninsula could partially return as soon as next month. The Michigan Department of Natural Resources recommendsthe Natural Resources Commission — the state’s hunting and fishing regulator — pass a rule that would prohibit recreational feeding of deer and elk in 11 counties: Alpena, Alcona, Cheboygan, Crawford, Iosco, Montmorency, Ogemaw, Oscoda, Otsego, Presque Isle and Roscommon. Those counties are where bovine tuberculosis, a disease that can spread in many mammals through shared feeding and is transmissible to humans, is of a high concern. In four of the counties — Alcona, Alpena, Montmorency and Oscoda — the disease is established in wild deer and cattle is subject to increased testing and movement restrictions. “In Michigan, to date, we know that there have been seven documented cases of TB in humans,” Dan O’Brien, a former DNR wildlife veterinarian and epidemiologist, said during a presentation to the Natural Resources Commission Thursday. “These are people that are actually sick with the disease — some of them very sick — that are due to the strains of bovine tuberculosis that are present in our deer and in our cattle.” RELATED: Michigan bill legalizing backyard deer feeding passes, but bans could remain Michigan House passes bill to lift deer baiting ban in the Lower Peninsula Bill aims to allow backyard wildlife feeding, but critics fear deer disease In 2019, the Natural Resources Commission prohibited feeding deer and elk in the Lower Peninsula, as well as baiting them for hunting purposes, to try to prevent the spread of bovine TB and chronic wasting disease. Sign up for our outdoors newsletter Want more coverage like this delivered directly into your inbox? Sign up for the Bridge Michigan Outdoors newsletter here. But feeding restrictions were lifted in the Lower Peninsula this year after legislation passed that allowed for 2 gallons of food to be spread within 300 feet of a residence. The legislation was introduced by state Rep. Ken Borton, R-Gaylord, who was motivated to run for office after being ticketed for feeding deer in his own backyard. While Borton is a fierce defender of the freedom to feed wildlife, he told Bridge back in July that he never intended for the legislation to allow the practice in all of the Lower Peninsula. “People who still live in those TB-restricted areas still would not be allowed to put bird feeders out,” Borton said.Donate But the legislation does not spell out exactly where those restrictions should occur. It says wildlife feeding practices mustalign with US Department of Agriculture standards or any agreements between the state and the federal government to control the spread of infectious diseases. The DNR, the Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development and the US Department of Agriculture Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service Veterinary Services currently have a memorandum of understanding related to bovine TB that details extra monitoring of the disease in Alcona, Alpena, Montmorency and Oscoda counties. The USDA agency recommended restricting feeding in the 11 counties suggested by the DNR plus Antrim, Arenac and Charlevoix counties. Bridge reached out to Borton to see how he felt about the DNR recommending the ban on deer feeding in seven additional counties, but he did not respond. A prohibition on baiting deer for hunting purposes, which is considered different than feeding deer for recreational purposes, remains in effect in the Lower Peninsula. In the Legislature, House Bill 4445, passed by the state House, would allow deer baiting during hunting season. The bill has been stalled in the state Senate Natural Resources and Agriculture committee since February According to a DNR memo, the department is “not recommending changes to baiting,” but with legislation introduced, the department suggested two baiting options for the Natural Resources Commission to consider if commissioners determine baiting should be restored. Both would continue baiting bans in the 11 counties.

articles.title: WATCH: President Trump addresses Nvidia’s CEO succession
Democrats launch Nvidia investigation, write scathing letter on Huang’s ‘scheme’ with Trump
articles.description: This Congressional investigation into Nvidia's China sales and its dealings with Trump is the second one, so far, since news of the alleged spy affair broke.
articles.content: Democrats on Thursday opened an inquiry into how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China. Earlier on Thursday, the company ousted its CEO Jensen Huang. He also agreed to testify to a different set of Republican-led Congressional committees. Huang was removed from the company he founded after he confessed to an extramarital affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. (He has since been accused of having more affairs, with Nvidia employees.) The alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, was an executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that U.S. officials suspect of helping route advanced Nvidia chips into China. The Democratic inquiry comes from Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee. As the minority party, they can ask questions but can’t compel answers. Their humdinger of a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asks the department to preserve records about an arrangement they find questionable and, they allege, illegal. “The scheme worked like this,” as the letter describes it. President Trump agreed to sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China as long as the chips, manufactured by Taiwan, were first shipped to the United States. On arriving, Trump added a tariff “effectively taking a cut of Nvidia’s sales to China through what appears to be an unconstitutional export tax system,” the letter said. Then the Commerce Department, under Lutnick, issued an export license. By the way, the deal between Trump and Nvidia to share revenue was public. In August 2025, Nvidia and AMD both agreed to share 15% of their revenue from chip sales to China with the U.S. government as part of a deal to secure export licenses, the AP reported at the time. But the letter questions why Lutnick continued to allow Megaspeed to buy chips even after he was reportedly informed by U.S. intelligence of their suspicions of Alice Huang and of Jensen Huang’s relationship with her. It questions why the department reportedly green-lit other Asian companies to buy Nvidia chips “with no physical presence at their listed addresses.” So the inquiry is aimed at the administration, not just at Nvidia and Huang. The letter also questions how Nvidia’s donations to Trump’s projects factored in. It notes that the export deal was approved after Trump learned of “Mr. Huang’s compromised position” in sleeping with an alleged spy, and after Nvidia donated $26 million toward Trump’s projects, including the ballroom. It appears to be asking if Trump used his knowledge of the affair to secure donations from Nvidia. Interestingly, in a “60 Minutes” interview with President Trump that aired on Sunday, Trump mentioned how he and his team had threatened an unnamed AI exec with jail, and after that, the exec “totally changed.” This Congressional investigation into Nvidia’s China sales and its dealings with Trump is the second one, so far, since news of the alleged spy affair broke. The Republican-led group involves leaders from the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and the House Intelligence Committee. That group has demanded that Huang come to them and testify in a closed-door session. They had threatened to subpoena him if he didn’t voluntarily agree. On Thursday, after his resignation, he agreed. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. articles.title: Maternal healthcare advocates lay out next steps
articles.description: A coalition of maternal healthcare advocates is laying out their policy wish list for Michigan’s next legislative term.
articles.content: Planned Parenthood's Power Family Health Center in Ann Arbor offers both medication abortion and in-clinic, procedural abortions. Abortion advocates say passing the Reproductive Health Act, which would remove state regulations on abortion facilities, is crucial for expanding access to patients - especially those in rural areas. But opponents say it’s “extreme” and “dangerous” legislation that would put patients’ health at risk.(Beth Weiler/Michigan Radio )A coalition of maternal healthcare advocates is laying out their policy wish list for Michigan’s next legislative term.Starting in January, Michigan Democrats will run the governor’s office, state Senate, and House of Representatives. The party last had a so-called “trifecta” from 2023-2024.The advocates see this as a chance to finish some unfinished business, like passing paid family and medical leave policies and getting rid of the mandatory 24-hour waiting period to have an abortion.Planned Parenthood Advocates of Michigan CEO Paula Thornton Greear predicts the federal support for family planning services will continue to fade in the coming years. She argues state officials need to quickly step in.“Incremental progress that we were facing the past two years just simply will not suffice. So, we want to see real wins for Michiganders very quickly,” she said during a press conference Thursday morning in Lansing.Thornton Greear said she has already been speaking with Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s team about plans.Unlike last time, Democrats are entering this upcoming legislative session with comfortable margins in both chambers.That could make a difference since, in the 2023-2024 session, one lone Democratic hold out could sink any bill. That’s what happened with efforts to repeal a ban on Medicaid reimbursement for abortions and to pass policies to address racial disparities in maternal health care.Mothering Justice executive director Danielle Atkinson said her group plans to be very involved next session in seeing campaign promises through.“We will be visible and we will be in all of the districts talking to people who voted for a change and come election time, come coffee hours, we will be showing up to support or hold accountable,” Atkinson said.However, even with the stronger Democratic majorities, none of these policy goals are a given.The business community has already signaled a desire to fight proposals for paid family medical leave. And some moderate Democrats may have hesitations to do away with things like parental consent for abortions.Concern for parental consent was a major source of criticism when a constitutional right to abortion was on the Michigan ballot in 2022. Voters still overwhelmingly approved the measure.But it’s not clear how much further the Democrats who flipped Republican seats would be willing to go. Republicans also might not be willing to lend support.Shanay Whittaker is with Reproductive Freedom for All, the campaign behind Michigan’s 2022 ballot measure. Her goals for next term include a state version of the federal Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances (FACE) Act, and new laws to keep Michigan abortion providers from being prosecuted for treating patients from other states with bans.“We hope to have continuing conversation on how we can expand access to all Michiganders. To make sure we can pass the FACE Act, that we can expand the reproductive health act by removing parental consent and having a shield law in place so we can protect providers,” Whittaker said.

articles.title: Jocelyn Benson wants to raise Michigan teacher pay. Union isn’t sold on plan
articles.description: The governor-elect wants to raise minimum teacher salaries to $60,000, but one of her biggest allies — the Michigan Education Association — isn’t yet on board. Others are also raising questions.
articles.content: Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson is advocating for a $60,000 starting teacher salary Average teacher starting pay in Michigan ranks 45th in the nation The Michigan Education Association says pay should be raised but for all people who work in schools The state’s largest teachers union is not fully on board with Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s proposal to combat Michigan’s teacher shortage by raising starting salaries to a minimum of $60,000. That’s over $16,000 above the current average starting pay in Michigan. Improving schools was one of Benson’s biggest promises during the election, and higher pay for teachers is a central plank of that plan. Doug Pratt, a spokesperson for the Michigan Education Association, told Bridge Michigan the state is facing shortages for bus drivers and paraprofessionals too, and “it’s not just a question of starting salary.” “As a state we need to increase compensation for every school employee, not just teachers.” (Editor’s note: The MEA is a sponsor of the Education Watch newsletter. The union had no part in the production or editing of this story.) Pratt said the union, whose president, Chandra Madafferi, is one of 15 leaders on Benson’s transition team, is committed to working with the incoming governor and the Legislature. “It’s a challenging thing to figure this out financially,” he said. Benson’s education plan advocates to “require starting teacher salaries of at least $60,000. This will be scaled up to provide additional compensation for experienced educators and staff commensurate with experience.” US Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has also called for a $60,000 minimum salary for teachers. Related: Donate Now, the hard part: Jocelyn Benson has big plans. Michigan has big problems Report: Funding, opportunity gaps hurting educational progress in Michigan Michigan is spending $150M on one-time ‘educator’ bonuses. Here’s how it works In response to questions from Bridge, Benson’s team said in a statement late Thursday: “Governor-Elect Benson was proud to run on a bold vision of lowering costs, raising wages, and transforming state government. She looks forward to laying out her first 100 days agenda, including a bold education agenda, to turn those priorities into action and deliver results for Michigan.” It’s unclear how much the proposal would cost to implement. But Jason Burns, a research specialist at the Education Policy Innovation Collaborative, previously told Bridge it would take about $350 to $400 million to raise teacher pay in line with public opinion. Benson’s team did not comment on how much the effort would cost or where the funding would come from. Public opinion polling shows people think teachers should start at $54,600 and average pay should be $71,445. Nearly 72% of respondents in a different poll support increasing starting teachers salaries. About 66.9% of respondents support a statewide minimum teacher salary. Burns told Bridge Thursday that details of a pay proposal matter but that a minimum teacher salary would likely raise pay for even teachers with some experience. “When you consider that the average starting teacher salary in Michigan is just a hair over $43,000 right now, there are a lot of teachers who are already in classrooms, who are not brand new, who are not making $60,000.” How Michigan schools pay teachers While some states have set minimum teachers salaries, Benson’s proposal would be a departure from how things currently operate in Michigan, where local districts set teacher pay, class sizes and other working conditions with local teachers unions. Districts rely on the state’s per-pupil funding to pay for employee wages and benefits. “It would be a pretty significant insertion of state policy into an area for, that as long as Michigan schools have been around, has been a local decision,” said Michael Van Beek, vice president for research at the free-market think tank Mackinac Center for Public Policy. Michigan’s average starting teacher pay of $43,093 ranks 45th in the nation, according to the National Education Association.The average teacher salary is $71,023 and ranks 22nd nationally, three spots lower than the year before.“We’ve slid on the overall average down to the middle of the pack,” Pratt said. “I think you’ve got to look at both: We’re definitely in the wrong place [on starting pay.] We’re moving in the wrong direction on the average.” Experts also acknowledge that the cost of living varies across the state, meaning a $60,000 minimum pay has higher purchasing power in some parts of the state. “If the state is saying we have to pay teachers a certain amount, then the state has to make sure the districts have the funds to do that,” said Jennifer Smith, director of government relations for Michigan Association of School Boards. State leaders have agreed to provide $150 million toward bonuses but how much each educator gets depends on how many students are enrolled in a district, how many qualify for bonuses and how a district negotiates with its local union if there is one. Other parts of Benson’ education plan include creating the “Michigan Education Guarantee,” which would “ensure a Michigan high school diploma means a student is college or career ready by creating a comprehensive, evidence-based statewide graduation standard.” This guarantee is championed by Launch Michigan, a bipartisan nonprofit whose vice chair is MEA President Madafferi. Van Beek said creating a state minimum would be “stepping into the territory that teachers unions typically have operated in.” Some other states have set minimum teacher pay. Tennessee schools will have a $50,000 minimum teacher salary next school year, up from the current $35,000. Van Beek said it’s important to remember that if districts increase pay, they will also be required to pay more into the public retirement system. “Everyone might look at the bright shiny headline number, which is the salaries, but teacher compensation is broader than that,” said Craig Thiel, research director of the Citizens Research Council of Michigan, In Arkansas, leaders raised the minimum teacher salary from $36,000 to $50,000 in 2023, with all teachers getting at least a $2,000 raise. Researchers found the raises significantly increased salaries in rural and high poverty districts and improved teacher retention. But researchers warn the effects of the policy will fade with time because of inflation. But the law also created a voucher program. “Not every law raising teacher salaries is a good one,” the National Education Association says on its website. “Some don’t come with adequate funding to help districts, especially rural ones, meet the new bars. Others are laden with poison pills.” Pratt said rising healthcare costs, availability of retirement options, class sizes and student behaviors all need to be addressed.“The details matter and now we’re moving past the statements of values 一which we agree with 一 to ‘alright, how do we implement it, how do we get this done,” he said.

articles.title: Nessel launches antitrust lawsuit against Mackinac ferry operator, alleging monopoly
articles.description: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has filed an antitrust lawsuit against the Hoffmann Family of Companies, a Florida-based private equity firm, which currently owns all of the passenger ferries that serve Mackinac Island. Nessel’s office alleges that the company’s acquisitions have created an illegal monopoly. “Every tourist, worker, and resident who rides a ferry to […]
articles.content: Shepler's Ferry (Photo by Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance)Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has filed an antitrust lawsuit against the Hoffmann Family of Companies, a Florida-based private equity firm, which currently owns all of the passenger ferries that serve Mackinac Island. Nessel’s office alleges that the company’s acquisitions have created an illegal monopoly. “Every tourist, worker, and resident who rides a ferry to the Island must buy a ticket from Hoffmann, and most of them must also pay Hoffmann to park for the duration of their visit,” the lawsuit, which was filed Thursday in state circuit court, argues. Historically, the island — which does not allow motorized vehicles — had been serviced by three passenger ferry companies, all separately owned. In 2016, the Star Line Mackinac Island Ferry purchased Arnold Transit Company when it went out of business, reducing the number of ferry companies to two; the Star Line and Shepler’s Mackinac Island Ferry. Hoffmann purchased Shepler’s in 2022 and the Star Line in 2024, which had rebranded as the Mackinac Island Ferry Company, eliminating all competition, and has since increased ticket prices for ferry riders. The lawsuit also lays out that Hoffmann owns “every dock on the Island, in St. Ignace, and in Mackinaw City that can serve passenger ferries,” as well as “the vast majority of long-term parking near those mainland docks, which most visitors need in order to reach the Island.” “Hoffman wields enormous monopoly power over two markets essential to the island’s well-being: ferry service to the island and long-term parking for anyone traveling to the island overnight, or even for a quick day trip,” Nessel said in a press conference announcing the lawsuit. “Since they consolidated their control in these areas, eliminating any competition for ferry service or parking, we’ve seen Hoffman do exactly what you’d expect a monopolist to do. They’ve raised prices, limited services, and leveraged their massive power in alarming ways, even threatening to suspend ferry service to Mackinac Island entirely if local government didn’t give them favorable extended agreements to let them keep hiking their prices.” In the past, when the Mackinac Island City Council has tried to rein in price increases, Hoffmann threatened to cease all ferry service, which the lawsuit describes as essentially holding residents and seasonal workers “hostage.” “Ferry access to the island is far and away the most common way tourists, visitors, residents, and workers move between the mainland and the island,” Nessel said. “90 to 95% of all traffic to Mackinac Island, which receives more than 1 million guests every year, comes by ferry service from Mackinac City or St. Ignace. That’s also how the island gets much of its freighted goods, including food and medical supplies. In the summer months, the ferry service lines run all day and well into the evening, with large commercial docks on the island and in each mainland city.” Patrons depart onto a Shepler’s Mackinac Island Ferry dock on Mackinac Island during the Detroit Regional Chamber’s Mackinac Policy Conference. May 26, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance The lawsuit also draws contrasts to the cost-per-minute charge of other ferries in the Great Lakes, including the Miller Ferry from Catawba Island, Ohio, to Put-in-Bay on South Bass Island in Lake Erie, the Kelleys Island Ferry from Marblehead, Ohio, to Kelleys Island in Lake Erie, and the Washington Island Ferry from Wisconsin’s Northport Pier to Washington Island in Lake Michigan — all of which charge around half the price-per-minute of the Hoffman ferries to Mackinac Island. Legislation put forward by state Sen. John Damoose (R-Harbor Springs) and signed by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in June sought to increase the ability of the island’s local government to restrict fare increases and exert oversight over the ferry companies. That law was approved by voters on Mackinac Island in the November general election. But the lawsuit notes that the oversight in the legislation will be delayed in going into effect — Hoffmann said publicly after the ballot measure passed that “it will continue to operate under its existing franchise agreements, which run through June 30, 2027, and that the new law cannot modify those agreements and will not affect the 2027 season.” The lawsuit is seeking “divestiture and other structural remedies to reopen these markets to competition, provide consumers with meaningful choices, and ensure fair market conditions for residents, businesses, and visitors,” a press release from Nessel’s office explained. Asked what those remedies might entail — including whether Hoffmann could be forced to sell one of its ferry companies — Nessel said the details would be up to the courts. Assistant Attorney General Jonathan Comish said the court could also seek to increase competition among parking operators, adding, “There were three separate ferry lines, so we would seek the court to force the divestiture of some ferry operations. Now, that’s a delicate procedure, often involving investment banks and lots of consultants to make sure that the transaction goes through in a way that’s healthy and restores competition in the long term.” A statement from the Hoffmann Family of Companies noted that they are aware of the lawsuit and will respond in court, and are “confident we will prevail, because we are not violating state or federal antitrust laws.” “As a reminder, the federal court has already twice rejected the City of Mackinac Island’s antitrust claims in its federal litigation against us,” the statement continued. “Most important: In April, AG Nessel issued a statement encouraging all parties to resolve the ongoing disputes. We wholeheartedly agreed with her and are in active mediation. We believe this lawsuit threatens to derail those efforts. While we are surprised and disappointed by this development, our goal remains the same: reaching agreement on a viable contract extension that serves the public interest and ensures sustainable ferry service for years to come.” Comish addressed questions about the previous lawsuits, which were dismissed for lack of standing. “The city asserted antitrust damages, which is a tricky thing that you have to allege in a private antitrust lawsuit saying that the harms you suffered were linked to anti-competitive conduct,” he explained. “Since we are the sovereigns, we don’t have to meet that requirement. So we have the ability to bring a lawsuit against anyone who violates our antitrust laws just because they violated the laws, so we get to skip that step.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Mackinac Island Mayor Margaret Doud said in a statement released by Nessel’s office that the city’s goal has been to ensure the ferry system serves the public. “This was never only an Island issue. More than 1.5 million people travel to Mackinac Island each year, and many of them are Michigan families,” Doud said. “Over 80% of the Island is designated as Mackinac Island State Historic Parks, which belongs to the people of Michigan. articles.description: WASHINGTON — Two top Democrats in Congress are calling on the Trump administration to delay new requirements for people on Medicaid, arguing there is not enough time for states to prepare before the change takes effect on Jan. 1. House Energy and Commerce Committee ranking member Frank Pallone Jr., of New Jersey, and Senate Finance […]
articles.content: Oregon Democratic U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden, shown on Nov. 9, 2026 at the U.S. Capitol, was one of two members of Congress who sent a letter to the Trump administration about Medicaid work requirements. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — Two top Democrats in Congress are calling on the Trump administration to delay new requirements for people on Medicaid, arguing there is not enough time for states to prepare before the change takes effect on Jan. 1. House Energy and Commerce Committee ranking member Frank Pallone Jr., of New Jersey, and Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden, of Oregon, wrote in a letter released Thursday that officials must use their “discretion to give states additional time to implement work reporting requirements and protect eligible beneficiaries from losing coverage.” The two lawmakers, who will become chairmen in early January when Democrats regain control of Congress, added that failure “to permit states to delay implementation despite known operational deficiencies will worsen preventable coverage losses for which Congressional Democrats will hold the Trump Administration accountable.” Medicaid and the ‘big, beautiful’ law Republicans included several changes to Medicaid, the state-federal health program for lower income Americans and some people with disabilities, in the “big, beautiful” law they approved in the summer of 2025. The provision raised in Pallone and Wyden’s letter requires Medicaid enrollees between the ages of 19 and 65 to work, participate in community service, or attend an education program for at least 80 hours a month. The law detailed several exceptions, including for pregnant people, parents of dependent children, people who have complex medical conditions, tribal community members, those in the foster care system, people who were in foster care who are below the age of 26 and individuals released from incarceration in the last 90 days, among others. Republicans also included a carve-out for people who are “medically frail” or who otherwise have “special medical needs (as defined by the Secretary).” This summer, CMS released a rule telling states how to determine if someone is “medically frail” and therefore doesn’t need to meet the 80-hours-a-month requirement. But that aspect of the law’s implementation is on hold after a federal judge issued a ruling in an ongoing lawsuit, an aspect that Pallone and Wyden wrote makes it even more difficult for states to enforce the new rules once they take effect in the new year. Pallone and Widen urged Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz to reconsider what types of diagnoses the administration believes make a person “medically frail.” “In one example, even a diagnosis of cancer could be insufficient to meet CMS’ extra-statutory definition of ‘medically frail,’” they wrote. Millions projected to lose access to healthcare The two also called on Oz to approve any “good faith exemptions” states have sent to CMS to ensure those Medicaid administrators have more time to implement the changes. “Congress gave CMS flexibility in the statute for a reason; the agency should not direct states away from good faith exemptions out of concern that they highlight the shortcomings of this policy—not when Americans’ access to health care hangs in the balance,” they wrote. “We intend to rigorously oversee CMS’ determinations on good faith exemptions and its decision to demand states to proceed with implementation even when out of compliance with federal requirements.” The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office released a report in July 2025 showing that changes throughout the “big, beautiful” law would result in 10 million people losing access to healthcare. West Virginia state officials said this week that come January, about 40,000 of the 160,000 Medicaid enrollees in the state will likely lose access to the program due to the new work requirements.

articles.content: Google says its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model can give more helpful answers to complex questions, including “questions with multiple parts, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests.” The new model can break down your questions and address each part in its responses. It’s available starting today in search, the Gemini app, all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, and in Google Antigravity for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Robby Stein, VP of product at Google Search, says it’s “now the new default model in AI Mode & being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews.” Google says Gemini 4 Hydrogen also gives users a wider range of links in its responses by “conducting simultaneous queries across all the relevant subtopics.” Its responses have more visuals, too, like images, comparison tables, graphs, and maps. One of Stein’s examples shows the AI generating an interactive animated driving simulation in response to a user’s question about how phones locate which lane of a highway a car is on in areas without cell service. Google says the new model also has improved language understanding “across all supported AI Mode languages.” [Media: https://twitter.com/rmstein/status/2120941443359576166?a=NQ8Q5PwHUHcmejMYRl4&s=20] Users have more thinking level options with Gemini 4 Hydrogen, as well, including low, medium, high, and a new “xhigh” mode. According to Google, the new model “delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence” compared to Gemini Flash 3.8, and it “matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class,” like Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Terra.

articles.title: Mayor Mamdani, FDNY Commissioner Bonsignore provide update on deadly building collaps
articles.content: Rescue efforts in Flatbush, Brooklyn ended Thursday afternoon, the FDNY said, as debris cleanup begins after Wednesday's deadly building collapse.Mayor Zohran Mamdani held a news conference with other officials to provide an update on Thursday afternoon.He said eight people were killed, including two children and six adults. Two construction workers were among the dead, and 18 people were hurt, including four firefighters. One person is in critical condition and the others are stable, Mamdani said.The names of the victims were released Thursday evening."These were our friends and our neighbors, parents and children, young families building their lives in our city, and immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Trinidad and beyond," he said. FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the department was still in the search-and-rescue phase at that time, but was also doing general debris removal. She said the rain will "definitely hinder" efforts at the scene, but firefighters will be there until they "are 100% sure there are no more people trapped." Bonsignore said FDNY members train extensively for these types of situations. Mamdani praised the efforts of the firefighters who responded to the scene within one minute of the initial 911 call."Just because we expect this courage from the FDNY does not make it any less extraordinary," he said. The mayor said more than 250 fire and EMS personnel have responded around the clock. He also thanked the New Rochelle Fire Department, which volunteered its services overnight. Mamdani said the city's Department of Buildings and law enforcement are leading the investigation with Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez as a partner. The investigation covers both the construction site and the building that collapsed. The mayor said five companies are tied to the collapse site and to about 100 other sites citywide that will also be investigated."If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable," DOB Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said. The mayor urged residents to avoid the impacted area in Flatbush as there are vacate orders, street closures and buses being diverted.The vacate orders are for 1323, 1325 and 1327 Flatbush Ave. That street is also closed between Clarendon Road and Bedford Avenue. Buses B41, B49, B103, B8 and BM2 are all being diverted.

articles.title: Nebius tests the neocloud playbook with $40 billion in planned spending
articles.description: Nebius plans to fund its $40 billion AI infrastructure expansion through customer prepayments and loans, even as delays at a Microsoft data center raise questions about its financing model.
articles.content: In its third-quarter earnings call Thursday, the neocloud company Nebius laid out $40 billion in planned spending for 2027, far more than Wall Street had expected. It’s an ambitious plan, but it rests on a string of planned projects that are already starting to show cracks. Nebius plans to fund the buildout by relying on customer pre-payments and loans backed by customer contracts — essentially using the future value of its data centers to finance their construction. But that can be a risky strategy if those projects get bogged down by delays or cancellations. “Building at this scale is hard, and delays are part of our industry right now,” CEO Arkady Volozh said during Thursday’s earnings call. “We are not immune.” The earnings announcement comes on the heels of reports that Microsoft is cooling on neocloud deals that aren’t delivering on time. That’s a problem for companies like Nebius, whose financing strategy is becoming more dependent on repayments. Because if it can’t get to capacity on time, it will keep piling on costs while revenues slip. One of Nebius’ largest customers is Microsoft, which is paying for AI computing capacity at a Vineland, New Jersey, data center that is now months behind schedule. Nebius’ contract with Microsoft is worth up to $19.4 billion, but it’s already letting deadlines slip. Only just over half of the Microsoft capacity is now planned for delivery by the end of the year, with the rest coming in Q2 2027. The delay is because DataOne, the third-party operator of the site, “decided to wind down the temporary generation faster than it was expected,” according to Andrey Korolenko, chief product and infrastructure officer, as the site switches over to Bloom Energy fuel cells. Still, that transition wasn’t entirely by choice. In August, the investigative site Floodlight identified at least 45 natural gas generators in operation at the DataOne site, even though it had not received any permits for operating gas generators. New Jersey regulators fined the DataOne facility $1.1 million in response, finding that the use of the generators violated federal law. DataOne is also facing a noise-complaint lawsuit from nearby residents over a constant humming noise allegedly emitted by the data center. According to Nebius’ summary of its Microsoft contract, Microsoft can terminate affected service after a grace period if dates are missed and no alternative capacity is offered. The tranches were originally meant to be deployed in 2025 and 2026, so a Q2 2027 delivery date falls well beyond that window. The contract also includes financial penalties for late delivery. Nebius said that Microsoft “has been part of the planning process.” Nebius did not say whether Microsoft has agreed to the new dates, but Microsoft has not publicly canceled anything. TechCrunch has reached out to Nebius, Microsoft, and DataOne for comment. On the call, Marc Boroditsky, Nebius’s chief revenue officer, said the company’s deals with Microsoft and Meta both came with significant prepayment, which arrived long before delivery. But Bloomberg reported last week that Microsoft is tightening oversight on projects run by third parties, including Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, and debating whether it’s worth signing new agreements. Microsoft also sent employees to the site in New Jersey, per Bloomberg. In its own quarterly earnings report, Microsoft noted that its capex spend was lower than expected due to third-party delays. The company is clearly not above pulling back from planned agreements where its partner doesn’t meet its share of the bargain. Bloomberg also reported that Microsoft won’t use an option to more than double its Nscale agreement for a Texas data center and recently stopped being an anchor customer for Nscale’s planned Essex site after power delays. Nebius says the delays it faces are coming from sites it doesn’t control, with the data centers it is building itself coming online on time or ahead of schedule. Those, Nebius says, will supply most of its new capacity from 2027. New deals signed in Q3 came with prepayments that more than cover the cost of building capacity behind them, says Boroditsky. Nebius ended the quarter with $7.4 billion in cash. Total prepayments plus asset-backed financing of investment-grade contracts are expected to cover up to 85% of the $40 to $45 billion 2027 capex spend. CFO Maria Del Dado Alonso Sanchez named Microsoft and Meta as contracts that can be financed this way. Boroditsky also said Nebius could “tap prepayments to shore up any additional cash requirements.” Nebius forecast 2027 revenue of $12 to $13 billion, and said it expects to break even on a pre-tax basis by the fourth quarter. Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571% from a year earlier. Roughly a third of that was a one-time payment tied to a new partnership model. Nebius cut its 2026 revenue forecast by $200 million to $3 billion, citing delays to third-party sites like New Jersey. Shares ended the day down 17%. articles.title: Ann Arbor residents invited to weigh in on city's extensive parks system
articles.description: Ann Arbor has about twice the number of parks for an average city of its size. Officials are seeking residents' input on their park needs and wants.
articles.content: Leslie Woods Nature Area in Ann Arbor( City of Ann Arbor)The City of Ann Arbor is asking residents for feedback about its extensive park system, as part of the process for developing a new strategic plan.Parks and Recreation Director Josh Landefeld said Ann Arbor has twice the number of parks as an average city its size. But he says needs are always changing, especially now, as the city rezones itself to accommodate more housing. "Are we meeting the needs that are out there, are we meeting the wants that are out there," he asked. "And how do Ann Arbor parks continue to provide positive experiences, consistent experiences for those that are moving into those new spaces or those new zoning areas."Landefeld said city parks are held in perpetuity for residents, so any decision to sell parkland, or swap a park for parkland somewhere else, would have to be approved by voters.The city is holding two workshops this week for residents to weigh in. The first is from 4-7 p.m. Thursday at Ann Arbor District Library, 343 S 5th Ave., and the other is from 11 a.m.-1 p.m. Saturday at Veterans Memorial Ice Arena, 2150 Jackson Ave.Residents can also respond to an online survey.Ann Arbor spends about $20 million a year on its parks. That includes an $8.5 million parks millage, $6 million in user fees, and $6 million from the city's general fund.
