articles.title: Michigan’s first Native American member of Congress outlines priorities for 4th district
articles.description: Democrat Sean McCann beat Republican incumbent Bill Huizenga in Michigan’s 4th District, covering Allegan, Van Buren, Kalamazoo and surrounding counties. It's the first time the area has been represented by a Democrat since 1933.
articles.content: ( Sean McCann for Congress)Michigan's Fourth Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives will be held by Democrat Sean McCann, who narrowly beat Republican incumbent Bill Huizenga. The fourth district covers Allegan and Van Buren Counties as well as areas of Berrien, Calhoun, Kalamazoo and Ottawa counties. McCann's victory also makes him the first Native American person to represent Michigan in Congress. Speaking with Stateside host April Baer, McCann said he's planning on supporting legislation to reverse Medicaid cuts, making food benefits more accessible and ending the war in Iran. "I'll be trying to reassert Congress' authority and power that it's ceded over the years to the executive [branch]," he said. "It's one of the reasons this tariff policy was able to move forward as it did because Congress has basically become a rubber stamp to the President's agenda." The 55-year old Detroiter got started in public service as a city commissioner in Kalamazoo. He served on the commission for a decade and then was elected to the Michigan House in 2010 and later in the Michigan State Senate. A citizen off the Potawatomi nation, McCann said he plans to oppose Enbridge Line 5 and join the Native American caucus in Congress. "As a representative of Congress I hope to have a respectful town hall where maybe not everyone agrees, but everybody gets a chance to be listened and know that they're heard," he added. "It's not just you call my office, you send me an email—it's that I'm there and present and available ... to anybody who wants to come and meet and speak with me." Over the next two years, McCann is hoping to bring back congressionally directed spending to the 4th district. "That's something I really prided myself on as state senator... was to bring back everything from fire gear and fire trucks to investments in senior centers and major infrastructure projects," he said. Full interview with Sean McCannApril Baer: For the first time since 1933, Michigan's fourth Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives will be stationed by a Democrat. Sean McCann narrowly beat Republican incumbent Bill Huizenga in a race to represent Allegan and Van Buren counties. There are portions of Berrien, Calhoun, Kalamazoo and Ottawa counties as well. His victory also makes him the first Native American person to represent Michigan in Congress. Sean McCann, welcome to Stateside. It's great to have you.Sean McCann: Great to be with you. Thanks for having me on.Baer: You're someone who's been around the block politically. You got your start in public service as a Kalamazoo City Commissioner before moving on to the Michigan House and the Michigan State Senate, where you have been serving since 2010. And during that time, you've played a pretty key role in one of the state's most significant election reforms. And that's ending partisan gerrymandering. What prompted you to decide to take a stab at a congressional seat?McCann: The gerrymandering reform was critical to me, and it was really noticeable early on in my time in the Michigan House, that it was one of the key reforms we needed. And imagine watching this play out in real time over the last two years as to all the reasons why it's so critical and important to our democracy, to not be able to let either party get to sort of tilt the playing field to their advantage and to the disadvantage of voters. So that's something that I couldn't be more thrilled to have seen come about in the time in the Michigan legislature that I've had. And it's a core piece of democracy. So, did it create a district here that's balanced? It seems like it did. I think that's good. You want representatives who are responsive to the voters and not necessarily able to just sort of pursue one agenda without any checks and balances on their role in Congress. So that's been very important to me in my time. How long it took a ballot initiative, it wasn't going to get done through the Michigan legislature, unfortunately, at the time. But here we are. And I think it's been of service to the people of Michigan.Baer: Were there things you felt you could accomplish in Congress that you weren't going to get done at the state and county levels where you had been serving?McCann: Yeah. I mean, that's what really motivated me to take this next step. And it was encouragement from other members of Congress for this race. And I was at the end of my state Senate term and that sort of didn't necessarily make this plan to do this. But more and more, as we looked at the issues that are confronting the families of Southwest Michigan, it became more and more clear that I needed to step up and run for the seat and accomplish what we've accomplished. And that's really to turn around some of these huge challenges that people are facing with affordability in their lives.We see it ourselves with our grocery budget and our two kids, and we want to have a family that reaches the American dream. This tariff policy that's been so chaotic, and particularly to Michigan with our near and dear neighbors, Canada, it's just not been productive to have it be executed, certainly the way it has been. And, if we go back to my time in the state House, 2013, while I was there in my second term, was when we had the opportunity to accept or not the expansion of the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid expansion in the state of Michigan. And over time, we came to insure over a million people in Michigan under expanded Medicaid. And to see that getting rolled back by the One Big Bill in Washington was deeply troubling. And that really drove also this desire to bring this change about and to run for Congress.Baer: Sean, as I mentioned earlier, you're one of two Anishinaabe people who were elected to join Congress this year. We've got Peggy Flanagan coming in to a Senate seat in the state of Minnesota. Is there anything that you would want people to know about how tribal identity has informed your public service over the years?McCann: Yeah, I'm really proud of my tribal identity. It's been a great opportunity to connect with some of the tribes that are based in or nearby the Fourth Congressional District. And I expect it to be something that is a factor in how I make my priorities here, representing the district here in Washington, D.C. There are some key tribal issues that overlay with the state of Michigan. Line five, for example, is a big one, and the Match-E-Be-Nash-E tribe in Wayland is in the fourth Congressional District.Then you have the Nottawaseppi Huron Band of Potawatomi, which is in Fulton, just outside the fourth Congressional District, but with a casino presence in the Fourth Congressional District. And then down I-94 to the Pokagon Band, Potawatomi and Dowagiac. Also, again with a presence in the fourth. And these are constituents of mine. I feel like I have a special connection to them, and I'm going to keep working to know the issues better and better.Baer: Sean, you ran a campaign against someone who had a great deal of name recognition across West Michigan and who'd been doing the job for ten years. How did you tailor your campaign to voters in the district? And I'm just kind of curious what kinds of things you were hearing for them that may have given you a sense of what they wanted?McCann: A couple of things really, I think, stood out. One was the lack of sort of town halls and connectivity with constituents, and that's something that people were very hungry for as I did my listening tours and my circulating around the congressional district, that people wanted to be heard. And I think we can and should be able to do that as a country, as a representative of Congress, in a safe and respectful way.And that's what I hope to lay out here in the next two years. Is that exactly the way to have a respectful town hall where maybe not everyone agrees, but everybody gets a chance to be listened to and know that they're heard. It's not just you calling my office, you send me an email. It's that I'm there and present and available, not just at sort of private functions or company tours, but available to anybody who wants to come and meet and speak with me. And so that I can listen to them.And then the second piece is that this is a unique district where there has not been congressionally directed spending, community investments that are one time special investments here to this district, brought back specifically by the congressional representative. And that's something that I very much plan to pursue in my role in the next two years. In fact, it's going to start up rather quickly. So to anyone listening, we're going to develop a process for how we can take that input from whether it's organizations or industry or local governments, how we can get that rolling as quickly as possible. That's something I really prided myself on as a state senator representing the Greater Kalamazoo-Portage area was to bring back everything from fire gear and fire trucks to investments in senior centers and major infrastructure projects. And I think that that is a void that I'm looking to fill very much here in the Fourth Congressional District.Baer: Do you see those as being difficult deliverables, given the state of the federal debt now above $30 trillion?McCann: Certainly that's a big part of the picture. I think that congressionally directed spending represents a very small portion of that, but a very critical one. And really, it's more of a basis of fairness. Every other member of the congressional district in Michigan, Democrat or Republican, has been bringing community investments back as part of their role. So it's really, for me, a process of joining that process. But we certainly have, beyond some of these other issues we've talked about, a $40 trillion plus national debt that we've got to get under control.There have been presidencies, administrations, and congresses that have actually gotten the annual deficit under control and actually started to make some progress on reducing the national debt. I'm very much there to do that. We absolutely need to do that for ourselves and our future generations.We have got to not let this national debt crush our country. So we're going to have to be very fiscally responsible. But when you're spending billions and billions of dollars on this reckless war of choice in Iran versus bringing those resources back to your district that multiply investments through the local economies and lift up all of our prosperity here in the United States. Those are some of the places that we need to have our dollars be spent.Baer: May I ask, there are many conversations going on right now about what the first few agenda items will be. There are leadership conversations that have been happening at the lower levels before the work of actual legislating gets going in session. But I'm curious if you could maybe talk to us about one or two pieces of legislation that really need to be handled within the first couple of months of the new term.McCann: Yeah. I'm going to be part of shaping that agenda, that first 100 hours, that first 100 days. And I'm excited to do that. I don't think it's going to be a big surprise. We're going to be looking at changes and restoration of affordable health care. Reversing the Medicaid cuts that came through the One Big Bill. Making sure that food assistance is there for hungry families, SNAP, the provision of SNAP and the farm bill are going to need to be critically important to making sure kids don't go hungry. I'm really proud, by the way, of the fact that the state of Michigan and our budget was able to deliver free school lunch and breakfast for all school-age kids. That's a huge point of pride for me. Now we need to make sure that that's happening at the federal level as well.I hope we're going to end the Iran war as quickly as possible. I'll be supporting a War Powers Resolution if that's what it takes to do that. And, trying to reassert Congre

articles.title: Michigan reproductive justice advocates lay out priorities for incoming Democratic trifecta
articles.description: Danielle Atkinson, the founder and executive director of Mothering Justice Action Fund, said that she is “cautiously optimistic” about the incoming Democratic trifecta to work with organizations like hers on prioritizing legislation to support caregivers and to improve maternal and child health outcomes. She also described some of these policy priorities as having the potential […]
articles.content: Danielle Atkinson, the founder and executive director of Mothering Justice Action Fund, speaks at a roundtable of advocates discussing priorities for the incoming Benson administration and legislative term on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Danielle Atkinson, the founder and executive director of Mothering Justice Action Fund, said that she is “cautiously optimistic” about the incoming Democratic trifecta to work with organizations like hers on prioritizing legislation to support caregivers and to improve maternal and child health outcomes. She also described some of these policy priorities as having the potential to be impactful early wins for Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s administration — such as passing paid leave laws, which Atkinson noted her organization has done the research and feasibility studies to put them on the table. “You have the support. You have the majority. Something that can be done really quickly that can be meaningful, and then stop the bleeding,” she said. “Unfortunately, it’s not the sexiest thing. But these cuts that are coming down from the federal government are going to be really harmful, and people are going to feel it, and they’re going to feel it silently, and they’re going to blame this incoming administration, deserve it or not. So they have to stop the bleeding and make sure that Michigan has an answer to what has happened at a federal level.” Atkinson joined other reproductive justice advocates in Lansing Thursday to discuss policies and priorities that they hope to see taken up in January when Democratic majorities take power in the Legislature alongside Benson assuming the governor’s office. Shanay Watson-Whittaker, the director of Michigan campaigns with Reproductive Freedom for All, for example, laid out two specific pieces of legislation that she hopes to see passed. She advocated for establishing a state-level Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances (FACE) Act, which would make it a criminal offense to interfere with access to a health facility that provides reproductive health services, as well as a state-level shield law, which provides legal protection for both reproductive healthcare providers and patients who receive reproductive care coming from states where it is illegal. Paula Thornton Greear, the president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Action Fund, speaks at a roundtable of advocates discussing priorities for the incoming Benson administration and legislative term on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance) Paula Thornton Greear, the president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Action Fund, similarly mentioned shield laws as a priority — including for providers of gender-affirming services — as well as access to medication abortion and telehealth services. She also pushed for legislators to end the 24-hour waiting period for abortions and parental notification requirements. With Democrats set to control both chambers of the Legislature as well as the governorship, the advocates described a ‘mandate’ from Michigan voters to enact legislation that expands access to health care, including reproductive healthcare. “Incremental progress is not enough anymore, and Michigan has a real opportunity to take a lead across this country,” Thornton Greear said. “We need things written into law. Executive orders are not strong enough; they can be torn down and broken, and they end. So we need to collectively push to have things written into law. An executive order is a promise written in pencil.” Cassy Jones-McBryde, founder of the Michigan Chamber for Reproductive Justice and executive director of the Michigan Equity Action Fund, warned against the same problems that the last Democratic trifecta, from 2023 to 2024, faced. “I was heartbroken when we also had a trifecta not so long ago, and we still didn’t get the promise of what the trifecta was,” she said. “We need to be audacious with our asks now. We have learned a few things from this administration. We know that we can be just as aggressive as the ways they took things from us, we can advocate and get things passed now that we have the promise of what this new administration here in Michigan will be.” Cassy Jones-McBryde, founder of the Michigan Chamber for Reproductive Justice and executive director of the Michigan Equity Action Fund, speaks at a roundtable of advocates discussing priorities for the incoming Benson administration and legislative term on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance) But Atkinson, speaking to Michigan Advance after the roundtable conversation, expressed hope about the bigger majority that the Democrats now hold and how it will prevent any one legislator from stalling key priorities. “We are hopeful that this cohort of elected officials will not be as worried and timid because there’s only a few people holding the majority together, and we have weak legislators,” she said, “We don’t need legislators like that, and we have fewer of them in this — well, we’ll see. True colors will show, but because there is a nice cushion. I’m really hopeful that the leadership will be able to hold a core together to get these ambitious but meaningful and funded policies across the finish line.” Thursday’s conversation also considered how policies outside of healthcare access do directly impact those conversations — including the harsh immigration policies of the Trump administration. Dr. Seydi Sarr, an advocate and the founder and CEO of the African Bureau for Immigration and Social Affairs, described how immigrants in Michigan — including many who worked to mobilize voters for the Benson campaign and state-level Democratic candidates — are living in a culture of fear of being detained by ICE. “Driving without a license in Michigan is a deportable offense. Taking your children to the hospital, taking your children to school, going to do grocery shopping can get you arrested,” she said, referencing stalled efforts to allow undocumented residents of Michigan to obtain drivers licenses. “You can end up in detention, and you could be deported. So when we have a trifecta, we have to make sure that we hold our community, our elected officials, accountable to their promises.” Jones-McBryde also discussed social determinants of health impacting access to reproductive health outcomes that she hopes to see addressed under the Benson administration — including legislation to address water affordability and eviction protections. Atkinson, who was announced as a part of Benson’s inauguration team on Thursday, said following the roundtable that, while she hopes to take her position on that team to celebrate the victory for Benson’s supporters, she also intends as an advocate to “stay visible in the administration, so that they see me and I’m a squeaky wheel.” Whitmer directs state agencies to strengthen privacy protections for reproductive health data Benson’s transition team — which is distinct from the team on which Atkinson holds a position — has faced criticism over her choice of members with strong ties to DTE Energy and the controversy-ridden Michigan Economic Development Corporation. “I understand the criticisms and I also have concerns, but it’s about the undue influence that they might have, and the best way to combat that is with more representation,” Atkinson said. “So you know, just asking who’s there for childcare, who’s there for wages.” Accountability was a strong theme throughout the conversation, with Thornton Greear noting that she has seen a trend of greater “self-accountability” among incoming leadership, who understand the message from voters about what is expected of them in the next term. “You can have hope, but it is really quite useless without strategy,” she said. “The governor-elect’s office knows full well that the federal administration is not done coming after Planned Parenthood or other providers. Just look around the corner, and you’ll see that they are poised to do something once again detrimental to Title X, which will impact so many Michiganders. I think it’s incumbent upon us to continue having that dialogue, to work with the governor-elect’s office to plot a course forward, to be around the table collectively with her, and actually plot out what we can get done.” Atkinson, who often advocates specifically for the “sandwich generation” — people responsible for both childcare and for elder care of parents — also added that she hopes to see Benson establish task forces to examine the actual administration of policy and the nuances of how different departments can work together. “They have to deliver. They have to be specific,” she added. “They have to be able to say with their full chest, Black women need this, and when we do this for Black women, it will affect and help everyone.”

OpenAI, Google, Anthropic hit with lawsuit seeking halt to frontier AI development
articles.content: A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups has sued five major artificial intelligence (AI) companies in a bid to halt further model development and deployment, alleging that the companies cannot adequately prevent their systems from causing serious harm, including cyberattacks.The lawsuit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court on Thursday, names Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX. The plaintiffs are seeking a court order to stop the companies from developing or deploying new AI models, citing documented instances of harmful AI activity, including cyberattacks, and concerns about the risks posed by increasingly autonomous systems.The complaint was filed by the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI. It alleges that the companies have violated California’s unfair competition law by endangering public health and interfering with the use of property, including computer systems.The plaintiffs also claim they have had to divert resources from other planned activities to address the potential harms associated with the companies’ AI systems.The filing points to incidents involving AI agents carrying out cyberattacks against government websites and companies. It also references a reported July incident in which OpenAI’s ChatGPT allegedly hacked into another AI company’s systems on its own.The complaint raises concerns about the development of increasingly autonomous AI systems capable of managing tasks and learning with limited human intervention. It argues that inadequate safeguards could allow such systems to cause significant harm and make human oversight more difficult.The lawsuit follows growing debate over AI safety, as technology companies continue to develop models with increasingly advanced capabilities. Some industry leaders have acknowledged the potential risks and called for stronger safeguards, while US policymakers have so far largely relied on companies to manage safety concerns.The companies named in the lawsuit did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Democratic state officials, USPS battle over Trump mail ballot rule ahead of 2028 election
articles.description: The U.S. Postal Service faces renewed calls to drop restrictions ordered by President Donald Trump on mail ballots, setting up a major clash between states and the federal government ahead of the 2028 election. Postal worker unions, civic groups and Democratic secretaries of state are demanding the Postal Service rescind a rule that imposes sweeping […]
articles.content: A voter uses a drive-up ballot box outside the Main Library in Salt Lake City, Utah, on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)The U.S. Postal Service faces renewed calls to drop restrictions ordered by President Donald Trump on mail ballots, setting up a major clash between states and the federal government ahead of the 2028 election. Postal worker unions, civic groups and Democratic secretaries of state are demanding the Postal Service rescind a rule that imposes sweeping new requirements on states if they want ballots delivered through the mail. As part of the rule, states must submit the names of likely mail voters to the federal government. The U.S. Supreme Court blocked the Postal Service from implementing the rule for the midterm elections. But the decision applied only to this year’s elections, leaving its ultimate fate unclear. With the midterms over, opponents of the rule have quickly turned to pressuring the Postal Service to abandon the restrictions — warning that the Trump-backed rule undermines the USPS’ closely guarded image as outside of partisan politics. “We should not allow a policy that threatens public confidence in the Postal Service neutrality to remain in place while its long-term status is debated in court,” Jonathan Smith, president of the American Postal Workers Union, said at a news conference in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. The rule’s future carries significant consequences for states with large numbers of mail voters. Eight states — California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington state — authorize all-mail elections. Nationwide, at least 33.9 million mail ballots were cast in the November general election, according to the University of Florida Election Lab. The Postal Service declined to answer questions from States Newsroom on Thursday, citing pending litigation. Executive order Trump signed an executive order in March directing Postmaster General David Steiner to put forward a rule requiring states, at least 90 days before a federal election, to notify the Postal Service whether they intended to allow ballots to be sent through the mail. States would then have to submit to USPS at least 60 days before the election a list of voters planning to vote by mail. Separately, the executive order required the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, with help from the Social Security Administration, to compile a list of voting-age U.S. citizens living in each state and then provide that information to state officials at least 60 days before each federal election. The order did not tell states how to use the data. The Supreme Court didn’t make clear its position on the mail ballot rule if it comes before the court again in the future. But Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who agreed with the decision to halt the rule for the midterms, wrote in a concurring opinion that there was “at least a fair prospect” the rule falls within the Postal Service’s authority. The Trump administration and some Republican states argued the rule would provide additional security safeguards. Ahead of the election, Republican officials in 11 states, led by Missouri, urged a federal judge not to pause implementation of the rule. “The Rule — if implemented — would help bolster the security of mail voting in Missouri and reduce the risk of fraud,” Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, wrote in an August court declaration. Hoskins’ office didn’t respond to a request for an interview this week. The other states included Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina and South Dakota. On Thursday, those Republican-led states, as well as Texas, filed a notice in court that they will appeal a D.C. district court’s preliminary injunction of the mail ballot rule to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. The move kicks off the next round of legal fighting over the rule. The White House didn’t respond to a request for comment. Opponents of rule filed suit Democratic states argued the rule encroached on their power to run elections. The U.S. Constitution assigns states the responsibility of administering elections. Multiple lawsuits were filed against the executive order in the spring. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, an appointee of President Barack Obama in Massachusetts, issued a preliminary injunction halting USPS from implementing the rule, which the Supreme Court declined to block. “This executive order is trying to force federal control over who can and cannot receive a ballot in the mail,” Chelsey Wininger, executive director of the Democratic Association of Secretaries of State, said at the Tuesday news conference. When the Postal Service published the final version of the mail ballot rule in August, the agency wrote that the rule doesn’t place the Postal Service in the role of an election administrator or dictate how states run elections. States maintain complete control over their voter registration rolls and decide who votes by mail, the USPS wrote. “States also retain complete autonomy to determine the extent to which they utilize the postal system as an aspect of their elections,” the USPS statement said, adding that the rule was consistent with the Constitution. During a USPS Board of Governors meeting on Tuesday, the board members didn’t discuss the mail ballot rule, according to a recording of the Tuesday meeting posted to the Postal Service website. The meeting mostly focused on the agency’s difficult financial condition, though postal workers received praise for their performance during the election. “In this election, the USPS did exactly what we always do,” Steiner, the postmaster general, said. “We put our heads down and we got the job done.”

How Amplitude ships product improvements in 1–2 days with OpenAI
articles.description: Built primarily on OpenAI models, Amplitude’s proactive product agent, Wave, identifies what to build, helps teams ship changes with coding agents, and measures the impact.
articles.content: Built primarily on OpenAI models, Amplitude’s proactive product agent, Wave, identifies what to build, helps teams ship changes with coding agents, and measures the impact. Lift in agent engagement vs. control after one day Estimated time to ship a product improvement with Wave Lower mean model cost per dispatch for GPT‑6.1 Sol in Amplitude’s Data Science Agent evaluation. Model cost for GPT‑6.1 Sol in Amplitude’s Opportunity Investigator evaluation. Amplitude has always helped teams see how people actually use their products. Its proactive product agent Wave helps teams turn those insights into shipped improvements. Amplitude describes Wave as roughly 80% powered by OpenAI models, including GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Luna, and GPT‑Image‑2.5 Flare. Wave turns product insights into implementation plans teams can ship to coding agents, including Codex, then measures the impact. Amplitude estimates that Wave can help teams ship product improvements in 1–2 days, down from roughly a month. On Amplitude’s own homepage, Wave helped personalize suggestion cards, driving a 160% lift in card-driven sends. Wave is Amplitude’s proactive product agent. Teams give it a product area and the goals and metrics they want to improve. Wave brings together Amplitude data, session replays, customer feedback, and code to identify and prioritize opportunities, develop solutions, and coordinate implementation with people and coding agents. It then tracks outcomes and uses those learnings to inform the next round of improvements. Behind that workflow, Amplitude uses different OpenAI models for different tasks. GPT‑6.1 Sol supports the opportunity manager and deep investigations into code and data. GPT‑6 Luna handles frequent, lower-cost tasks such as scanning code and running small evaluation checks. GPT‑Image‑2.5 Flare generates product mockups using screenshots from session replays as visual references. When an opportunity is ready to build, teams can send it directly from Wave to coding agents, including Codex, with a technical plan and acceptance criteria to guide implementation. “The idea with Wave is you have a unified platform with agents that comb through massive amounts of session replays, analytics, and code to find opportunities to improve products,” explains Jacob Newman, Principal AI Product Manager at Amplitude. Amplitude tested Wave on its own homepage, where generic suggestion cards were meant to help users start a conversation with an AI agent. Wave discovered that people often bypassed them: in a sample of 100 session replays, 80 users typed their own questions and only 12 selected a suggestion. Wave proposed personalizing the cards using recent charts, dashboards, or the page a user had come from. It illustrated the change and produced a technical plan, including preserving free typing and showing generic suggestions when personalization context was unavailable. After a brief review, the team handed the work to a coding agent and A/B tested the change. In the experiment readout Amplitude shared, messages sent through homepage suggestion cards increased 160% relative to control after one day. “It is a great example of how non-groundbreaking things that just get ignored can increase the adoption of features in unexpected ways.” explains Eric Carlson, Senior Principal AI Engineer at Amplitude. Wave’s tasks place different demands on its models. A deep investigation needs strong reasoning and well-supported conclusions. A small check repeated hundreds of times needs to be fast and inexpensive. Amplitude evaluates quality, latency, and cost for each task, then assigns models accordingly. For Wave’s Opportunity Investigator, Amplitude evaluated whether models corroborated findings, avoided false positives, incorporated evaluator feedback, recovered from tool failures, and kept claims aligned with evidence. GPT‑6.1 Sol scored 4.06 out of 5 overall, compared with 3.62, 3.52, and 2.94 for three alternative models. It led on all five investigation criteria and had the fastest median investigation time, at 54 minutes. In a separate evaluation of Wave’s Data Science Agent, GPT‑6.1 Sol scored 67.5 out of 100, compared with 69.3 for another leading model, at a mean model cost of $1.28 versus $2.63 per dispatch. GPT‑6.1 Sol also scored higher on tool-contract compliance, estimation and uncertainty, and evidence grounding. For high-volume work such as scanning code and running small evaluation checks, Amplitude uses GPT‑6 Luna to keep latency and cost low. Splitting work across specialist agents lets the team reserve more expensive reasoning for the tasks that need it the most. For generating wireframes and mockups, OpenAI’s image generation model scored 80.3 out of 100 for solution wireframes, compared with 63.9 for another image generation model. Amplitude’s evaluation covered communication quality, product fidelity, instruction adherence, text and UI legibility, and visual coherence across 15 opportunities. Customers across industries are already using Wave in beta to identify and ship product improvements. Wave analyzes session and analytics data, then develops recommendations with a proposed fix, technical plan, and acceptance criteria. From there, teams can control the level of automation. Most teams send bug fixes straight to coding agents, while new features and bigger bets get a human review. For changes that reach launch, the path from discovery to execution can be short: among customer-launched experiments, flags, and guides, one in four went live the same day Wave surfaced the opportunity, half in under four days, and two in three within a week. Interpolated from supplied milestones; the curve is illustrative, not individual observations. “Our ambition with OpenAI is to make self-improving products the way companies build software,” says Skates. As OpenAI’s models get better at reasoning and coding, teams will be able to delegate more investigation and implementation work to agents, ultimately resulting in better products reaching users faster. Amplitude is already seeing it, as agents find and help deliver improvements in its own product while the team works on other priorities: “I think teams will be surprised by how much they can accomplish when their software is working alongside them to make the product better.” Product updates, practical guides, upcoming events, and more. articles.title: Ars Live: What drone attacks on data centers mean for modern life in the cloud
articles.description: A livestream Ars discussion is happening on November 17 at 1 pm Eastern Time.
articles.content: Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Commentary: How the election results may have saved the planet
articles.description: Among all the reasons to celebrate the wonderful midterm election results, I would particularly like to emphasize how they have literally created an opportunity to save mankind’s future on this planet — that is, by stopping Trump’s race toward climate destruction and allowing the United States to once again become a leader in positive climate […]
articles.content: The Michigan State Capitol, visible through wildfire smoke. July 16, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.Among all the reasons to celebrate the wonderful midterm election results, I would particularly like to emphasize how they have literally created an opportunity to save mankind’s future on this planet — that is, by stopping Trump’s race toward climate destruction and allowing the United States to once again become a leader in positive climate policies. This could not be more timely. Let me explain. First, some data on the extent of the climate crisis. While the issue of climate change unfortunately received almost no attention during the election campaign (in part due to some dubious recommendations by campaign advisors for “climate hushing”), one might have still noticed the almost weekly occurrence of climate-related weather disasters throughout the year … both in the U.S. and around the world. The evidence that massive global climate change is happening is absolutely incontrovertible. Every year now brings new temperature records, and just this past October was globally the warmest October ever recorded. Atmospheric CO2 rating on Election Day (Nov. 3, 2026) was 428.84 ppm, continuing a pattern of record-high ratings (vs. about 280 ppm in “pre-industrial” times). CO2 ratings have now been climbing every year for decades, with trends increasing from less than 1.0 ppm/year in the 1960s to over 2.5 ppm/year in the 2020s. Indeed, climate scientists are warning that Earth’s “life support systems” are breaking down, and that “The climate emergency is already here.” A new United Nations report concludes that we have already missed the original goal of limiting global temperature increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius. However, with urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse gas emissions (e.g., 18% by 2030 and 45% by 2035), we could limit the increase to a level of 1.7-1.8°C and return to 1.5°C by the end of the century. This is where the crucial importance of the recent U.S. election comes into play. As the world’s largest economy, the United States is positioned to have a massive influence on world policy and actions regarding climate. Hence the positive actions that President Biden took toward reducing greenhouse gas emissions were vitally important … and, in contrast, the immensely negative steps during Trump’s second administration are tremendously damaging. Trump EPA to strip greenhouse gas limits for power plants, a key Biden climate policy It is no exaggeration to say that if the U.S. continued Trump’s recent path regarding climate-related actions, those urgent savings targets would be completely unfeasible. Indeed, Trump’s actions to undermine climate policy and increase greenhouse gas emissions are so numerous and so extensive that it is not possible to summarize them all in one editorial. But here are a few examples. In terms of international agreements, Trump not only has withdrawn (again) from the Paris Agreement, but also from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF). Domestically, Trump has pursued an incredible list of actions to support, finance and deregulate coal and oil interests, while also removing funding and blocking development of wind and solar energy projects. (Trump actually said in January 2026, “My goal is to not let any windmill be built.”) This past September, Senators Schumer and Whitehouse released an extensive report detailing the dozens of ways that the Trump administration has rewarded the fossil fuel industry for its huge support of Trump’s presidential campaign. Some examples include: 26 senior officials across EPA, the Department of Energy (DOE) and the Department of the Interior (DOI) previously worked for fossil fuel or other polluting industries. Trump weaponized his EPA, DOE, DOI, DOJ, etc., on the fossil fuel industry’s behalf — from canceling grants for renewable energy projects on false pretexts to leasing swaths of public land to fossil fuels. Trump attacks clean energy to take out fossil fuel’s competitors: The Trump administration attacks fossil fuel’s competitors, especially wind and solar. More than $1.8 billion in taxpayer funds have been paid to companies to cancel wind projects, and over 160 projects are frozen. Among the most consequential of Trump’s many actions is his rescinding of the “endangerment” finding by the EPA, that was the core basis for the government to be able to regulate greenhouse gas emissions. States can also be important leaders in advancing climate action. In that regard, the 2026 election is also very significant in that it produced five new states that now have Democratic “trifectas” (i.e., Democrats control the governorship as well as both chambers of the legislature). Michigan is one of those five states (the others being Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin). The existence of Democratic trifectas has become very important, due to the unfortunate shift in the Republican Party under Trump to be against any pro-climate policies. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The Michigan story in that context is very illustrative. Back in 2023, when Michigan had a Democratic trifecta, we passed a very significant legislative “climate” package. It established for the first time a clear state policy relating to climate change, as well as making some important additions to Michigan’s landmark renewable energy and energy efficiency law (PA 295 of 2008). When Michigan passed that climate policy package in 2023 (PA 235 to strengthen the renewable energy requirement and PA 229 to strengthen the utility energy efficiency standard), not a single Republican voted in support of either of those pieces of legislation. Since the Republicans captured control of the Michigan House of Representatives in 2024, not a single piece of climate-friendly legislation has been passed. Re-establishing a Democratic trifecta in Michigan and those other key states should provide excellent opportunities for advancing pro-climate policies. Bottom line: We are at a crucial crossroads for the future of this planet. With these outstanding election results, we’ve been given an opportunity to reverse our current path toward a climate crisis. Among the many issues that our newly elected representatives need to deal with, let’s hope that they make sure that one of the priorities is the climate. Postscript: It is important to note that the primary policy solutions to the climate challenge … renewable energy and energy efficiency … are both cheaper than fossil fuels, and also create more local jobs. So saving the climate is also good economic policy. Let’s get to it!

articles.title: No, AI agents did not discover a previously unknown Maya site
articles.description: “I woke up and checked the agents' reports. 'DAMN!' They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses,“ Pietro Miotti wrote on his blog. | Image: Pietro Miotti Armed with a team of AI agents, Google researcher Pietro Miotti claimed earlier this week to have discovered a potentially unmapped Maya site in Mexico. There was just one problem: The site had already been discover
articles.content: Armed with a team of AI agents, Google researcher Pietro Miotti claimed earlier this week to have discovered a potentially unmapped Maya site in Mexico. There was just one problem: The site had already been discovered and was published in an academic journal last year. The incident, which sparked criticism among archeologists online, underscores a growing tension in science as amateurs wielding increasingly powerful AI tools parachute into specialist fields, often without the expertise needed to understand what they are looking at. Miotti said the idea to use AI to search for archeological sites came to him while traveling in Peru, when he began wondering what historic explorers might do with access to modern technology. He settled on lidar, a laser-based mapping technology that can produce detailed three-dimensional images of the environment, and set a team of 48 AI agents to comb through NASA lidar data for signs of undocumented sites. As “Peru isn’t well covered” by public lidar data, Miotti wrote, he shifted his focus to the Maya region. The agents flagged numerous promising locations, including “one major village [that] doesn’t seem to have been registered” in existing records. Miotti, who described the research to The Verge as a personal side project done without any Google compute or resources, said he then reached out to Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to check whether the apparent discovery was already known, including through unpublished research. Using the agents to translate his correspondence into Spanish, Miotti said INAH told him it had no record of a registered site at that location. “It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive,” Miotti wrote on his blog. Miotti stressed that he is not an archeologist and emphasized that the finding would need to be verified with fieldwork. Nevertheless, he hailed it as proof that “we’re on the brink of a revolution across every science” and called for the “entire planet” to be mapped with lidar so AI agents could “help us find the rest.” Had he been an archaeologist familiar with the region, however, Miotti might have spotted a problem: The site was already known, and had been documented in an academic journal more than a year earlier. Archeologists were quick to point out the oversight on social media. In a series of posts on Bluesky, Sarah Parcak, an archeology professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, stressed the importance of carefully checking findings against existing research. “This is why we have peer review,” Parcak wrote, adding that just because the Mexican government doesn’t have something in its database doesn’t mean it is unknown or unmapped. Other archeologists echoed her criticism, slamming the project for spreading misinformation and taking credit away from archeologists, who have been using advanced digital tools in their work for decades. “This was a personal project that I was excited to share,” Miotti told The Verge. “I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.” He added that as a non-archaeologist, he had not realized a site not being registered wasn’t the same as it not having been mapped, adding that expert knowledge “is needed to verify what the agents find.” He also addressed the limits of his AI tools: “My agents and I missed it. Archaeologists rightly don’t publish the coordinates of sites, so checking whether a site is already known means comparing images against figures in papers, not searching a database. That’s much harder for agents, and it’s something these tools need to get better at. When people pointed it out, I updated the post and the blog as soon as I could to credit their work.” Nevertheless, Miotti said this was an example of how agents could be used to help experts sort through large amounts of data. He said he has been encouraged by the archaeologists and PhD students that he said were reaching out to him “excited about the workflow and wanting to know how it works and whether it could help with their own survey data.” “Our ‘problem’ is not discovering new sites,” Elizabeth Graham, a professor of Mesoamerican archaeology at University College London, told The Verge. “Most of us working in the Maya area know about tons of sites not explored or excavated or mapped, most of these found on foot,” she said. Graham also critiqued the use of the word “discover,” noting that local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area. While she credited Miotti with doing a decent job of using AI to map the mounds from lidar data — “the interpretation of lidar data can be tricky” — Graham argued the bigger obstacle is funding for research. “The fact is, there just isn’t the funding to excavate or map sites as there was in the past, so in a way it doesn’t matter how many more are ‘discovered.’” The controversy reflects a broader problem with AI in science, perhaps most visible with OpenAI’s recent advances in mathematics. While AI tools are increasingly capable of producing genuinely impressive results, they don’t always engage with the existing research those findings build upon. The result can be claimed breakthroughs that have, as is the case here, already been made by someone else, or a general failure to credit earlier work. Even when the findings are actually new, they can lack context a specialist would bring. Ultimately, amateur use of AI tools often ends up shifting the burden of establishing what has actually been found and why it matters to actual experts, work that would ordinarily be part of making a scientific discovery in the first place. Ivan Šprajc, a professor of archaeology at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts in Ljubljana and a coauthor of the paper documenting the site, told The Verge he wasn’t particularly impressed by the agents’ work. Archeologists have been using lidar and “other sophisticated remote sensing tools for quite some time,” he said, adding that “just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.” He told The Verge that while it is commendable that Miotti checked in with INAH, doing so is “not sufficient” as the institution does not have access to all possible information. “The fact that INAH has no official knowledge of a particular cluster of archaeological features does not necessarily mean that it has not been spotted or even explored by archaeologists.” Šprajc said that he worries the growing use of AI tools by amateurs could overwhelm archeologists with claims of new discoveries. “Just today I have received an email from another AI ‘discoverer,’ so I am a little bit concerned about being flooded by this kind of message,” he said. He also raised another potential risk of amateurs publicizing the locations of archeological sites: attracting looters. “But as long as these findings do not lead to looting, I don’t see a major problem,” he added.

articles.title: Mayor to give residents say in spending Detroit budget in neighborhoods
articles.description: Each of the seven City Council districts will receive a $250,000 allocation, which could be used on projects such as park improvements, recreational enhancements, beautification projects and other neighborhood needs.
articles.content: Detroiters will have a chance to decide how a portion of the budget gets spent in their neighborhoods, thanks to a new pilot initiative Mayor Mary Sheffield launched. Sheffield announced the city’s new participatory budgeting process, which proposes $250,000 per City Council district to be spent on infrastructure-type projects in neighborhoods that residents will propose. Participatory budgeting allows residents to directly decide how to spend public funds. While Sheffield was a Detroit City Council member, she asked former Mayor Mike Duggan’s administration to allocate funding toward a participatory budgeting program to provide residents a choice in how to spend money in their districts. “It took a long time to get here, but I’m very proud to announce that under this mayoral administration, residents will now have a direct say in how to dedicate a portion of city funds to their neighborhood projects in the city,” Sheffield said. “This will ensure that the people who live, work, and raise families here have a voice in the investments that shape their communities.” Funds will be geared toward small to medium-scale capital improvement projects, including: parks and recreation center enhancements, street or sidewalk upgrades, community safety infrastructure or neighborhood beautification. How it works for Detroit neighborhoods Each of the seven City Council districts will receive a $250,000 allocation, which could be used on projects such as park improvements, recreational enhancements, beautification projects and other neighborhood needs. MORE: Will Mary Sheffield follow through on participatory budgeting? What Detroit can learn from participatory budgeting processes in NYC, Boston and Brazil Denzel McCampbell wants direct democracy to drive council decisions Leadership roles will be open to the public. Design committee members collaborate with residents, community organizations and the city to establish the rules and procedures of the process. Starting Monday, Nov. 16, residents can apply to volunteer for the design committee, which will be responsible for setting up rules, proposal guidelines and voting eligibility. The city of Detroit held a news conference on Nov. 12, 2026, to discuss plans for participatory budgeting. Credit: City of Detroit Flickr Applications for the delegate committee members, which will review public input and refine the ideas into project proposals, will open in the spring. They can sign up at www.detroitmi.gov/pb and the city will choose a total of 16 committee members, who will be required to attend an orientation on Jan. 9, 2027, and meet weekly for five weeks, followed by up to six meetings through March, said Tanya Stoudemire, chief financial officer. Phase two involves decision making, in which residents submit their project ideas and vote on them. The city will open an application window in February 2027 for the budget delegate committee, which will manage and develop the ideas into proposals and create a final list of projects. Phase three involves implementation. Residents can be involved by applying to serve on a committee, attending participatory budget community meetings, submitting ideas and voting on finalized projects. Public ideas will be accepted in May 2027, refined between June-September, and voted on in October 2027. Areas of need in Detroit Mose Primus, president of the Yorkshire Woods Community Organization, highlighted many positives in his neighborhood, including community gardens, park and green spaces, a flower garden, and the potential for building out a bee farm. But problems such as living on blocks full of trash and abandoned homes need to be addressed in his neighborhood and surrounding areas, he said. He and his neighbors often see squatters in abandoned homes, many of which are owned by people outside of Detroit and left to sit, Primus said. “We have abandoned apartment buildings that the city needs to crack down on the ownerships of these buildings, because it makes the neighborhood look bad,” Primus said. “Even some vacant houses that are owned by LLCs and people from out of the state, they don’t want to sell them.” Ros Haskins and Larry Chatfield, president and vice president of the Bagley Community Council, said for the most part, the Bagley neighborhood is in good shape. The neighborhood could use some updated bus shelters and benches, adding that most stops require riders to stand. And, they would like to see a public park in the area. “The closest park to us is Palmer Park,” Haskins said. However, they want to highlight the neighborhood’s Motown history, having housed musical legends such as Stevie Wonder and Marvin Gaye, with a musical note sculpture and sign that reads: “Bagley, home of the Motown stars.” “We have several different Motown musicians that grew up in Bagley. We’ve been working on ways to market that in a positive way for Bagley,” Haskins said. Detroit City Council President James Tate (center) and Council Member Denzel McCampbell (left) speak at a Nov. 12, 2026, news conference. Credit: City of Detroit Flickr City Council President James Tate anticipates his colleagues will approve the budget item next year. His constituents have often sought investments in upgraded sidewalks, beautification, neighborhood street signs and improving recreational centers with kitchens. “I think, because this program is geared toward capital projects, it won’t satisfy all of those concerns that folks have because they do want programming, and maybe we can expand to that direction in future years,” Tate said. During the previous budget cycle, City Councilmember Denzel McCampbell urged the administration to use the participatory budget process. “We’ve heard a lot about beautification, park improvements, more amenities for seniors and families like pickleball courts, “McCampbell said. The District 7 council member recently held a roundtable with Cody High School students to identify their neighborhood needs, some of which included employing youth to help seniors with lawn care services, along with a community hub to help with various issues, such as “substance use disorder, health, and homelessness” along with providing a wellness and hangout hub for teenagers. Dana Afana is the Detroit city hall reporter for the Free Press. Contact: dafana@freepress.com. Follow her: @DanaAfana.

articles.title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
articles.description: Gemini 4 Hydrogen isn't getting a slow, security-conscious release like Carbon and Argon.
articles.content: Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen. These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen's purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google's ecosystem use. With Google's recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company's products. Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it's 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces "fabricated claims" by more than 5x, according to Google's analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash's score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands
articles.description: Nectar's new AI agent automates influencer marketing, helping brands discover creators, manage outreach and partnerships, and track campaign results.
articles.content: Nectar, an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results. Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research. Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically. Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN. The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult. Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords. Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular. Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets. “Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.” Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals. Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers. The company plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents. This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic.
