Michigan’s US Senate results challenge the claim that criticism of Israel alienates Jewish voters
articles.description: As Jewish voters overwhelmingly supported Democratic candidates in last week’s midterm elections, new polling data shows that the Democratic Party’s Jewish support was not an outlier and likely won’t change anytime soon. At the same time, growing opposition to unconditional U.S. support for Israel could create opportunities for Democratic candidates in 2028 who take a […]
articles.content: Former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a primary election night watch party in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)As Jewish voters overwhelmingly supported Democratic candidates in last week’s midterm elections, new polling data shows that the Democratic Party’s Jewish support was not an outlier and likely won’t change anytime soon. At the same time, growing opposition to unconditional U.S. support for Israel could create opportunities for Democratic candidates in 2028 who take a more critical approach to the Israeli government’s policies. Polling data released after the election by J Street, a progressive Jewish organization that advocates for a two-state peace solution between Israel and Palestinians, indicated that 72% of Jewish voters cast ballots for Democrats in the 2026 midterm election. That number has remained consistent compared with past cycles. The organization’s polling also found that 70% opposed unconditional U.S. aid to Israel. That’s comparable to the 68% who in 2022 said they supported restricting aid if it expanded Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The survey of 800 self-identified Jewish voters was conducted by GBAO Strategies from Oct. 28 to Nov. 3 among those who cast their ballots on Election Day or prior to Election Day. It has a margin of error of +/- 3.5 percentage points. J Street polling data on Jewish voters opinions in the 2026 midterm election about aid to Israel. (J Street PowerPoint) Jewish voters remain reliably Democratic, even as views on U.S. aid to Israel shift Some 2026 candidates were critical of the Israeli government over conflicts with its Arab neighbors, as well as the outsized spending against them from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, including U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan. That stance exacerbated tensions among Michigan Jewish Democrats, some of whom called for voters in the U.S. Senate race to leave their ballots blank or vote instead for the Republican nominee, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers. Although J Street did not specifically poll Michigan’s U.S. Senate race, Tali deGroot, the group’s vice president for digital and political strategy, said those factors did not sway Jewish voters in Michigan from supporting El-Sayed. “The vast majority of Jews voted for Democrats across the country,” deGroot said. “It was just another chapter, ‘Will the American Jewish community abandon the Democratic Party?’ And the answer is no. The American Jewish vote is a reliably Democratic vote.” Tali deGroot, vice president of digital and political strategy at J Street. (Photo courtesy of J Street) In terms of the moral conflict that faced American Jews at the ballot box this year, deGroot said “American Jews support a relationship with Israel that is grounded in values and shared interest.” Few races better illustrated those tensions than El-Sayed’s contest against Rogers, following a contentious Democratic primary against U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) that appeared, at least on the surface, to damage his standing with some Michigan Jewish voters. But once all the votes were counted, El-Sayed defeated Rogers by 7 percentage points, a much wider margin compared to the Senate race between U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) and Rogers in 2024, which was within a single percentage point in a Republican wave election. An analysis by Millions of Michiganians, the super PAC for Progress Michigan, a nonprofit that supports progressive policies, found that El-Sayed’s share of the vote in 72 precincts with large Jewish populations was just 1.3 percentage points lower than Slotkin’s share in those same precincts in 2024. New polling made public on Friday, however, complicates the narrative that a majority of Michigan Jewish voters chose El-Sayed. The Jewish Majority, an organizations dedicated to “ensuring that the authentic priorities of the Jewish community are accurately represented in public life, released a survey of 833 Michigan Jewish voters that found 50% of those surveyed voters backed El-Sayed, compared with 43% who supported Rogers; 4% left the Senate race blank and 3% who voted for another candidate. In Oakland County — home to the largest share of Michigan’s Jewish population and many of Metro Detroit’s major Jewish institutions and congregations, including Temple Israel, the target of an antisemitic terrorist attack in March — 52% of Jewish voters said they chose Rogers compared to the 39% who voted for El-Sayed. The senator-elect, however, won the county by 14 points. The Jewish Majority findings indicate that 93% of self-identified Jewish Democrats and Democratic-leaning voters backed Benson for governor. That compares with just 70% who supported El-Sayed for Senate, although Benson’s campaign was not targeted by tens of millions of dollars in outside spending as was El-Sayed’s. Also, the 70% figure matches the national numbers that J Street obtained in its own polling. Still, Jim Gerstein, the principal at GBAO, in a call last week presenting J Street’s polling data, cautioned against looking at precinct-level data in areas with a large Jewish voting population as a way to distill how the community voted in the 2026 election. “These precinct level data, they also have non-Jews in those precincts, so we don’t know which way those votes went and what percentage of those were moved by Jewish voters versus the larger number of people in those precincts that are not Jewish,” Gerstein said. “The other thing is, in the precincts where they are overwhelmingly Jewish, those Jews are going to have different perspectives than Jews who live in less Jewish-dominated precincts.” Millions of Michiganians also argued that El-Sayed performed well among Jewish voters despite an active campaign by Nonnegotiable Michigan. The coalition of rabbis and Michigan Jews said they could not vote for El-Sayed unless he publicly recognized the right of Israel to exist as a Jewish state, and ensured the safety of American Jews if elected. Nonnegotiable also championed a write-in campaign for “Emma Lazarus,” a 19th-century author and Jewish political activist. Jewish groups disagreed over what the election results showed Millions of Michiganians noted that there were only 470 anti-El-Sayed write-in votes across the 72 precincts that it polled, and just 253 undervotes, meaning that less than 0.25% of total voters in the governor’s race, decisively won by Democrat Jocelyn Benson, chose to leave the ballot blank for El-Sayed. Nonnegotiable Michigan represented Michigan Jews who opposed El-Sayed, but deGroot said that opposition represented only a small portion of Jewish voters who considered Israel a top issue. She believed El-Sayed did well to shift his general election campaign away from Israel and AIPAC toward “the issues that affect the vast majority of Michiganders: affordability, healthcare, cost of gas, issues that the American Jewish community is actually voting on.” That notion tracks with the J Street polling, which indicated that the future of democracy and the cost of living were by far the top concerns for Jewish voters, at 44% and 34% respectively, while policy toward Israel stood at just 14%. J Street polling data on top priorities for Jewish voters in the 2026 midterm election. (J Street PowerPoint) Debbie Rosenman, a member of the progressive Michigan Indivisible Fighting 9 activist group, supported El-Sayed because of his progressive values and the issues he championed. Rosenman said Jewish voters like her shared those values and voted accordingly. David Kramer, a Democratic fundraiser and member of Nonnegotiable Michigan who ended up publicly supporting Rogers, said he had “zero regrets” about the stance he and other Jewish Democrats had taken during the election. “I think that we spoke from a point of moral clarity and a position of caring about Jewish safety and security, and our place in the community,” Kramer said. “Even though Abdul failed to meet us on those points, we still put an important marker down, and it’s a template for other candidates and for other elected officials. It was never about just one race and one person.” Israel policy could reshape the Democratic coalition heading into 2028 While there was no way to avoid the U.S.-Israel relationship being a political football in the years to come, deGroot warned candidates and outside groups against the “instrumentalization and weaponization” of the Jewish vote, because the data shows that younger American Jewish voters are becoming more progressive, and are shifting toward ending military aid to Israel. “Something we found in this cycle is that a candidate’s willingness to buck AIPAC was an indication of their general willingness to buck the status quo, and I expect that to continue,” deGroot said. “Voters want to see candidates say the status quo is not right, and we’re going to change it.” Rosenman said that Jews who supported El-Sayed could easily transfer their support to another progressive candidate in the presidential election if they had preconditions on the U.S.-Israel relationship. That was especially true if that presidential candidate possessed qualities they saw in El-Sayed, like his ability to communicate complex issues. State of the Race: Democratic U.S. Senate race pits old guard, vanguard in battle for party’s soul Rosenman also said that many American Jews were waiting to give the Israeli government a chance to reform itself before they fully agreed to completely reexamine its ties. That could depend in part on the outcome of Israel’s recent parliamentary elections, which left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Opposition parties and Arab-led parties collectively won enough seats to prevent Netanyahu’s bloc from securing a majority, leaving the formation of a new governing coalition uncertain. If Netanyahu were to lose power, Rosenman said progressive Jews like her could be more “patient” with Israel if it becomes more “open-minded and responsive to the needs of the Israeli people and their neighbors.” Another factor is El-Sayed’s performance as a senator, and if he can deliver on his baseline promises for healthcare and ending the corrupting influence of money in politics. “I think there were a lot of people who were elected who he can find partners with, and so we’re going to be watching him,” Rosenman said. “And based on how he does, or what the impression is of how he’s doing, that will have an effect on how people feel, because I don’t think Jewish voters are changing their values.” November 13, 20265:10 amThis story has been updated with additional polling data.

articles.title: Trump administration pursues a second round in the courts on birthright citizenship
articles.description: WASHINGTON — A federal judge in the District of Columbia on Thursday seemed weary of the Trump administration’s arguments that it should be allowed to proceed with its second attempt to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship. During the hearing, Judge Christopher Reid Cooper pressed Department of Justice attorneys to clarify when the second executive […]
articles.content: Hundreds gathered outside the U.S. Supreme Court on May 15, 2025, to protest the Trump administration's effort to strip birthright citizenship from the Constitution. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — A federal judge in the District of Columbia on Thursday seemed weary of the Trump administration’s arguments that it should be allowed to proceed with its second attempt to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship. During the hearing, Judge Christopher Reid Cooper pressed Department of Justice attorneys to clarify when the second executive order went into effect, because no date was included when President Donald Trump signed his executive order in August. Cooper also questioned the advocacy groups that brought the suit, led by the American Civil Liberties Union, if he should make a decision on whether to grant a preliminary injunction or wait, as he was concerned about issuing a ruling that would be redundant because there is a similar case out of Maryland. He noted that the judge who handled the first challenge to the president’s executive order in 2025 was also presiding over the second attempt and had more knowledge about the issue. This is the Trump administration’s second try at curbing birthright citizenship. In June, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the president’s executive order that would deny citizenship to babies born to parents who were either in the United States on a temporary visa or were immigrants without legal status. The case was brought by the ACLU, ACLU of New Hampshire, ACLU of Maine, ACLU of Massachusetts, ACLU of the District of Columbia, Legal Defense Fund, Asian Law Caucus and Democracy Defenders Fund. They are representing immigrants and their children who could be subject to the new executive order, and the groups previously challenged the first executive order relating to birthright citizenship. Trump’s recent executive orders would deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents deemed part of a designated terrorist organization and to parents who purposefully came to the United States to gain citizenship in what critics call “birth tourism.” The executive order also aimed to deny citizenship to children born to foreign diplomatic staff and children born in U.S. territories where Congress has not passed a law granting citizenship. Passports potentially revoked? Cooper, who was appointed by former President Barack Obama, wanted to know when children would be subject to the second executive order, which Trump signed on August 6. Lucia Goin, an ACLU staff attorney, said there is concern that the second executive order is retroactive and that children who were issued passports would have them revoked by the State Department if the order went into effect. She added that the order does not have a set date, compared to the first executive order that made clear that any child born 30 days after the order was signed would be subject to it. Ty Turley Trejo, a DOJ attorney, said the Trump administration views the order as going into effect when it’s published. Cooper questioned if that meant a child who was born before the Aug. 6 order was published, such as on Aug. 4, would be subject to the order. Trejo said the executive order would not apply to the newborn, or any child born before the executive order was signed. Cooper said if he decided to proceed with the case, he would issue an order soon.

articles.content: CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI. The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried. In Chicago, many families showed up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!”Read full article Comments

articles.title: Netflix releases new trailer for Ray Gunn
articles.description: "It's hard being the only honest players in a crooked game."
articles.content: We caught the first trailer for the upcoming Netflix animated film Ray Gunn in September and were charmed by director Brad Bird's blend of a Jetsons-like future with classic 1930s noir detective thrillers. Bird has described it as a mashup of The Maltese Falcon and Buck Rogers, and the latest trailer definitely gives off that energy. As previously reported, Bird has directed some of our all-time favorite animated films: The Iron Giant (1999), The Incredibles (2004), and Ratatouille (2007), with the latter two snagging well-deserved Oscar wins. He's been kicking around the idea for Ray Gunn for the last 30 years, working on his many other film projects while the Ray Gunn script—co-written by Matthew Robbins, who also co-wrote 1987’s Batteries Not Included with Bird—“stayed in a filing cabinet at Warner Brothers,” the director said earlier this year. The film’s inspiration came when Bird heard the opening of the B-52s’ “Planet Claire” (a personal favorite that also provides the soundtrack to the new trailer) and initially thought it was a cover of Henry Mancini’s theme music from the classic TV show Peter Gunn. Bird is a longtime fan of film noir and hard-boiled detectives, and he came up with the idea of a futuristic detective named Ray Gunn (a play on "raygun," of course). “It’s film noir and a hard-boiled detective story, but it’s got a lot more comedy and a lot more action than the average film noir,” said Bird.Read full article Comments

Michigan Democrats promised lower costs. Here are 7 ideas (it won’t be easy)
articles.description: Michigan Democrats dominated competitive races by appealing directly to voters’ pocketbooks. Now, the big question is whether they can deliver — and how soon after they take office in January.
articles.content: Michigan Democrats won big elections by focusing on lowering costs of living, making necessities more affordable Experts, advocates say state leaders have options to improve residents’ economic circumstances, though some would be costly Democrats will have majorities in state legislature and Congress, but still need to work with Trump administration to change federal policy In Michigan and across the nation, Democrats dominated competitive races by appealing directly to voters’ pocketbooks, promising to tackle high costs and fight back against President Donald Trump’s tariffs and Iran War. This story also appeared in Bridge Michigan Now, the big question is whether they can deliver — and how soon after they take office in January. Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson said after her double-digit win that she’ll be working with legislative leaders to identify options for “quick relief,” beginning with “the bills families feel every month.” Related: Michigan GOP reckons with Trump, leadership revolt after drubbing 5 Michigan cities voted to create ‘health action’ boards. Now what? Michigan’s next House speaker wants ‘transformational’ change At the federal level, “money in your pocket” was a campaign mantra for Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed. He and fellow Democrats are angling to reverse or revise some of Trump’s signature second-term actions, from tariffs and the Iran War to spending cuts on Medicaid and food assistance. But political and economic realities could hamper Democrats’ ambitions. Federal lawmakers will still need Trump’s signoff to pass laws, and state leaders are limited in what they can do to effectively combat systemic economic issues, especially if the state budget is stretched thin. Experts and advocates who spoke with Bridge Michigan this week said there are opportunities for relief if officials are able to spend or have the appetite to push for long-term changes. Still, “there is no silver bullet, there is no fix where suddenly gas prices go down, groceries are more affordable and everything else,” said Eric Lupher, president of the Citizens Research Council of Michigan. Boost wages For many Michigan families, wage stagnation or decline is as much of a cause of affordability issues as higher costs of living, said Patrick Schaefer, an economic security policy analyst for the Michigan League for Public Policy. “This crisis of affordability is not new for everyone,” Schaefer said. “Affordability is not a one-sided issue. It is not just about costs, and it’s not just about wages. It is a multi-variable equation in which wages and costs are a large part of it.” Benson, in her winning campaign for governor, said she wanted to guarantee a minimum salary of $60,000 for teachers. As of last year, Michigan starting teacher pay ranked 44th nationwide at $41,645. House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri, D-Canton, says he wants to ‘return some normalcy’ to the state House after two years in the minority. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya) House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri recently told Bridge that Democrats are still working on their legislative agenda. But he told Bridge he wants lawmakers to “start tackling why our household median income in Michigan is lagging behind our peer states,” among other things. Depending on political will, building on recent increases to the state’s minimum wage and increasing worker protections and labor participation could be on the table. But doing so would likely require significant political capital — lawmakers in 2025 brokered a deal on minimum wage increases only after months of infighting and a spirited challenge from restaurant owners. Policymakers have also tried to boost wages by attracting companies with high-paying jobs to the state, though middling returns on incentives to draw such companies have caused consternation among lawmakers in recent years. Congress could also move to increase the $7.25 federal minimum wage, which hasn’t increased since 2009, although that impact could be limited because most Americans already earn more than that. More tax credits, supports Under term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan expanded its Earned Income Tax Credit for lower-income workers and introduced programs like Rx Kids, a first-in-the-nation cash assistance program for moms that has improved health outcomes but drawn scrutiny from legislative Republicans. Benson previously told Bridge she wants to expand Rx Kids and work with the Legislature to create a new $5,000 caregiver tax credit. Long-term, advocates say expanding eligibility for childcare scholarships and increasing the number of providers available is another way the state could make a tangible difference in family budgets. Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson addresses reporters in Detroit following a commanding election night victory. (Lauren Gibbons/Bridge Michigan ) One likely limitation: The cost of it all. Much will depend on how federal changes to payments for programs like food assistance and Medicaid play out in the state budget, as well as updated revenue estimates state officials will receive in January. Some advocates have argued that additional taxes on the state’s wealthiest residents, either via surcharges or taxes on inheritance, could be a way to boost revenue without hitting middle- and lower-income residents’ bottom lines. “We have tools at our disposal to increase revenues without necessarily burdening the median family or median worker that we could then use to pay for some of these programs,” Schaefer said, acknowledging that suggesting new tax hikes “becomes very unpopular.” Revisit tariffs The Trump administration’s tariff strategy was a hot topic in the midterms as critics blamed the new import taxes and retaliation from other nations for rising costs of groceries and other necessities. Trump — who has defended his aggressive tariff strategy as a means to protect US manufacturing interests — will remain a key decision-maker in setting trade policy, but advocates argue there’s an opportunity for federal and even state officials to push for change. President Donald Trump is continuing to tax imports after the US Supreme Court struck down many of his initially tariffs. (Mark Schiefelbein/Associated Press) “Tariffs are a pretty important first step” for taking on the cost-of-living issues Michigan residents are facing, said John Sellek, spokesperson for the Michigan Smart Trade Alliance. Congressional Democrats are reportedly preparing a two-pronged approach to wind back some of Trump’s tariffs through investigations and legislative challenges. An analysis from the National Taxpayers Union Foundation found the import taxes have cost Michigan residents an estimated $27 billion since January 2025, an estimated $6,485 per household and the third-highest statewide total in the country. The federal government collected $233 billion in tariff revenue from January through late September, though refunds ordered by the US Supreme Court are cutting into that, with about $140 billion to be counted as revenue. The import tax was about $77 billion in 2024 before Trump was reelected. Reconnect with Canada Michigan and other states bordering Canada have borne the brunt of Trump’s tensions with the United States’ northern neighbor, from retaliatory tariff costs to a drop in foreign tourism. Where many other pressures on people’s pocketbooks don’t have a quick political fix, Sellek argued a friendlier relationship with Canada would show “fairly rapid” improvements for businesses and consumers alike. Canadian and American flags are shown on the Gordie Howe Bridge under construction between Windsor, Ontario and Detroit, May 22, 2026. (Paul Sancya/Associated Press) El-Sayed, who called Trump’s tariff policies “chaotic,” “ham-fisted” and “self-serving” on the campaign trail, recently told MS Now that resolving trade issues with Canada should happen “immediately.” State officials have little control over foreign relations, though that hasn’t stopped outgoing Gov. Gretchen Whitmer from working with sources both in the US and Canada. On Tuesday, Whitmer sent a letter to federal officials asking for the government to eliminate food tariffs imposed from 2025 onward and reimburse Michigan residents for higher grocery costs. In an October debate, Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson declared she would “negotiate a contract between Michigan and Canada” to alleviate the state’s tariff burden. It’s not clear she would have the authority to do so, however, because the US Constitution only gives Congress the power to levy tariffs and approve formal treaties with foreign governments. Following her election, Benson was more measured, offering to work with the Trump administration and Congress “to protect the people of Michigan from the harm that these tariffs have caused.” Suspend gas taxes Gas prices skyrocketed across the country in recent months amid the US and Israel’s ongoing war with Iran, and prices in metro Detroit at times topped $5 per gallon. According to AAA, average prices have dropped considerably from those highs in recent weeks and currently sit at $3.95 per gallon, roughly a dollar more than this time last year. Because the crude oil that goes into making gasoline is a global commodity, prices can be volatile and are influenced heavily by international affairs in addition to supply and demand. Gas prices have topped $4 a gallon for a record number of days in 2026. (Jordyn Hermani/Bridge Michigan) One factor US policymakers can control is the taxes collected at the pump. Michigan has the sixth-highest gas tax in the nation, at 52.4 cents a gallon, and the federal gas tax is another 18.4 cents per gallon. On the campaign trail, state and federal candidates alike floated temporary gas tax holidays as a possibility to give drivers a little relief. But doing so even for a short time would come with a big cost: those taxes are the primary funding source for critical road repairs. “When you cut out the primary funding mechanism for this, well, now you’re stuck with a problem,” said Adam Hoffer, director of excise tax policy at the Washington, DC-based Tax Foundation. “You’re either going to need to raise taxes somewhere else, or you’re going to need to tax some other item or product, or this becomes deficit financing.” “None of those are great options,” he continued. Benson has said she’s open to considering short-term state gas tax reductions. On the day after the election, she noted the state should also consider revisiting how road repairs are funded “so that we are identifying new sources of revenue that can help pay our bills in the state, but also streamlining how things are spent so that we’re reducing costs as well.” Address healthcare costs Costs of healthcare have continued to surge, resulting in a growing number of uninsured Americans. Looming federal changes to Medicaid under the Trump-backed “big, beautiful bill” could lead to more people losing their existing health coverage. Voters in five Michigan cities approved measures to create new citizen-led boards that will recommend ways to lower costs and improve healthcare policies. It’s unclear how those boards will function in practice, and they won’t have any direct authority to change policies. Some winning candidates like El-Sayed championed a “Medicare for All” single-payer federal healthcare system, a longtime progressive priority. That could require new or higher taxes, but proponents argue it would reduce overall costs by eliminating out-of-pocket costs. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Michigan, is an unabashed supporter of Medicare for All. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Associated Press) At the federal level, convincing Trump to walk back some of his signature policies adopted with a Republican-led Congress will likely be a tall order for Democrats, as would any significant expansions to government-backed healthcare the GOP has historically opposed. Man's secret use of synthetic testosterone for cows nearly destroyed his heart
articles.description: Doctors warn that such life-threatening cases are becoming more common.
articles.content: For 11 years, a Massachusetts man had an alarming array of health problems, most notably that his heart kept failing. He landed in the hospital over and over again, needed life support at one point, spent years going to specialists, and underwent a barrage of tests along the way. But through it all, he never revealed a key detail behind his ailments: He was taking powerful, illicit synthetic testosterone derivatives (aka anabolic-androgenic steroids, or AAS). One of the drugs he took was approved only for use in animals; it's primarily used to beef up cows. Left in the dark, his doctors had to puzzle this out on their own. In a case report in this week's issue of the New England Journal of Medicine, they explain how they did it. They also offer a warning: These cases will only become more common, and clinicians need to know what they look like.Read full article Comments

Nonprofit Director Urges East Lansing to Expand Support for Unhoused Residents
articles.description: Punks With Lunch Executive Director Kelsea Hector presented to the East Lansing Human Rights Commission on Monday.
articles.content: Amid ongoing concern about a possible serial killer targeting unhoused individuals on the Lansing River Trail, the director of a Lansing-based organization that aids the area’s homeless community spoke to the East Lansing Human Rights Commission. Kelsea Hector is the executive director of Punks with Lunch, or PWL, a local nonprofit organization that serves unhoused individuals in the Greater Lansing Area, including Ingham, Eaton and Shiawassee counties. Hector said PWL distributes around 700 to 800 lunches weekly to people experiencing homelessness, a number that is steadily increasing due to a growing need. At Monday’s Human Rights Commission meeting, Hector recommended steps the City of East Lansing could take to support the homeless population. Hector suggested a care model that emphasizes housing and provides resources for overdose prevention, addiction counseling and mental health services. She stressed that any real solution will be built with input from unhoused people. Hector recommended the City of East Lansing and the HRC publicly recognize the safety of unhoused people as a fundamental human rights issue and support a pause on encampment sweeps across the region. “We go where people are,” Hector said. “Our model works because we meet people exactly where they are.” Many unhoused people in East Lansing grew up in the city and wish to stay, Hector said, but a lack of resources and negative encounters with police are pushing them into neighboring communities like Lansing. At the same time, Lansing is still clearing encampments while local shelters operate at full capacity, and people can spend years on a waitlist before receiving public assistance they need to become housed. Hector described a systemic Catch-22 in transition programs: individuals who have been on the streets for years may eventually receive subsidies that allow them to secure housing. However, vital support from the government and most nonprofits stop too soon once they become housed, leaving underlying issues unresolved. “We put them in four walls, and we say ‘good luck’ and then we walk away … and we wonder why people end up back on the streets,” Hector said. According to PWL, individuals routinely return to the streets because their new environments lack community enrichment and long-term support systems. Currently, East Lansing’s only homeless shelter, Haven House, primarily serves families rather than individuals. Through trust PWL has built within the local homeless community, PWL outreach teams conduct weekly check-ins in East Lansing, tracking displaced individuals and distributing food and supplies to a population Hector notes is very real, but increasingly less visible. “We’ve seen people panhandling a lot in downtown East Lansing that we’ll stop and provide connections to services [and] make sure we talk to them,” Hector said. Highlighting the realities of how unhoused individuals interact with local law enforcement, Hector shared an encounter involving an unhoused man named Gary. “He [Gary] was in East Lansing on a scooter. He had a rotisserie chicken [in] his hand that he was eating because he did not have a plate. He had just bought it, and a police officer stopped him because someone called and told her [the officer] that someone was eating a chicken suspiciously on the side of the road,” Hector said. “She took his chicken away, she threw it in the trash, and then she took him to jail. These are the common stories that we hear. A lot of people will stay away from East Lansing because of the way that they’re treated.” Lansing drew national attention this fall for a series of violent deaths on the River Trail that have raised concerns a possible serial killer is targeting homeless people in the area. Still, the scary circumstances have not earned the unhoused population sympathy from some. “In reality, people keep getting swept. We have a lot of murders that have happened in the last year on the [Lansing] River Trail. We continue to see increases of community stigma and violence on our unhoused people,” Hector said. “Because of this, we’ve had people who have experienced threats on the River Trail now. There’s a group of kids going down and harassing people and saying that they’re going to be next.” Do you have a question that you would like ELi to investigate? Just click here! articles.title: US senators demand end to Iran war funding in bill averting shutdown
articles.description: WASHINGTON — The possibility of a government shutdown next month increased somewhat Thursday as a group of U.S. senators said the stopgap spending bill must cut off funding for the Iran war. Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, as well as Vermont independent Sen. Bernie […]
articles.content: U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, is among four senators who say a stopgap spending bill must cut off funding for the Iran war. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)WASHINGTON — The possibility of a government shutdown next month increased somewhat Thursday as a group of U.S. senators said the stopgap spending bill must cut off funding for the Iran war. Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, as well as Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders, wrote in a joint statement that a short-term funding bill “must include language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.” Legislation must be enacted by Dec. 11 to avert a shutdown. “The American people do not want more war in the Middle East — but that is what President Trump has given them. Congress cannot allow Trump to continue his conflict — we must force him to end it,” they wrote. “Not doing so will only prolong the American people’s pain, and opens the door to further escalation as he has threatened.” Washington state Sen. Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, said Tuesday that leaders on the panel were debating how long the stopgap spending bill should last and whether to add any restrictions to how the Trump administration can spend the funding. “We’re exploring all options at this point,” she said. Murray said during the brief hallway interview in the Capitol that Democrats did not intend to approve the tens of billions of dollars in additional funding that the Trump administration requested this summer for the Iran war. Any short-term funding bill will need support from Democrats to move through the Senate, where at least 60 votes are needed to advance major legislation. While Republicans hold a majority of 53 seats for the rest of this year, it’s not enough to pass bills without bipartisan support. But, President Donald Trump’s signature will also be needed unless there are veto-proof margins in each chamber, an unlikely prospect with Republicans in charge of the House and Senate. That makes avoiding another government shutdown when funding expires a complicated balancing act. Bennet, Duckworth, Sanders and Van Hollen wrote in their joint statement that the midterm election results showed voters want Congress to end the “illegal and disastrous war with Iran.” “This conflict has driven up the cost of gas, groceries, and fertilizer,” they wrote. “More than 20 American service members have been killed and hundreds more wounded, while achieving none of President Trump’s stated goals and harming civilians across the region.” House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York speaks to reporters Nov. 12, 2026, at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom) House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, asked about the possibility of adding language to an appropriations bill to end the war, said he didn’t want to get ahead of bipartisan negotiations. He said that Connecticut Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro, ranking member on the House Appropriations Committee, was “working through all of our Democratic priorities to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11.” “I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine, to Pete Hegseth’s war machine over in the Middle East,” Jeffries said. “Taxpayer dollars should be spent to make life more affordable for everyday Americans, not to drop bombs overseas in an endless war that Donald Trump and Republicans promised they would not get the country into, but turned around and did the exact opposite.”

Michigan Democrats promised lower costs. Here are 7 ideas (it won’t be easy)
articles.description: Michigan Democrats dominated competitive races by appealing directly to voters’ pocketbooks. Now, the big question is whether they can deliver — and how soon after they take office in January.
articles.content: Michigan Democrats won big elections by focusing on lowering costs of living, making necessities more affordable Experts, advocates say state leaders have options to improve residents’ economic circumstances, though some would be costly Democrats will have majorities in state legislature and Congress, but still need to work with Trump administration to change federal policy In Michigan and across the nation, Democrats dominated competitive races by appealing directly to voters’ pocketbooks, promising to tackle high costs and fight back against President Donald Trump’s tariffs and Iran War. Now, the big question is whether they can deliver — and how soon after they take office in January. Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson said after her double-digit win that she’ll be working with legislative leaders to identify options for “quick relief,” beginning with “the bills families feel every month.” At the federal level, “money in your pocket” was a campaign mantra for Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed. He and fellow Democrats are angling to reverse or revise some of Trump’s signature second-term actions, from tariffs and the Iran War to spending cuts on Medicaid and food assistance. But political and economic realities could hamper Democrats’ ambitions. Federal lawmakers will still need Trump’s signoff to pass laws, and state leaders are limited in what they can do to effectively combat systemic economic issues, especially if the state budget is stretched thin. Related: Michigan GOP reckons with Trump, leadership revolt after drubbing 5 Michigan cities voted to create ‘health action’ boards. Now what? Michigan’s next House speaker wants ‘transformational’ change Experts and advocates who spoke with Bridge Michigan this week said there are opportunities for relief if officials are able to spend or have the appetite to push for long-term changes. Still, “there is no silver bullet, there is no fix where suddenly gas prices go down, groceries are more affordable and everything else,” said Eric Lupher, president of the Citizens Research Council of Michigan. Here are seven ways Democrats could get started. Boost wages For many Michigan families, wage stagnation or decline is as much of a cause of affordability issues as higher costs of living, said Patrick Schaefer, an economic security policy analyst for the Michigan League for Public Policy.Donate “This crisis of affordability is not new for everyone,” Schaefer said. “Affordability is not a one-sided issue. It is not just about costs, and it’s not just about wages. It is a multi-variable equation in which wages and costs are a large part of it.” Benson, in her winning campaign for governor, said she wanted to guarantee a minimum salary of $60,000 for teachers. As of last year, Michigan starting teacher pay ranked 44th nationwide at $41,645. House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri, D-Canton, says he wants to ‘return some normalcy’ to the state House after two years in the minority. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya) House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri recently told Bridge that Democrats are still working on their legislative agenda. But he told Bridge he wants lawmakers to “start tackling why our household median income in Michigan is lagging behind our peer states,” among other things. Depending on political will, building on recent increases to the state’s minimum wage and increasing worker protections and labor participation could be on the table. But doing so would likely require significant political capital — lawmakers in 2025 brokered a deal on minimum wage increases only after months of infighting and a spirited challenge from restaurant owners. Policymakers have also tried to boost wages by attracting companies with high-paying jobs to the state, though middling returns on incentives to draw such companies have caused consternation among lawmakers in recent years. Congress could also move to increase the $7.25 federal minimum wage, which hasn’t increased since 2009, although that impact could be limited because most Americans already earn more than that. More tax credits, supports Under term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan expanded its Earned Income Tax Credit for lower-income workers and introduced programs like Rx Kids, a first-in-the-nation cash assistance program for moms that has improved health outcomes but drawn scrutiny from legislative Republicans. Benson previously told Bridge she wants to expand Rx Kids and work with the Legislature to create a new $5,000 caregiver tax credit. Long-term, advocates say expanding eligibility for childcare scholarships and increasing the number of providers available is another way the state could make a tangible difference in family budgets. Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson addresses reporters in Detroit following a commanding election night victory. (Lauren Gibbons/Bridge Michigan ) One likely limitation: The cost of it all. Much will depend on how federal changes to payments for programs like food assistance and Medicaid play out in the state budget, as well as updated revenue estimates state officials will receive in January. Some advocates have argued that additional taxes on the state’s wealthiest residents, either via surcharges or taxes on inheritance, could be a way to boost revenue without hitting middle- and lower-income residents’ bottom lines. “We have tools at our disposal to increase revenues without necessarily burdening the median family or median worker that we could then use to pay for some of these programs,” Schaefer said, acknowledging that suggesting new tax hikes “becomes very unpopular.” Revisit tariffs The Trump administration’s tariff strategy was a hot topic in the midterms as critics blamed the new import taxes and retaliation from other nations for rising costs of groceries and other necessities. Trump — who has defended his aggressive tariff strategy as a means to protect US manufacturing interests — will remain a key decision-maker in setting trade policy, but advocates argue there’s an opportunity for federal and even state officials to push for change. President Donald Trump is continuing to tax imports after the US Supreme Court struck down many of his initially tariffs. (Mark Schiefelbein/Associated Press) “Tariffs are a pretty important first step” for taking on the cost-of-living issues Michigan residents are facing, said John Sellek, spokesperson for the Michigan Smart Trade Alliance. Congressional Democrats are reportedly preparing a two-pronged approach to wind back some of Trump’s tariffs through investigations and legislative challenges. An analysis from the National Taxpayers Union Foundation found the import taxes have cost Michigan residents an estimated $27 billion since January 2025, an estimated $6,485 per household and the third-highest statewide total in the country. The federal government collected $233 billion in tariff revenue from January through late September, though refunds ordered by the US Supreme Court are cutting into that, with about $140 billion to be counted as revenue. The import tax was about $77 billion in 2024 before Trump was reelected. Reconnect with Canada Michigan and other states bordering Canada have borne the brunt of Trump’s tensions with the United States’ northern neighbor, from retaliatory tariff costs to a drop in foreign tourism. Where many other pressures on people’s pocketbooks don’t have a quick political fix, Sellek argued a friendlier relationship with Canada would show “fairly rapid” improvements for businesses and consumers alike. Canadian and American flags are shown on the Gordie Howe Bridge under construction between Windsor, Ontario and Detroit, May 22, 2026. (Paul Sancya/Associated Press) El-Sayed, who called Trump’s tariff policies “chaotic,” “ham-fisted” and “self-serving” on the campaign trail, recently told MS Now that resolving trade issues with Canada should happen “immediately.” State officials have little control over foreign relations, though that hasn’t stopped outgoing Gov. Gretchen Whitmer from working with sources both in the US and Canada. On Tuesday, Whitmer sent a letter to federal officials asking for the government to eliminate food tariffs imposed from 2025 onward and reimburse Michigan residents for higher grocery costs. In an October debate, Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson declared she would “negotiate a contract between Michigan and Canada” to alleviate the state’s tariff burden. It’s not clear she would have the authority to do so, however, because the US Constitution only gives Congress the power to levy tariffs and approve formal treaties with foreign governments. Following her election, Benson was more measured, offering to work with the Trump administration and Congress “to protect the people of Michigan from the harm that these tariffs have caused.” Suspend gas taxes Gas prices skyrocketed across the country in recent months amid the US and Israel’s ongoing war with Iran, and prices in metro Detroit at times topped $5 per gallon. According to AAA, average prices have dropped considerably from those highs in recent weeks and currently sit at $3.95 per gallon, roughly a dollar more than this time last year. Because the crude oil that goes into making gasoline is a global commodity, prices can be volatile and are influenced heavily by international affairs in addition to supply and demand. Gas prices have topped $4 a gallon for a record number of days in 2026. (Jordyn Hermani/Bridge Michigan) One factor US policymakers can control is the taxes collected at the pump. Michigan has the sixth-highest gas tax in the nation, at 52.4 cents a gallon, and the federal gas tax is another 18.4 cents per gallon. On the campaign trail, state and federal candidates alike floated temporary gas tax holidays as a possibility to give drivers a little relief. But doing so even for a short time would come with a big cost: those taxes are the primary funding source for critical road repairs. “When you cut out the primary funding mechanism for this, well, now you’re stuck with a problem,” said Adam Hoffer, director of excise tax policy at the Washington, DC-based Tax Foundation. “You’re either going to need to raise taxes somewhere else, or you’re going to need to tax some other item or product, or this becomes deficit financing.” “None of those are great options,” he continued. Benson has said she’s open to considering short-term state gas tax reductions. On the day after the election, she noted the state should also consider revisiting how road repairs are funded “so that we are identifying new sources of revenue that can help pay our bills in the state, but also streamlining how things are spent so that we’re reducing costs as well.” Address healthcare costs Costs of healthcare have continued to surge, resulting in a growing number of uninsured Americans. Looming federal changes to Medicaid under the Trump-backed “big, beautiful bill” could lead to more people losing their existing health coverage. Voters in five Michigan cities approved measures to create new citizen-led boards that will recommend ways to lower costs and improve healthcare policies. It’s unclear how those boards will function in practice, and they won’t have any direct authority to change policies. Some winning candidates like El-Sayed championed a “Medicare for All” single-payer federal healthcare system, a longtime progressive priority. That could require new or higher taxes, but proponents argue it would reduce overall costs by eliminating out-of-pocket costs. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Michigan, is an unabashed supporter of Medicare for All. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Associated Press) At the federal level, convincing Trump to walk back some of his signature policies adopted with a Republican-led Congress will likely be a tall order for Democrats, as would any significant expansions to government-backed healthcare the GOP has historically opposed. The amazing disappearing exoplanet
articles.description: An exoplanet seems to have stopped transiting in front of its host star.
articles.content: One nice thing about discovering exoplanets is that, once you work out how long their orbits take, they continue to show up like clockwork. The timing is so regular, in fact, that we can use variations to detect the gravitational influence of additional planets in the same exosolar system. And the precise timing is useful in that we can rely on it to point telescopes at the system when we know some of the light we detect has passed through the planet's atmosphere. Except when we can't. On Monday, researchers reported on an exoplanet that simply stopped showing up. TOI-2535b is a hot Jupiter-sized planet we've been observing as it transits between its host star, TOI-2535, and Earth for about seven years now. But it recently stopped showing up, and researchers suspect that's due to an unseen companion orbiting in a different plane.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Muhith Mahmood becomes Hamtramck’s first Bangladeshi mayor a year after election
articles.description: Mayor Mahmood hopes to unite Hamtramck residents across a variety of religions, political affiliations and ethnicity. The post Muhith Mahmood becomes Hamtramck’s first Bangladeshi mayor a year after election appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: Mayor Mahmood hopes to unite Hamtramck residents across a variety of religions, political affiliations and ethnicity. Hamtramck Mayor Muhith Mahmood was sworn into office Nov. 8 at the Hamtramck Community Center. Muhith Mahmood was sworn in as Hamtramck’s new mayor on Sunday during an inauguration ceremony at the Hamtramck Community Center. “Let us build bridges, respect our differences and work toward our common goals. As I begin my service as mayor, I pledge to lead with integrity, fairness, humility and dedication. Together, let us move forward. One Hamtramck, one community, one future,” he said during his inauguration speech. The former Hamtramck City councilman is the city’s first Bangladeshi mayor. This comes after a yearlong battle for the city’s top job. Mahmood says although every problem cannot be solved overnight, he will work to unite everyone across ethnic, faith and political backgrounds. “We may come from different backgrounds, but we share the same hope, same neighborhoods, clean streets, reliable services, good schools and a green future for our next generation…. Every resident deserves to feel welcome, respected and represented,” he says. Mahmood says this moment reflects the importance of every voice in Hamtramck as shown through their cast ballots. “This achievement belongs to everyone who helped make it possible. Our journey has shown why every voice deserved to be heard and every ballot deserved to be counted. Hamtramck is a special American city,” he says. This new change in office comes after a Wayne County judge ordered the Wayne County board of canvassers to count 37 absentee ballots last month. The ballots were found in the city clerk’s office days after the election last year. Last year, Adam Alharbi was declared the winner. Alharbi, the Yemeni American engineer for the Department of Commerce, has served as mayor since January. The recent count put Mahmood in a 12-point lead over Alharbi. The ballots were certified after hearing arguments about Mahmood’s residency. Alharbi alleges Mahmood does not live in Hamtramck. Mahmood maintains he lives in Hamtramck; his family lives in Troy. During the inauguration ceremony at the Hamtramck Community Center, Democratic State Sen. Stephanie Chang told people to move forward together “This is such an important time for the city of Hamtramck to be able to come together, celebrate our diversity and really build on many of the strengths that this community truly does have. I’m looking forward to continuing to be a partner to the city of Hamtramck. Congratulations,” she says. Rep. Tonya Myers Phillips, who serves the Michigan’s Seventh House District, was also in attendance. “All of us are so excited on behalf of the state of Michigan to partner with our new mayor and our city council and community members to just keep Hamtramck moving forward. To advocate for more affordable, housing, utilities, basic needs and business opportunities,” she says. Gias Talukder, owner of Bengal Auto Sales in Hamtramck, says the new mayor represents all people. “Please, to all to the Yemeni American community, and Polish American community, the American community, and the Bangladeshi community, please let’s welcome Muhith Mahmoud. Let’s respect the result of the vote and work together,” he says. Mohammed Ahad is the President of the Bangladeshi American Business Association of Michigan. He’s a business owner and former resident of Hamtramck. He says he came out to celebrate Mahmood’s oath ceremony. “I am a business owner also in Hamtramck; there is another hope from Muhith Mahmoud and his council: please bring the business to Hamtramck,” he shares. But he adds that Mahmood should work for all Hamtramck residents, not just business owners. Mahmood says he was elected by all people, not just Bangladeshis. “I got elected by every culture and ethnicity that voted for me. As you can see, there has been chaos going on for the last year and we overcame it. Now it’s time for peace and for us to move the city forward,” he says. Talukder notes that he also hopes Mahmood focuses on keeping a strong police and fire force as well as fixing the roads in Hamtramck. Mahmood says he needs leaders from different communities to work together and focus on the future. “We all want one Hamtramck, and we all want to work together,” he says. He says that Alharbi did a great job in his run. He looks forward to working with him for the betterment of the community. Alharbi did not attend the inauguration. He plans to pursue a legal appeal to recount the 37 ballots and Mahmood’s residency, despite the Wayne County judge telling both parties to stop fighting to allow the residents to heal and move forward. Mahmood began his new role as mayor on Monday, Nov. 9. The inauguration program also included Bangladeshi cultural programming.

SoftBank’s billion-dollar loss may have put a cap on AI’s natural gas ambitions
articles.description: SoftBank lost over $3 billion preordering natural gas turbines to power AI data centers. Here's what the loss means to power markets.
articles.content: SoftBank might not be the first to invest in a hot trend, but when it does, it goes big. Witness its $30 billion bet on OpenAI in early 2025 or its announcement in February that its SB Energy subsidiary would spend $33 billion on a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas power plant. If you can’t be first, be biggest, I guess. That philosophy apparently spilled over into procurement, where orders were also supersized. Starting about two years ago, SoftBank reportedly put down deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines, almost 50% more than it needed. The decision to over-order undoubtedly helped secure turbines and speed up SoftBank’s projects. “SB Energy did not have a choice except to overbook turbines in the future if they wanted some turbines right away,” Peter Gardett, CEO of Noreva, told TechCrunch via email. The energy world was caught off guard by the swiftness and magnitude of AI’s rising power demands. Queues for turbine orders now extend into the early 2030s. As natural gas was shaping up to be a go-to power source for the AI boom, CEO Masayoshi Son bet that by deploying his investment firm’s significant war chest, he could corner a portion of the market. If the AI world wanted power for its data centers, it would have to come to him. Now that bet appears to have fizzled. SoftBank announced a $7.1 billion quarterly loss on Tuesday, with over half of that stemming from losses related to power-generating equipment. The investor had paid turbine manufacturers nonrefundable deposits to secure orders, and now it considered much of those worthless. The move was also a costly bit of price discovery, Gardett said. Rather than overpay and potentially still be short of turbines, SoftBank overpaid and over-ordered. “This charge is just that price discovery finally happening,” Gardett said. The magnitude of that misplaced bet — over $3 billion — reflects some of the electricity mania that has overtaken the AI world. Faced with years-long waits to connect to the grid, many hyperscalers and developers have turned to natural gas as a sort of energy security blanket, something that is proven and familiar. As AI data centers spend more time in operation, their operators are getting a better feel for what’s required to keep them operating. Natural gas might seem like a safe bet, but there are still risks, including winter curtailments when supplies dip and demand spikes, Brent Nelson, senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics, told the Equity podcast Wednesday. In light of that, Nelson said the grid might still be their best bet. Most data centers would be best served by a grid connection, albeit a smaller one than they might normally request. To make up for the shortfall, large batteries are a cost-effective choice, Nelson said. They’d help shave peak loads or ride out requests from the utility to curtail electricity use. Data center operators might be coming to that same conclusion, leading the natural gas market to develop more slowly than SoftBank expected. SoftBank’s natural gas-related losses are unlikely to have a domino effect, leading to mass cancellations of gas power plants. AI’s power demand appears to be too large for that. For now, natural gas is riding high, though SoftBank may have found its ceiling. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. articles.title: Mamdani Signs a Law Letting Housing Nonprofits Bid First on Distressed Buildings
articles.content: In New York City, "COPA" now means more than a swinging nightclub. On Tuesday, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act (COPA) into law, giving nonprofits and community groups first dibs on certain New York City buildings. It will go into effect in November of 2027. COPA requires building owners to notify the city's housing department when they want to sell certain properties, including distressed multifamily buildings with four or more units and buildings with 100 or fewer units subject to certain affordability rules. The city then allows eligible nonprofits and community groups to make offers on these buildings before private buyers. These groups have 20 days to submit a statement of interest in buying the property and 70 days to make a first offer. The groups, according to the law, also have "a right of first refusal if an owner receives an offer from a person other than a qualified entity." COPA was first proposed back in 2020, and a different version of the bill passed City Council in December of 2025. That version, however, was vetoed by former Mayor Eric Adams on his last day in office. This year, the City Council, led by COPA's main sponsor, Council member Sandy Nurse, pushed through a scaled-back bill that applies to 2,100 buildings (instead of 10,000), according to amNY. Before City Council's vote, Nurse said that the city cannot build its "way out of this crisis," and COPA is necessary to preserve existing housing, reported The New York Times. Although the toned-down version of COPA may alleviate some of the real estate industry's concerns, critics of the law, like Manhattan Institute senior fellow John Ketcham, have argued that COPA still poses other problems. In December of 2025, Ketcham wrote in City Journal that COPA "rests on the flawed premises that nonprofit ownership is inherently superior to private ownership and that city government should tip the scales in favor of nonprofit ownership." While COPA's supporters believe that nonprofits will best protect tenants and maintain buildings, Ketcham also noted that "there is little reason to think that nonprofits would be better at addressing cold boilers, leaky roofs, and other maintenance needs." Nonprofits, just like private landlords, can also evict tenants, he added. And as The New York Times has pointed out, a 2025 report from New York University's Furman Center has warned that opportunity to purchase laws like COPA, especially in softer markets, could discourage investments by "imposing timing delays and legal process costs." Erik Engquist of The Real Deal argued that "COPA doesn't improve the difficult economics of buying and operating distressed buildings," as the few nonprofits able to buy these buildings have been allowed to bid on them without COPA. "It just adds a layer of bureaucracy," he wrote in October. Adding layers of bureaucracy to the housing market instead of stripping them away is not out of character for New York City under the Mamdani administration. Just last month, the city's rent freeze took effect. And while some tenants who are lucky enough to score frozen rent now may embrace city intervention in housing, it is unlikely that giving the government more control of the market will meaningfully bring down prices in the long run.
