articles.title: 5 Michigan cities voted to create ‘health action’ boards. Now what?
articles.description: Voters in five Michigan cities have approved measures to create citizen-led boards to recommend ways to lower healthcare costs.
articles.content: Michigan will receive nearly $1.6 billion in opioid settlements by 2040.(ERIC HOOD /Eric Hood - stock.adobe.com / 123721416)Amid growing concerns over medical costs, voters in five Michigan cities last week approved measures to create new citizen-led boards that will recommend ways to lower costs and improve healthcare policies.How the boards will function is not clear, nor is the source of funding for the successful ballot campaigns. Liberal “dark money” groups spent nearly $3 million on the initiatives, which were spread across two toss-up congressional districts represented by Republicans who lost their reelection bids.But with healthcare costs top of mind for many, voters agreed to establish “citizens’ advisory health action” committees by wide margins in Benton Harbor ( 80% approval ), Lansing ( 66% approval ), East Lansing ( 69% approval ), Kalamazoo ( 69% approval ) and Portage ( 55% approval ).Now, it’s up to local governments in those cities to set up the boards, prompting fears of additional costs and uncertain outcomes.“If the voters want it, then we’ll set up a committee and we’ll do it,” Lansing Mayor Andy Schor told Bridge Michigan ahead of the election, expressing ambivalence and acknowledging the proposals made a political point.The cities will be limited in how much they can impact a sprawling national healthcare system with mind-numbing complexities, often opaque financing and Medicaid eligibility changes that are expected to reduce coverage and cost providers millions of dollars.But the new committees will be able to advise officials whose policies could support local health providers in ways that drive down costs, said Ryan Cohn, a spokesperson for City Action Michigan, the nonprofit driving the effort.“Voters sent a clear message,” said Cohn, who works for a Florida-based public relations firm, Sachs Media. “They want action on healthcare costs, and they’re done waiting for Congress to deliver it.”A late-October poll of Michigan voters showed high costs were a top concern, with health insurance or medical costs the primary driver.Local amendments, local concernsThe local proposals amended city charters to create seven- or eight-member committees to:1. Hold public forums to hear firsthand accounts from community members about how healthcare costs affect them2. Hold public forums to learn more about the role of federal and state policies in determining healthcare costs3. Track federal and state officials’ votes on healthcare legislation4. Prepare a “Healthcare Action Plan” for city leaders by Oct. 1 of each even-numbered yearCity councils then must hold public hearings by Oct. 15 of the same year for public discussion on the action plan. Advisory committee members will not be paid for their efforts, but must have necessary “research, analytical and community engagement skills,” according to the new rules.Some local officials have called the effort misguided.In October, the Kalamazoo City Commission passed a resolution unanimously opposing the local ballot measure. In public meetings, Mayor David Anderson expressed concerns about the ongoing financial burden organizing and running health advisory committees might impose on taxpayers.“Who’s gonna pay for all this work going forward in perpetuity? City residents,” Anderson said. “The cost of this will end up being a reduction in resources for something else that we might care a lot about.”Kalamazoo Commissioner Chris Praedel criticized the use of dark money to push the proposal, warning that it was “critically important for the public to think through how this sets a precedent or how this could impact things in a very dark, mischievous way.”It’s unclear how much the initiative will cost cities going forward. Committee members aren’t paid, although they can be compensated for costs, according to ballot language.“I would not envision it would be a lot,” said Alex Little, city manager in Benton Harbor.Political impactThe proposals were notable for the way that they intertwined policy and electoral advocacy — the amendments were only proposed in largely Democratic cities within battleground congressional districts — and campaign advertising prominently attacked the Republican incumbents.Those lawmakers, US Reps. Tom Barrett and Bill Huizenga, were both unseated in close races in the Nov. 3 election. Democrats Will Lawrence and Sean McCann will replace them in Congress, respectively.Critics suggested the petition drives used to put the proposals on local ballots were designed to collect voter data and spread negative information about the incumbents.In an election where Democrats saw sweeping gains, approval rates for the ballot proposals in the five liberal-leaning cities generally lagged behind support for major Democratic candidates like Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson.Chokwe Pitchford, a Berrien County commissioner whose nonprofit was paid by City Action Michigan to build support for the proposals, dismissed concerns that the initiative could set a precedent where municipal government itself becomes a platform for political advocacy.“Everyone has access to these tools, and if the other side wants to push a ballot proposal about the Second Amendment or about pro-life policies — if the voters vote for it, that’s democracy,” Pitchford said in an interview.The only representative of the City Action Michigan (formerly Community Action Michigan) that the campaign had not reported paying as of mid-October, Texas Charter Township trustee Barb Hammond, declined repeated requests for an interview with Bridge.What’s next?Local officials are now attempting to figure out how the new committees will work and what their responsibilities are.Municipal advisory boards or committees tend to focus on specific city operations like parks, libraries or transit systems, said Little, the Benton Harbor city manager. But “this is more of a study group to understand price and services for healthcare,” he said.Benton Harbor faces another challenge, he said: The city’s hospital closed 40 years ago, and the city — one where the median income is just above $31,000 and among the lowest in the state — may not have enough residents with healthcare and financing backgrounds to serve on the board.Moreover, he and others said it might seem like local governments can do little to shape healthcare policy. Benton Harbor’s public health initiatives are run through the county health department, for example.And decisions in a national healthcare system with its “infinite complexity” are mostly guided by federal and state policy, said Scott Greer, a University of Michigan professor who researches the ways in which political systems operate and shape health policy decisions.Still, the biennial reports that the committees produce will force “hyper-local” conversations that otherwise might not happen, Greer said.A community might explore how much emergency care is provided to homeless people, and therefore shift policy to extend more routine care to the homeless as a way to keep chronic conditions in check, Greer suggested as an example. That could be a cost saving for the system as those patients then rely less on expensive emergency room care.Benton Harbor, meanwhile, is facing hundreds of thousands of dollars in extra costs to pay for ambulance services because so many local patients are uninsured, said Little, the city manager. Perhaps an advisory committee focused on healthcare can find a solution, he mused.Cohn, at City Action Michigan, said the advisory committees can also offer collective voices that can reach Lansing.Pitchford, in Berrien County, argued the reports can be tailored to “the preconditions of your community.”“You might have an infant mortality crisis, you may have an obesity crisis, you may have pollution in the water, pollution in the air,” he said. “How do we gather all of that information, put it into something that is actionable, and take that to Lansing and to Washington, (DC) so that citizens can lobby their government on behalf of the changes to healthcare that they believe in?”Spokespersons for East Lansing and Portage said city officials now will review next steps.The moneyThrough mid-October, the ballot committee for City Action Michigan reported receiving $2.8 million in donations, exclusively from dark-money nonprofits from outside Michigan not required to disclose their donors.They include American Opportunity Action, Cityscope, Global Impact Social Welfare Fund and Global Impact Ventures — all of which have been known to channel funding to liberal political initiatives while masking donor identities.Much of the funding was spent on ads supporting the proposals and to pay canvassers who collected signatures to get the initiatives onto local ballots.City Action Michigan also disclosed giving $100,000 to Pitchford’s 501(c)(4) nonprofit, Berrien Forward.Pitchford said the money, reported as a grant, was used to pay 17 canvassers to promote the proposals in Benton Harbor and Kalamazoo.“These were older Black women from churches, young people who were getting involved with the election process for the first time, who got trained on knocking doors, and we used that funding to invest in the election,” he said.It’s a “fair criticism” to note that neither he nor the voters know where the money came from, Pitchford acknowledged.He said he makes “value-based assessments” when groups approach him to work on their issues. “No funder, no group has ever asked me to do anything that I don’t believe in,” Pitchford added.___This story was originally published by Bridge Michigan and distributed through a partnership with The Associated Press.

articles.title: El Niño's mild winter could predict trouble for Michigan wildlife and agriculture
articles.description: Experts predict this El Niño will push Michigan toward a milder, drier winter, though polar vortex shifts and lake-effect snow could still bring sharp weather swings.
articles.content: (Adobe Stock)NOAA predicts impactful El Niño effects this winter, pushing Michigan toward a milder, drier season.Greater variability in weather is also predicted, with negative effects on certain native wildlife and agriculture.Polar vortex disruptions and lake effects may bring an added layer of variability.Jonathan Overpeck, University of Michigan professor and Dean of the School of Environment and Sustainability, spent a formative part of his childhood in Michigan.“You know, we'd build a snow fort in December, and it would still be there in February. And now, you know, we get these warm temperatures, and the snow fort will be gone. But then it'll get cold again," he said. "So we can get subzero weather even though we're getting warmer temperatures. But it'll just be more variable.”According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), a massive El Niño is already affecting the Great Lakes region. The warm and cozy fall broke records in parts of Michigan this year, and the winter weather has barely started.The hugely impactful climate pattern, coupled with polar vortex disruptions, is likely to fundamentally shape this winter and the year to come. In Michigan, the effects could be both positive and negative and could be a big player in wildlife survival and agricultural success.What is El Niño?“Of course, many people always ask, ‘Well, what is something thousands of miles away from the Great Lakes? What does that have to do with us?’ And the answer is that these events are so large and involve just thousands of square miles of ocean that they basically influence the flow of the jet stream in both hemispheres, both the North and the South. And of course, the jet stream is what controls our day-to-day and week-to-week weather patterns here,” explained Jeff Andresen, state climatologist and professor at Michigan State University.El Niño is a part of a periodic and natural cycle of weather patterns that drag across the globe every few years. It has to do with the shape and physics of living on a sphere made mostly of water, traveling around the sun and being unevenly heated.“This is one way that the climate system attempts to rebalance itself, and (as) it overheats in certain areas, it cools off too much in others,” said Andresen.Julia Cole, professor at the University of Michigan, explained the science and geography behind the phenomenon. She said that the equatorial Pacific is warming. The water warms the air over it. It then rises all the way up in the atmosphere, and starts to change the normal air flow that occurs around the globe.“It's like sticking a stick in the river, right? It changes the flow downstream. It changes the flow of the upper atmosphere that connects the tropics and the extratropics,” said Cole. It shifts the polar jet stream north, allowing for warmer conditions farther north as well. ”What's happening in the Pacific is able to affect the global climate and climate variability as far away as Michigan, mainly by changing the way the atmosphere circulates.”Climate change is basically supercharging it on one end, adding heat and energy to the system, creating more extreme and unpredictable patterns.Cole’s research on this was recently published in Science magazine. It used modern and fossil coral records to reconstruct historic sea surface temperatures. Her team found an unprecedented increase in variability, particularly over the last 40 years.“It's amazing to think that these corals growing in the tropical Pacific are responding to some of the same rhythms that we here in Michigan might be feeling,” said Cole.Wildlife and agriculture impactsOne of the predictions is that we will have increased variability. Which can mean what’s called winter “heat waves.”This can be hard on hibernating animals, especially pollinators and other insects that need a hard, cold winter or insulating snowpack. For some, the snowpack helps them stay warm; for others, like the woolly bear caterpillar that freezes solid all winter, there’s a cost to warming up and then having to freeze again. It could also allow invasive tropical organisms that would die off during a hard winter to survive.According to Yash Sondhi, an entomologist from Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, it can also cause some insects to “wake up” too early, leaving them without the proper resources in an early spring. If the plants haven’t fully grown out yet, but the insects are looking for food, they can starve.“ El Niño years mess up everything, but a lot of it is because they mess up the plant cycle, so then the animals just don't have anything to eat, so they emerge and they're just starving… So it does affect their population, but the assumption is that they can recover in the next year or two,” said Sondhi. “They have lots of natural fluctuations, but El Niño years the numbers really drastically fluctuate more than in non-El Niño years.”The variability also makes it hard to plan for agriculture, as it changes growing seasons and threatens plants with unusual cold snaps and mini heat waves.“ The variability, especially the occurrence of extremes, it's almost more challenging to manage or to deal with than these changes in mean. Humans for a long, long time have been able to deal with changes, in trends that are orderly. But when you change the extreme events or you change the variability, it's much, much more complicated. And that unfortunately is also a piece of what we're seeing currently in our part of the world.” said Andresen.It’s not all bad news, he explained.“If it is a mild winter, we tend to see an earlier start of the growing season. And for some elements of agriculture, that's not such a bad thing,” said Andresen. More growing time and more options for field work can be a positive result, he explained. But for some crops that overwinter, like Michigan’s famous fruit orchards, an early end to winter or increased temperature fluctuations have the potential to cause cold injuries on the plants.It’s complicatedDespite a lot of talk of warmer weather and polar jet streams pushed north, there is also a polar vortex disruption to contend with. And this week may not be the only wild card of the season; experts are watching for continued disruption later this month.And then, finally, lake effect will have complicating effects as well. A warmer winter could mean less lake ice cover, which could mean more lake effect snow. So the map of future weather predictions is currently a mosaic of impacts.Overpeck explained it best when he advised me to get some good coats, “ I love cold weather. Nothing beats sitting at a football game when it's below freezing, you know, and your feet are going numb.”

articles.description: A spokesperson for the city of Detroit confirmed the authenticity of a video making the rounds on social media.
articles.content: A viral video of two people attempting to board a Detroit city bus with horses in tow is real and officials are investigating. A spokesperson for the city of Detroit confirmed the authenticity of a video making the rounds on social media showing a pair of saddled horses being led onto a Detroit Department of Transportation (DDOT) bus through one entrance and then promptly exiting through another. The following embedded post includes profanity “It is a real video,” said Alexis Ware, deputy director of media relations for the mayor’s office, in an email. “DDOT has located the bus driver.” Related: Equine therapy: Horses help Michigan youth cope with mental health crises MDOT studying plan to create a fourth passenger rail route in Michigan Passenger train planned for Detroit transit hub at Michigan Central campus Transportation troubles create a lonely reality for older Michiganders A Facebook user named Ellessia Drew posted the video on the social media platform. According to CBS Detroit, she was driving on Seven Mile on Saturday when she caught the scene on camera. She told the TV station she turned down Strasburg Street and saw the horses. A Detroit television station, WXYZ-Channel 7, reported that the horses’ owner led them aboard the bus to draw attention to urban horsemanship and Black cowboys. In a Thursday statement, Ware said the city recognizes “that the actions in the video were meant to draw awareness to a positive cause. And we also acknowledge that this presented safety concerns for other passengers on public transit and for the horses themselves. “ “While DDOT welcomes service animals to ride the bus when they meet the requirements under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), it appears that these horses were brought on the bus for other reasons,” Ware said. Rwanda’s investment in children is paying off, with progress and priorities highlighted in a new budget brief
articles.content: UNICEF Rwanda in collaboration with the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning today launched Social Sector Budget Brief focusing on education, health, social protection and water, sanitation and hygiene, as preparations for the FY2027/28 budget begins KIGALI, 12 November 2026 – UNICEF Rwanda and the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning (MINECOFIN) today launched the FY2026/27 Budget Brief, an analysis of public spending in the four sectors on education, health, social protection, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), with the brief showing a nominal increase of 4.2 per cent in these sectors that are important for children. The launch comes as Government begins preparing the FY2027/28 budget, giving ministries and partners a shared evidence base for the choices ahead. Rwanda’s national budget for FY2026/27 stands at Frw 7,796.3 billion, 12.1 per cent higher than last year, with domestic resources now financing more than two-thirds of public spending. The combined allocation to education, health, social protection and WASH rose by 4.2 per cent to Frw 1,711.3 billion, or 22.0 per cent of the national budget. With inflation projected to peak at 10.5 per cent this year, the brief highlights the importance of protecting the real value of these allocations so that recent gains for children are sustained. “Rwanda has shown what steady investment in children can achieve. Fewer children are dying before their fifth birthday, more are finishing primary school, and far fewer families are living in poverty,” said Lieke van de Wiel, UNICEF Representative in Rwanda. “As the FY2027/28 budget takes shape, protecting these investments is one of the surest ways to build the healthy, skilled workforce that Vision 2050 depends on.” The brief shows that Rwanda continues to invest in services for children. Education is now about 88 per cent domestically financed, and domestic funding for social protection rose by two-thirds to make up for lower partner contributions. This investment has gone hand in hand with important gains for children. According to the seventh Integrated Household Living Conditions Survey (EICV7), poverty fell from 39.8 per cent in 2017 to 27.4 per cent in 2024, while extreme poverty more than halved over the same period, from 11.3 to 5.4 per cent. Stunting among children under five declined from 33 per cent in 2020 to 27 per cent in 2025, and under-five mortality dropped from 45 to 36 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2019/20 and 2025. In education, pre-primary net enrolment more than doubled, from 24.2 per cent in 2021/22 to 50.3 per cent in 2024/25. “Investing in people remains at the heart of Rwanda’s development agenda,” said Jeanette Rwigamba, Head of the National Budget Department at MINECOFIN. “This brief, which we developed together with UNICEF, gives us a common evidence base as we prepare the FY2027/28 budget. We look forward to working with line ministries and partners to make every franc count for children.” Looking ahead to FY2027/28, the brief points to a set of practical priorities: keeping allocations to child-focused sectors in step with rising prices; protecting maternal and child health, early childhood and nutrition programmes as external financing changes; building a stronger domestic base for WASH and social protection; and bringing child-focused sectors more fully into Rwanda’s climate finance architecture. The half-day launch at the Kigali Marriott Hotel brings together senior officials from MINECOFIN, the Ministries of Education, Health, Local Government and Infrastructure, the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda and the Local Administrative Entities Development Agency, alongside development partners, research institutions and the media. Participants agreed on priority actions to inform the FY2027/28 planning and budget process. UNICEF promotes the rights and well-being of every child, in everything we do. Together with our partners, we work in 190 countries and territories to translate that commitment into practical action, focusing special effort on reaching the most vulnerable and excluded children, to the benefit of all children, everywhere. For more information about UNICEF and its work for children in Rwanda, visit www.unicef.org/rwanda. Follow UNICEF Rwanda on Twitter, Facebook, Instagram and on our YouTube channel.

articles.description: The first Gemini smartglasses are a collab between Google, Samsung, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker.
articles.content: Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days. Now, Google is ready to take another swing at "intelligent eyewear" for the Gemini era after previewing its plans a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they're no impulse buy. These devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered. Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. Gentle Monster has gone a bit further with six styles, but Google hasn't told us any names for those yet. They come in dark red, pink, gray, and yellow colors and are available with clear, tinted, blue, or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster styles start a little higher at $449, and they will be available in the US and South Korea.Read full article Comments

Scott Colom wins Mississippi US Senate race
articles.description: This story was originally published on Mississippi Today. Colom, a district attorney in north […]
articles.content: District Attorney and U.S. Senate candidate for Mississippi Scott Colom speaks as he gives an update on state of Senate race against Cindy Hyde-Smith November 4, 2026 in Jackson, Mississippi. Colom, a district attorney, was declared the winner of a hard-fought battle for the Senate seat, and will be the first Black U.S. senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images)This story was originally published on Mississippi Today. Democrat Scott Colom has won a hard-fought U.S. Senate race in Mississippi, breaking Republicans’ dominance of statewide offices, ousting one of the state’s sitting senators for the first time since the 1940s and becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. Colom, a district attorney in north Mississippi, defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and independent Ty Pinkins. Colom on Wednesday secured a come-from-behind triumph that has stunned pollsters, pundits and forecasters across the nation. Hyde-Smith has held the Senate seat since 2018. Mississippi has elected only Republican senators for the last 40 years. The Democratic victory is an extraordinary upset in a state that President Donald Trump won by 23 points two years ago, and where Republicans have long maintained a stranglehold on state government and every statewide elected office. A source close to the Colom campaign said the Hyde-Smith had called him to concede on Wednesday evening. She did not immediately release a statement of her own. RESULTS: Mississippi 2026 midterm election results Democratic leaders see Colom’s victory as a stinging rebuke of the Republican Party’s agenda under Trump, who visited the state in the election’s closing days and pleaded with voters to send Hyde-Smith back to the Senate to help advance his agenda. The Associated Press called the race with 99% of precincts reporting. Colom led 49.2% to Hyde-Smith’s 48.7%. He led Wednesday night by 4,645 votes. Colom will now be the 55th Democratic senator to join the chamber, with Alaska’s Senate election still too close to call. The AP called the race for Colom based on uncertified results, and the campaigns have said legal challenges are possible. Colom’s long-awaited win caps more than a week of the nation waiting on Mississippi’s county election officials processing by hand thousands of affidavit ballots to determine the winner. Colom, 43, will be the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since John Stennis in 1982. He is also the first Black person elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since Reconstruction, when the state Legislature elected Hiram Revels in 1870 and Blanche Bruce in 1875. He is also the first Black person elected to any type of statewide office since Reconstruction. When asked about possibly becoming the first Black man in more than a century to win a U.S. Senate race in the state, Colom said he only wants to make sure he won’t “be the last.” “I don’t want anybody to say that I did anything to hurt the next person that has the talent, the work ethic, the ability to be able to reach for their dreams,” Colom said. “That’s my focus.” Most forecasters rated the Mississippi Senate race as safe Republican. But on the issues defining the midterms, voters left little doubt the elections would be a referendum on soaring consumer prices exacerbated by tariffs and the president’s unpopular war in Iran. Colom believed his strategy of tying Hyde-Smith to the high cost of gasoline and consumer prices would be enough to pierce the Republicans’ dominance in the Magnolia State. He began to pick up steam rapidly in the campaign’s closing weeks, receiving endorsements and resources from national Democrats. Colom traversed the state from end to end and, in the election’s homestretch, engaged in a near-nonstop media blitz aimed at galvanizing any voters tuned into traditional cable news shows or following the race on social media. In one viral ad, he mocked Hyde-Smith for suggesting voters upset over the rising price of beef should “pick another protein,” with Colom supporters saying they’d rather pick another senator. Another ad riffed off the Oscar-winning movie “Sinners,” which is set in Mississippi and his final ad before the election featured the home of slain civil rights hero Medgar Evers. Colom mobilized the Democratic base through energetic rallies and appearances with high-profile national Democrats. He also tried to persuade skeptical Republicans. In one 24-hour span just over a week before Election Day, Colom roamed the line outside a Trump rally for Hyde-Smith in northeast Mississippi, spoke to some of the president’s supporters, then headed to the other end of the state for a rally with former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. Dan Pffeifer, a political commentator and former senior adviser to President Barack Obama, said Colom “has run a campaign that is a model for Dems trying to flip very red states.” And his strategy worked. Colom managed to crack the GOP’s iron grip on the state by turning out large numbers of Black voters, flipping several crucial swing counties blue and convincing Republicans to cross over and vote for him. The most surprising feat was Colom winning DeSoto County, a reliably Republican stronghold in a Memphis suburb, by seven percentage points, something Democrats would have viewed as unthinkable last year. Colom also tempered his losses in Harrison County, a populous coastal county that has swamped statewide Democratic candidates over the last decade and become a red firewall for the state GOP. He also flipped Lafayette and Madison counties, two majority-white, affluent areas of the state that have become swing areas in recent elections. In a joint statement, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said Colom’s victory was historic and vowed to work with him “to fight for Mississippians’ health care, costs, and future in the 120th Congress.” “Scott is a seventh-generation Mississippian, proud husband and father of two, and District Attorney who has dedicated his life to keeping communities safe,” Schumer and Gillibrand said. “He has never stopped fighting for his neighbors, because Mississippi Matters – and he’ll continue to be a champion for Mississippi in Washington.” For many pioneering Black officials in Mississippi, Colom’s victory is the culmination of decades of organizing, campaigning and civil rights activism. It’s a moment that many never thought they would see in their lifetimes. Mike Espy, the first Black person to represent Mississippi in the U.S. House since Reconstruction and the first Black person to become U.S. agriculture secretary, unsuccessfully ran against Hyde-Smith twice. The former cabinet secretary served as an advisor to Colom, handed over his donor and voter lists to the campaign and hoped his losses “paved the road” for the soon-to-be senator, he told Mississippi Today in an interview. “There is a time and place for everything,” Espy said. “This is Scott Colom’s time, and his place is in the U.S. Senate. I’m so pleased with the way he ran his campaign, and I was happy to support him.” For Colom’s supporters, his victory brought a sense of poetic justice. Then-President Joe Biden in 2022 nominated Colom to a federal judgeship in northern Mississippi. A bipartisan coalition of Mississippi officials supported the nomination, but Hyde-Smith used her home-state “blue slip” privilege to oppose it. Had Hyde-Smith not blocked Colom’s nomination, he likely would have served on the federal judiciary for the rest of his life and never run for the Senate. But Colom decided to run and cast her as an out-of-touch politician who doesn’t represent Mississippi’s values. Hyde-Smith’s campaign called him a puppet of far-left national Democrats, with a spokesman calling Colom a stooge of Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and to billionaire donor George Soros. Hyde-Smith, a Brookhaven cattle farmer, was first appointed to the Senate in early 2018 by then-Gov. Phil Bryant to succeed longtime Republican Sen. Thad Cochran, who retired about halfway into the six-year term. She won two races against Espy, a special election in late 2018 to fill the end of the term Cochran started and a regular election in 2020, and hoped she would gain a third victory. Hyde-Smith left little doubt that she hoped to stymie Colom’s future as a judge. But in the end, her decision to block him from the federal judiciary cost her a seat in the Senate. articles.title: 7 customer service skills every human and AI agent needs (with examples)
articles.description: Learn the 7 customer service skills every human and AI agent needs, with real examples, a human vs AI comparison, and ways to train and measure them.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Every support conversation can win or lose a customer. How well the AI or human agent on the other end of the interaction listens and solves the problem decides which route the call takes. In isolation, one conversation may not seem like much. Added up across every call and chat, they decide whether a business keeps its customers or keeps replacing them. According to a Zendesk study, more than 50% of customers switched to competitors after a single bad experience. That shows the importance of customer service skills, even as AI continues to disrupt CX operations. Organizations that continuously upskill their CX team have a competitive advantage as customer expectations grow. This guide explores key customer service skills, why they matter for businesses, how to improve them, and how AI augments CX teams. Customer service skills are the soft and technical abilities that help a support team understand customer needs and resolve their problems effectively. These skills are broadly categorized into soft skills, like communication, patience, empathy, and adaptability, and technical skills, like product knowledge or incident management. We’ll explore seven of these skills in more detail: communication, problem-solving, conflict resolution, empathy, adaptability, personalization, and product knowledge. We’ll also touch on how each one applies to both human and AI customer support agents. Customer service skills are practices that help customer experience teams actively listen, understand, respond, resolve, and follow up on customer issues. These skills draw on practices from different disciplines, spanning communication, problem-solving, empathy, and conflict resolution. Equipping your team with the right customer service skills ensures a consistent, positive customer experience across all touchpoints. Traditionally, support teams develop customer service skills through training in both soft and hard skills. For example, you learn how to pause and listen, note customer frustration, and use respectful words to de-escalate situations. In addition, CX teams must be familiar with tools such as CRM and ERP to surface information during conversations. Increasingly, employees in CX need a high level of tech literacy to work with AI agents to surface relevant information and expedite solving the customer’s issue. In fact, the vast majority of customer service teams now use AI agents to streamline customer experience workflows. According to Gartner, at least 70% of customers will start their customer journey using an AI interface by 2028. Upskilling the CX team remains important, but architecting AI support agents around brand SOPs, security guardrails, knowledge base integrations, and third-party tools is key to unlocking the potential of AI-powered CX operations. Effective customer service speeds problem resolution, driving brand loyalty, retention, and revenue over time. Instead of waiting for incidents to escalate, CX teams proactively investigate customer-reported cases. They listen actively and give customers space to share their thoughts before then helping to resolve any problems or queries. The same applies to AI customer service agents. Even though they’re driven by generative AI, machine learning, and other software technologies, you architect them around workflows, principles, and policies that build trust. Whether AI, humans, or both, your goal is to resolve customers’ problems and make them feel heard. When integrating AI into CX workflows, Jannes Koopmann, Sr. AI Business Owner at 3Shape, stressed the importance of an empathetic tone and a human-like feel. As his company modernized customer support with AI agents, Jannes wanted to ensure customers feel understood throughout the entire process. Good customer service requires both humans and their AI counterparts to be competent across different skills. These are the skills needed for customer service, with examples of how human and AI agents apply each one. Clear communication prevents confusion, which causes customers to abandon calls or messages when seeking help. Communication skills require active listening, concise responses, and clear written and verbal communication. Human agents develop communication skills by listening to what customers say and choosing appropriate words in response. They avoid jargon for clarity and always clarify technical terms, whether in email, on a call, or via text. AI agents, particularly those powered by LLMs, excel at conversational responses. However, AI agents need specific guidelines for turn-taking and handling interruptions. For example, when a customer pauses mid-speech, a voice agent must respond within a specific window to sound natural. At the same time, it mustn’t talk over the caller or give unrelated answers. Both human and AI agents can communicate better when they share conversation context effectively. This means that AI and the CX team must have real-time access to conversational analytics to respond accurately. Example: A human agent says, “Let me confirm I have this right: your order shipped on Monday but never arrived.” An AI voice agent repeats back the key detail in the same way and pauses for the customer to confirm before it continues. Customers expect the support team to solve their problems quickly, whether human or AI. Resolving customer pain points is an essential function of CX agents, with a consistently high-quality service helping to build confidence in your brand. Human support personnel can speed up problem resolution by diagnosing issues systematically. This includes noting the customer's issues, confirming details to prevent miscommunication, and drawing on product knowledge to offer a solution. If a solution isn’t immediately available, the human agent communicates next steps to the customer. AI agents share similar problem-solving principles, but they leverage the LLM’s reasoning and predictive capabilities to resolve issues. Based on available customer data and context, AI evaluates possible resolution paths and chooses the one with the highest confidence score. Then, it lists steps that the customer can follow to solve their problem. Example: A customer reports a failed card payment. A human agent checks the account, confirms the card details, and walks the customer through the fix. An AI agent reads the same account data through a connected tool, picks the most likely cause, and shares the steps to resolve it. Despite best efforts, conflict might arise when conversing with customers. Equipping human and AI support agents with conflict resolution skills helps remove friction points, offer remediation, and remain professional throughout the exchange. When resolving conflict, human agents stay composed, follow conflict resolution procedures, and remain objective. They acknowledge the customer’s frustration and gradually work towards a common understanding. The goal is to rebuild trust through concrete action and ensure a fast resolution time. AI, on the other hand, supports conflict de-escalation by providing a clear escalation path. It uses natural language understanding (NLU) to identify when a customer is feeling frustrated, distressed, or angry. Then, it calmly and quickly hands off the conversation to a human agent. Similarly, an agent can transfer the call to a live support team if the customer explicitly requests it. Example: A customer says, “This is the third time I’ve called about this.” A human agent responds, “I’m sorry this hasn’t been resolved yet. I’ll own it from here and tell you exactly what happens next.” An AI agent that detects the same frustration offers a transfer to a human agent and passes along the conversation history with a warm transfer. Empathy is emotional intelligence that allows human agents to resonate with the customer’s feelings. It’s one of the most critical customer service skills because showing empathy builds rapport and creates a shared understanding with the customer. Human agents show empathy by acknowledging their customer’s feelings instead of interjecting with a response. By simply saying “I understand that you’re upset, and I’m ready to help,” you make the customer feel heard and respected. And that opens up further conversations. AI cannot truly feel emotions like humans do. However, AI can identify patterns that indicate frustration in a customer’s voice or textual response. Based on the sentiment it detects, AI can mimic the empathetic tone and choice of words that humans use to show empathy. Example: Both an AI and a human agent who detect frustration can acknowledge it directly by saying, “That sounds frustrating, and I want to get this sorted for you.” Customers reach out to businesses across channels, including email, chat, voice, and text. Adaptability lets the CX team maintain consistent messaging, especially when the same case requires several discussions. Human agents are trained to be competent across platforms. Each platform has its own interaction style, guidelines, and nuances. For example, emails allow time for proofreading to maintain professionalism. However, a call is more impromptu, requiring the agent to react to new information in the moment. AI agents can retain context across topics and conversations. Once configured, teams can deploy agents across different channels. By referring to historical context, AI agents can interact with customers in the tone, format, and style they prefer. Example: In chat, a human agent sends a short written summary the customer can refer back to. On a call, the same agent speaks more slowly and confirms details aloud. An AI agent follows the same rule by sending concise text replies in chat and natural spoken turns on voice. When customers reach out, they expect support agents to know who they are and the details of their case without having to repeat themselves to every new agent they come into contact with. Human agents personalize responses manually. For example, when responding to a ticket, agents review the customer’s past purchases and briefly ask whether they were happy with what they bought. Although it’s a simple gesture, customers feel valued because your team remembers who they are and what they prefer. AI agents can personalize responses more efficiently. Instead of manually checking records, they connect to a third-party CRM and retrieve historical data when supporting customers. Additionally, an AI agent can proactively collect data in real time and use it to make personalized product recommendations. Example: Instead of asking, “What did you order?”, a human agent says, “I can see you bought the Pro plan last month. Is that what you’re contacting us about?” An AI agent connected to a CRM can open with the same context. Customers expect support agents to know the company’s products, services, and policies. As a result, CX teams responding to queries must stay updated to provide confident, accurate responses. Human agents stay up to date by reviewing the latest product and service updates. They note policy changes, documentation updates, and pricing changes that might affect customers. AI agents work similarly, but they use tools like a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system and third-party integrations to provide accurate, helpful answers. For example, an LLM-powered chatbot doesn’t inherently understand a specific product the customer mentions. Instead of guessing, it retrieves information from your organization’s internal knowledge base to generate an answer. Example: When a customer asks whether a refund policy covers sale items, a well-informed human agent answers from the current policy. An AI agent retrieves the latest policy from the knowledge base and answers from it. The table below summarizes how human and AI agents apply each of the seven skills. articles.title: ElevenLabs brings free voice restoration to veterans, songwriters, and more patients
articles.description: ElevenLabs launches free ElevenMusic for artists with voice loss, partners with Wounded Warrior Project, and adds NYU Langone to 1 Million Voices.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Greg Kellner is a New York-based educator and community music leader. He has spent his life teaching through signing and playing guitar. In 2019, brain cancer took his singing voice, putting his teaching career on temporary hold. Seven years later, he was introduced to ElevenLabs via the Impact Program, and has since recreated his singing voice through ElevenMusic based on old recordings. Abdi Omar never had a spoken voice because of cerebral palsy. He designed his own voice from scratch using ElevenLabs Voice Designer. His voice is unique to him, and reflects his individuality. He is now a rap artist using ElevenMusic to help write and produce his tracks. On November 11 at ElevenLabs New York Summit, both Kellner and Omar took to the stage and performed new songs, using their ElevenMusic singing voices. They are two of the first recipients of the new initiative launched by the ElevenLabs Impact team at the Summit. Today, people living with permanent voice loss can now get free access to ElevenMusic, so artists who can no longer sing can keep composing and releasing music. ElevenLabs also welcomed a new 1 Million Voices partner in NYU Langone Health, one of the country’s leading medical centers. Through 1 Million Voices, ElevenLabs provides free, lifetime access to voice restoration for people living with permanent voice loss. The program has helped more than 11,000 people with ALS, motor neurone disease (MND), head and neck cancer, and other conditions speak again in a voice that sounds like their own. ElevenLabs aims to restore 1 Million Voices, a $1 billion in-kind commitment. It reaches people through nonprofit, clinical, and assistive technology partners around the world. On stage, Wounded Warrior Project® (WWP), the nation’s leading veterans service organization, was announced as another Impact Program partner. This collaboration will explore how ElevenLabs technology can help veterans maintain connection, communication, and independence. Until now, 1 Million Voices has focused on speech. Now, it extends to song. People with permanent voice loss can now access ElevenMusic for free to write and release music in their own voices. ElevenLabs is launching the program with Songwriters of North America (SONA), which will verify eligibility and distribute access to its members and the wider songwriting community. More partner organizations will join in the coming months. “Voice restoration has always been about more than getting basic needs met. It’s about being truly heard, in all the ways that make us human. With ElevenMusic, artists living with voice loss can keep creating, sharing their stories, and making music in a voice that’s entirely their own,” said Gabi Leibowitz, Head of Impact at ElevenLabs. The partnership with WWP® launches on Veterans Day and centers on veterans living with voice loss. ElevenLabs will lead an educational workshop for WWP teammates on how voice AI can support warriors experiencing permanent voice loss, blindness, or low vision. Beyond voice restoration, the two organizations will explore how voice technology can connect more veterans and their families to services and programs. “The needs of our nation’s veterans are complex, and we are committed to ensuring those who served have the quality of life they deserve,” said Chris Stuart, chief information officer at Wounded Warrior Project. “That includes harnessing technology, including AI, to reach more warriors with the care and support they need, whenever they need it. Partners like ElevenLabs help make that possible, and we’re excited to build a relationship that expands access to resources and helps us better meet the evolving needs of veterans.” ElevenLabs’ free voice restoration program is now being offered directly to patients at NYU Langone Health, one of the country’s leading academic medical centers. Through NYU Langone’s Rusk Rehabilitation, the program is available as an assistive technology resource for individuals experiencing permanent voice loss related to ALS, head and neck cancer, stroke, and other conditions. Eligible patients can access the program through their rehabilitation care team to create a personalized digital voice that sounds like their own, at no cost. 1 Million Voices is ElevenLabs’ $1 billion in-kind commitment to restore the voices of one million people worldwide, and has already helped more than 11,000 people with disabilities speak again in their own voice. People living with permanent voice loss can apply for free voice restoration through the ElevenLabs Impact Program. Nonprofits, hospitals, and other organizations that support people with disabilities can become a partner. Learn more about the Impact Program here. Create with the highest quality AI Audio

articles.title: CNN This Morning
Collections are coming for millions of student loans in default
articles.description: A long-postponed reckoning could be coming soon for millions of student loan borrowers who are now faced with garnished wages and seized tax refunds as soon as next year. Since pandemic forbearance finally expired last year, more than 9 million borrowers already are in default, owing a collective $234 billion, and millions more are late […]
articles.content: A soon-to-be college graduate tosses her cap for photos at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill in 2024. Student loan debt is crushing people across the country as pandemic forbearance ends, leaving some 9 million borrowers in default. (Photo by Sean Rayford/Getty Images)A long-postponed reckoning could be coming soon for millions of student loan borrowers who are now faced with garnished wages and seized tax refunds as soon as next year. Since pandemic forbearance finally expired last year, more than 9 million borrowers already are in default, owing a collective $234 billion, and millions more are late in their payments. Those borrowers are likely to face severe collection measures such as wage garnishment and seizure of tax refunds next year. Such collections have been repeatedly paused, most recently this past January. Betsy Mayotte, president and founder of The Institute of Student Loan Advisors, a nonprofit that advises borrowers, schools and employers, said she expects collections to start next year. “It’s heartbreaking,” Mayotte said. “People tend to get caught off guard when their tax refund is taken and if they’re struggling financially, a lot of times they’re counting on that refund to catch up.” Quotation I fear that unless something miraculous happens, I will default and my wages will be garnished for life. – Timothy Varro, a New York City attorney who owes $375,000 in student loans The Washington Sun reported in October that collections plans would likely be announced after the midterm elections. The U.S. Department of Education did not respond to a Stateline question. States with the highest default rate, Mississippi, Louisiana and New Mexico, had more than a quarter of borrowers living there in default, but even the lowest state rates were 15% for Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Utah and Wisconsin. That’s according to a Stateline analysis of Education Department data from the second quarter of this year. Defaults began to start up again in late 2025 and early 2026. In those two quarters alone, 13% of student loans went into default in Louisiana and Mississippi, and at least 5% went into default in every state, according to data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York based on credit reports. Older borrowers seemed to be struggling more than they were before the pandemic, according to the bank’s analysis. One of them is Timothy Varro, 40, who has made payments for the past 10 years but can’t keep up even with the interest on the roughly $120,000 he borrowed for college in New Jersey and law school in Rhode Island. Despite a good job as an attorney for a bank in New York City, the balance has ballooned to $375,000, and he can’t make the $2,000 minimum payment. It didn’t help that he graduated in a recession and took low-paying public service jobs at first. “I don’t have rich parents to pay this off for me,” Varro said in an interview. “This may be my conspiracy theory, but I think this is punishment. They’re trying to send a message that this is what’s going to happen if you’re lower or working class and you strive for upward mobility.” Varro said he worries about collection efforts because he’s supporting his fiancé in a small apartment in New York City and has been ill at times with epilepsy that requires breaks from work. “I fear that unless something miraculous happens, I will default and my wages will be garnished for life,” Varro said. “I don’t think it’s asking too much to just give us a payment plan that’s reasonable.” Even on a smaller scale student debt can be a burden when a college education doesn’t pay off as planned. Taylor Lewis, 26, owes $29,000 for her time at Kennesaw State University, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in media and entertainment. Taylor Lewis, 26, of Atlanta went into default on $29,000 in student loan for a degree in media and entertainment that didn’t help her get a job. (Photo courtesy of Taylor Lewis) “I was young, I was just trying to chase my dreams. I wanted to be a talk show host. I wanted to work in the media world,” Lewis said. “I was just young and stupid, pulling out loans every semester and thinking, ‘Yeah I could pay that back. I don’t care about that.’ They prey on undergraduate students. They know we don’t have anything to lose at the time.“ After graduating in 2023 Lewis found that her degree did not get her into the media world without more experience, and she now works as an assistant manager for United Parcel Service in Atlanta. After missing a payment by mistake, she said her loan went into default and she wasn’t allowed to rectify it without paying the full $29,000, which she can’t afford. She’s hoping to be offered a repayment plan and planning to go back to school, paying her own way this time, to get a degree in human resources. Some states, such as Maine, have initiatives to advise students on loans starting in high school. The state suffers too if young people fall into debt, said Mila Tappan, education affordability training manager at the Finance Authority of Maine, known as FAME. Maine is among the states that offer a tax credit for student loan payments to help keep and recruit educated workers. Connecticut has similar credits for employers who help with student loans. Maine had one of the lowest rates of new defaults at the peak in late 2025 and early 2026, along with other New England states such as New Hampshire and Vermont, but also Kentucky and Wisconsin. Maine’s finance authority offers student loan counseling through emails, webinars and in-person events. “We like to think that what we do makes a difference. Some of it is as simple as the mentality here in Maine, that you do what it takes to repay your debts,” Tappan said. Preston Cooper, a senior fellow at the conservative American Enterprise Institute, has written about the student loan crisis and lobbied for changes to benefit taxpayers, he said. He helped craft a process that could deny schools student loans if they can’t prove their degrees raise pay for graduates, for instance. Some private vocational schools have very high rates of late payment on student loans, as high as two-thirds for some that are mostly in the South, according to a 2025 federal report. Schools of medicine and health, on the other hand, often have little or no default. The current crisis caught a lot of student borrowers by surprise because they were allowed to stop payments during the pandemic without being classified as delinquent or in default, and the pause was extended many times. “The government did not do a very good job of communicating the fact that repayment was starting again for real. There were a lot of false starts,” Cooper said. “They would say the student loan payments are about to resume, only to extend the pause. “You had heartbreaking stories where people only found out they were delinquent on their loans when they suddenly got dinged on their credit.” Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org. Bangladesh and India ban toxic pesticide to boost suicide prevention and brain health
articles.content: Globally it is estimated 1 in 5 suicides are attributable to the ingestion of acutely toxic pesticides. Many of these deaths are easily preventable and occur in rural communities across Africa, Asia, Eastern Mediterranean, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Pacific Islands. Long-term exposure to toxic pesticides has also been linked to brain health and neurological risks among agricultural workers, and neurodevelopmental disorders among children. In September 2026, Bangladesh and India declared national bans on paraquat, regarded as one of the most dangerous agricultural chemicals due to its severe toxicity and links with suicide, Parkinson disease, and risk to farmer occupational safety. With this historic public health decision, Bangladesh and India join over 70 countries that have prohibited paraquat. Suicidal thoughts and behaviors can be impulsive and often occur during moments of acute distress. In these critical moments, easy access to a highly lethal means like paraquat can make the difference between life and death. Restricting access to lethal means of suicide is highly effective because it allows crucial time for suicidal thoughts to pass and the opportunity to intervene, preventing numerous potentially fatal actions. Evidence from a number of countries including the Republic of Korea, Malaysia and Sri Lanka demonstrate that national bans on paraquat and other acutely toxic pesticides have resulted in substantial reductions in pesticide-related suicides and overall suicide rates, without harming agricultural productivity. Based on international evidence, national regulatory action on paraquat in Bangladesh and India is anticipated to save thousands of lives and protect brain health. These momentous actions build on years of tireless work across government, civil society, academia, community, and the health sector, including WHO. WHO, in collaboration with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, have produced critical resources to support pesticide regulators in phasing out the use of acutely toxic pesticides linked to suicide, including the International code of conduct on pesticide management: guidance on pesticide regulation to prevent suicide, the brochure Preventing suicide by phasing out highly hazardous pesticide, as well as a resource booklet Preventing suicide: a resource for pesticide registrars and regulators. In addition, a WHO study demonstrated that national bans on acutely toxic pesticides are among the most cost-effective interventions for mental health and have been included in WHO’s Menu of cost-effective interventions for mental health.

articles.title: Southern Michigan communities turn to regional management of growing deer herds
articles.description: On opposite sides of the state, Kent County, and the cities of Farmington Hills, Farmington and Southfield, have turned to regional coalitions to manage growing deer populations.
articles.content: A group of deer pause in the middle of a roadway in Kent County( Kent County Deer Management Coalition)Communities in southern Michigan with growing deer populations are increasingly pursuing a regional approach to managing herds.The coalitions' goals are multi-faceted: human safety, by reducing car crashes with deer, reducing overbrowsing and protecting biodiversity in natural areas, and keeping herds of deer out of neighborhoods and people's yards. The Kent County Deer Management Coalition involves partners like Grand State Valley University, the state Department of Natural Resources, the state Department of Transportation, the Kent County Road Commission, and multiple local governments.Jerry Byrne, the managing director of the Kent County Road Commission, said until recently, Kent County held the unenviable position of the county with the most car crashes involving deer in the state of Michigan. Oakland County has now taken that No. 1 spot, he said.The Kent County coalition is taking a number of steps to reduce human-deer conflicts, Byrne said. One non-lethal approach is mowing the sides of roadways, so deer and drivers can see each other and avoid accidents.Other actions include arranging with the state DNR for additional permits to allow farmers to shoot more deer on their properties, and an app that connects farmers willing to allow hunters access to their lands to hunt deer. Soon, the coalition will also be working with communities that want to have professional sharpshooters reduce the size of the local herd.He says they do not use the word, "cull," to describe these activities."When people think of a cull, they think we are going to eliminate the herd," Byrne said. "We are going to help manage the herd so it's sustainable for the environment — and the deer are not going to then be harvested with a car."The coalition has also hired a wildlife biologist to oversee the programs and conduct surveys to identify problem areas in the county experiencing lots of deer-human crashes and other conflict. A deer management coalition involving Farmington Hills, Farmington, and Southfield has also hired a wildlife biologist.Karen Mondora, the city manager for Farmington Hills, said a wildlife biologist has a unique set of skills the cities don't possess."This wildlife biologist will coordinate with the Michigan Department of Natural Resources to implement the cities' respective deer management plans, which were adopted in 2025," Mondora said, "and they'll also respond to and document resident emails and phone calls regarding wildlife concerns."Mondora said the biologist will also develop and recommend educational resources for the community, and not just related to deer."Really, we do get a lot of inquiries about coyotes and geese and turkeys that seem to be more prolific these days," she said.The Southeast Michigan coalition just concluded its first winter deer reduction program, involving sharpshooters from the USDA Wildlife Services Department. Mondora said they designed the first herd reduction to be somewhat conservative. Seventy deer were killed, she said, with 2,300 pounds of deer meat donated to local food banks via the Michigan Sportsmen Against Hunger program.Mondora said community support for the management program is "mixed," but the primary concern for elected officials in the cooperating cities is safety for people.Efforts to explore a similar regional effort in Washtenaw County communities are already running into political opposition from the Humane Society of Huron Valley, which also opposed the hiring of professional sharpshooters in Ann Arbor in 2015. That program was abandoned by the city council four years later.But in October, a majority of the council approved a resolution directing city officials to study the possibility of a regional deer management program.Whether such a program would include neighboring Scio Township is unclear. Township trustees tabled a resolution to fund a deer management study in early October, after pushback from the Humane Society, some residents and some trustees.Officials with the Humane Society of Huron Valley, along with others, say government programs to shoot deer to manage the size of deer herds are cruel and unnecessary. They say humans should change their own behaviors to avoid conflict with deer, including limiting suburban housing development, slowing down while driving, not planting things in yards that deer like to eat, and, if necessary, sterilizing deer.

articles.content: Your support helps make our show possible and unlocks access to our sponsor-free feed. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said Americans "temporarily" put their trust and hope in Democrats during the midterm elections, but if his party doesn't act boldly when it takes control of Congress, he is concerned they will lose that trust. The 42-year-old, seen as a progressive, said the voters were clear: Democrats need new leadership and an ambitious legislative agenda. "I deeply appreciate Senator Schumer," El-Sayed told NPR's Leila Fadel on the video podcast Newsmakers. "But this is about leadership from the American public, and if all we do is kind of go back to what we've been doing in a moment where we've been given a mandate, I worry that we may not earn our mandate." El-Sayed said he wants Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., to challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., during the December leadership elections. Van Hollen, a 67-year-old progressive, made headlines in 2025 when he traveled to El Salvador to visit Maryland resident Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was wrongfully deported by the Department of Homeland Security without standard due process. "He's willing to take risks when it matters — flying down to see Kilmar Abrego Garcia was a real risk," El-Sayed said of Van Hollen's trip to El Salvador. "I want folks to sort of think about what it means to earn that mandate that we just got. To me, it means taking righteous risks and righteous fights." Beyond changing the Senate leadership, El-Sayed said Congress needs to end the war in Iran, pass "Medicare for All" and abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). When asked how — with Democrats a few seats short of a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate — El-Sayed said he's willing to work with his new Republican colleagues. "I've had a number of conversations with U.S. senators who said some really, really terrible things about me," El-Sayed said. "You know, we talked about auto policy because we make cars in Michigan." He said he hasn't yet spoken to President Trump, who posted "Mr. Veto" on social media following the resounding Democratic midterm victory. "Donald, if you're listening, there's a lot we could work on," El-Sayed said. "Happy to have a meeting. Let's figure out what we can work on and get done." The former Detroit public health official even floated the idea of naming major healthcare legislation after Trump. "Put his name on it," El-Sayed said. "He'll probably pass it. I'm not above doing that. I don't care what it's called." At the same time, he appeared to welcome a standoff with the president over healthcare. "I dare Donald Trump to veto. I dare him," El-Sayed said, "because if you want to make the argument that Democrats want to deliver for you, do that. Make him veto it." During the campaign, Trump called El-Sayed a "jihadist lunatic" who was "on the side of terrorists." El-Sayed said he saw this bigoted name-calling from "a mile away," when he decided to run, but said he knew Michigan voters wouldn't buy it. "The opposition decided to make my name such an issue and my faith such an issue," El-Sayed said. "And so, you know, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed is as American as Mike Rogers. It's as American as Donald Trump. It's as American as whatever JD stands for. It is an American name." In January, Vice President Vance will swear in all the new senators-elect. During the campaign, Vance called El-Sayed a representative of "terrible evil" and a "little weasel." "I hope he doesn't make it awkward," El-Sayed said of Vance. "There is, as I said, a delicious irony in the fact that he is constitutionally obligated to swear me in." El-Sayed's win is historic — he is the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. When taking the oath, he said he will likely swear on the Quran, but he's deciding which one. Right now, he said, it might be the one that Thomas Jefferson owned or the oldest Quran in his state, which is at the University of Michigan. "Whatever my name is, however I pray, it's not the book that you swear on. It's the book you swear allegiance to," he said, referring to the Constitution. "This document is the reason that, no matter how I pray, that I could run for office and that the folks in my state could elect me. What an amazing thing." Michigan Senator-elect El Sayed discusses Democrats’ ambitions
articles.content: NPR's Leila Fadel speaks with U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) about his win in the midterms and what's at the top of his agenda once he begins his first term in Congress. LEILA FADEL, HOST: Abdul El-Sayed is one of the breakout figures of the newly elected Democratic Congress. Voters in Michigan elected the epidemiologist and former public health official to serve in the Senate. He will be the first Muslim to join the Upper Chamber come January. That victory did not come easy, though. Republicans, including President Trumps (ph), viewed a bigoted vitriol against him. Members of his own party thought he leaned too far left. With all that behind him now, I sat down with Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed as part of our Newsmakers series to hear what comes next and why he wants new leadership in the Senate.ABDUL EL-SAYED: I deeply appreciate Senator Schumer. He and I built a partnership over the course of, you know, my campaign. He was very, very supportive of that campaign. I'm grateful for that. But this is about leadership for the American public. And if all we do is kind of go back to what we've been doing in a moment where we've been given a mandate, I worry that we may not earn our mandate.FADEL: So you see Senator Schumer as a leader of the past, not the future?EL-SAYED: I think the American public has been very clear about that, and I think we need to move forward into a future where we're taking the reins and fighting to win.FADEL: Do you have concerns that this moment that your party has could be squandered?EL-SAYED: Absolutely. People are fed up with politics generally, and they have very temporarily put their trust in us. What we do next dictates whether or not they want to continue to trust us. They just asked you - tapped you in to go and help. Go help. There is no point to these jobs, aside from doing the things that the public needs you to do.And right now, people are struggling under the weight of an affordability crisis that is crushing them at every single turn. I think we put the political strategy secondary and say, what are the things we need to do to solve those problems that sit in the lives of everyday people? And if we've done that, the politics will solve themselves.FADEL: OK. So let's talk about what's possible because you are going into a divided government, which historically a lot doesn't get done. So I just want to tick through a lot of the top issues that drove so many voters to understand what you think you can really get done with the Trump administration. Can you make things more affordable in the months ahead?EL-SAYED: Yes.FADEL: How?EL-SAYED: End the war. Stop the tariffs.FADEL: Can you expand healthcare?EL-SAYED: Yes.FADEL: How?EL-SAYED: Make sure Medicaid tax cuts don't take hold, bring back the ACA subsidies and then start toward the path of Medicare for All. There's a public consensus that we should be guaranteeing healthcare here. Then there's a political consensus that says we can't. Now, the only reason that there's a difference between the public consensus and the political consensus - meaning both parties - is somebody's money. It is pharma money. It is insurance money. I stood up against that money. If we put down a bill tomorrow that said we were going to eliminate all the gaps in Medicare and we were going to extend it to children and people under 55, that thing would have 95% support in the public. Let's go do it.FADEL: But it has to have that support in Congress.EL-SAYED: Sure. And then I dare Donald Trump to veto. I dare him. Because if you want to make the argument that Democrats want to deliver for you, do that. Make him veto it. Make him. I bet you he'll put his name on it. He'll probably pass it.FADEL: You faced a really ugly campaign against you that really leaned on bigoted tropes about your ethnicity, your religion, and that started at the top. You know, you had the president of the United States saying, you're a Jihadist lunatic. And Republican - now colleagues - in the Senate saying things about you, as well. Can you work with people who were spewing such vitriol against you?EL-SAYED: You know, this is not the first time I heard any of that. I don't really care what you've said about me in the past. I care that people in Michigan have healthcare, that they can afford their gas and groceries and that we're building an America that is befitting of the American dream.FADEL: So you would sit down with, like, say, Senator Ted Cruz, who called you a Jihadist leprechaun...EL-SAYED: Sure.FADEL: ...And said...EL-SAYED: If he wants to help us get money out of politics, put money in pockets to pass Medicare for All, sure.FADEL: You recently called President Trump the dumbest effing guy who ever was president.EL-SAYED: True.FADEL: You've also said Democrats should drop the decorum and treat the president as the unserious fool that he is.EL-SAYED: True.FADEL: Why are you taking that approach?EL-SAYED: Because he's a bully, alongside being a narcissist. And the only way you deal with bullies is to stand up to them. They bully you because it makes them feel strong. And the way you take on a bully is to bully back because then they learn that this does not make them feel strong. It makes them feel weak, and they don't like to feel weak. And so I think it's important for us to stand up to him.FADEL: Do you think this could just push him away? - this type of approach, calling him dumb and unserious.EL-SAYED: No, because he cannot stand being disliked. So his biggest incentive now - you know, I'm going to say this and it's probably going to reach his desk, and he won't be able to resist it - he wants me to like him. So, Donald...FADEL: You think he wants you to like him?EL-SAYED: ...Call my office. We can have a meeting.FADEL: There was another moment in your victory speech where you referred to the vice president as JD Habibi, and it's really become kind of a touchstone, right? There are hats being made. There are T-shirts being made. There are explainers being written by The Associated Press, like, it means beloved, but it can mean bro or pal. Did you know when you said that, that it was going to become this thing?EL-SAYED: You know, it's funny. Normally, when I speak, I speak off the cuff. I knew there was a lot I needed to get through in that speech, so I actually wrote the speech. Habibi wasn't in the speech. But it was one of those moments where, you know, JD Vance is a very particular kind of politician who represents the worst of the instincts of our politics because he is so focused on his own ascension. And so when I said it, like, it was almost like, I'm so sorry for you. You know, you have mercilessly attacked me for this thing about me that I'm actually really quite proud of. You know, I love my heritage, and it makes me no less American than you. So welcome to this moment where you are forced to reckon with the fact that both your politics lost, and they're ugly on their own terms.And I think, you know, that sort of sense of both I empathize for you because somewhere along the line, somebody should've loved you harder, and also, I'm going to tag you at this so you'll never, ever be able to escape the fact that people are going to call you an Arabic word in your politics.FADEL: What will it be like to be sworn in by him?EL-SAYED: You know, I hope he doesn't make it awkward. I won't (laughter).FADEL: Have you decided what you're going to swear in on?EL-SAYED: I will likely swear in a Quran. Which Quran, we - we're not sure. I mean, Thomas Jefferson had a copy of a Quran. There's also - the University of Michigan holds the first Quran in the state of Michigan. It's very, very old, and that might be the choice. And whatever my name is, however I pray, it's not the book that you swear on. It's the book you swear allegiance to.Yesterday, I got to spend a little bit of time in the National Archives with the original copy of the Constitution. And, you know, it was one of those moments where I was like, this document is the reason that no matter how I pray, that I could run for office and that the folks in my state could elect me. Not every country has that, and, like, we should not take it for granted.FADEL: Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed or Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.EL-SAYED: Leila Fadel...FADEL: Thank you for your time.EL-SAYED: Thank you for the lovely interview.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)FADEL: In my full Newsmakers interview with El-Sayed, he talks about possible Democrat-led investigations of the Trump administration and why he's never shied away from embracing his name, religion and ethnicity.
