articles.title: Michigan’s Black voters sent a message to candidates in midterms: ‘You’ve got to earn it’
articles.description: Autumn Butler, deputy executive director of progressive advocacy group Michigan United, said that on Election Day, she saw lines of people waiting to cast their ballots in cities across Michigan — driving what she expects to be significantly higher voter turnout among Michigan’s Black voters than the last midterm election in 2022. “Everywhere we went, […]
articles.content: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 03: People vote at a polling location on November 03, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. Americans go to the polls in consequential midterm elections, where control of the House and the Senate is at stake for the remainder of President Donald Trump's second term in office. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)Autumn Butler, deputy executive director of progressive advocacy group Michigan United, said that on Election Day, she saw lines of people waiting to cast their ballots in cities across Michigan — driving what she expects to be significantly higher voter turnout among Michigan’s Black voters than the last midterm election in 2022. “Everywhere we went, people were coming out. They were excited. They were ready,” she said. “Anecdotally, just looking at the Black cities throughout the state of Michigan, I definitely saw a great enthusiasm for people to turn out.” As the election results are certified and more detailed voter turnout data emerges, the main takeaway that James Johnson, the political director of a social justice nonprofit Detroit Action, had for candidates in the future seeking to court Black voters is that “The overall lesson is you’ve got to earn it.” “I think it shows that Black people will turn out and they will vote when you speak to them and speak to their issues. But you can’t do the wash, rinse, repeat of the traditional campaigning, or just dump a bunch of mail and commercials in here,” he continued. Johnson said candidates need to be “on the ground” and “touch some grass” to actually talk to Black voters and earn their vote. “It is not something that you can just put in your back pocket and bank on. However, if you do earn it, we will show up, and we will show up for you,” he said. James Johnson is the Political Director of Detroit Action. Tameka Ramsey, executive director and convener of the Michigan Coalition on Black Civic Participation and Black Women’s Roundtable, similarly emphasized, “Everybody needs the Black vote. We’ve seen it across this country.” As for what actually drove that higher turnout that Butler witnessed, she said that the cost of living, including healthcare costs, was a driving factor for many. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE “Struggling with gas, struggling with groceries, and this war has touched a lot of people who have been hearing that the government has enough money for wars, but it doesn’t have enough money for safety net programs here in the country,” Ramsey said. An exit poll from the National Coalition on Black Civic Participation noted that over 36% of Black voters surveyed nationwide listed inflation as the top issue threatening voters and their families, and over 18% listed housing. That drive to the polls stemming from the issues, Johnson said, also showed that turnout was not driven by a “cult of personality” — Black voters were largely not turning out specifically to vote for Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson or Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, but instead because they believed change needed to come on issues like housing and healthcare. He did, however, call the results of the U.S. Senate race “a repudiation of the ideas of Mike Rogers as much as it was an acceptance of Abdul El-Sayed being the person who was carrying those ideas.” Voters wait in line outside the Department of Elections in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance) The highly contentious Senate election led to significant conversation about whether or not El-Sayed could mobilize Black voters, especially after he lost Wayne County in the primary to U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens. But Stevens herself turned off many Black voters just days before the midterms when she went with Rogers to the Perfecting Church in Detroit to announce her endorsement of his Senate campaign, despite having previously endorsed El-Sayed, a move that Ramsey said led some members of that church to feel “used.” “When you talk about specifically anti-Blackness, you brought someone to a place of Black power whose entire career was based on diminishing Black power, and that is motivating because now I know that this person is attacking me in my home, at the home base,” Johnson said about Stevens’ decision not only to make her endorsement of Rogers, but to do so in what he called “the organizing base of Black political power in this country since its inception.” U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina), center left, speaks during a press conference supporting U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, center right, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 at North End Church of God in Christ in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Johnson noted historical friction between Black and Arab communities in metro Detroit — but reminded, “We’re not a monolith, and we also don’t think in such tribalistic terms.” El-Sayed’s presence in Detroit throughout the campaign, and his background as the health director for the city and for Wayne County, was also helpful in developing his trust among Detroit’s Black voters, Ramsey said. “Abdul has worked in Detroit. He has worked around Black people. He has worked with Black people, and he understands,” she explained. “Abdul has worked in Detroit to decrease the health inequalities in Detroit. I mean, getting little kids glasses that were considered problematic in school. So there can be race problems between groups, but I don’t think with Abdul it was as bad as they thought.” Tameka Ramsey Johnson also highlighted another candidate who he said did a good job engaging with Black voters in his own district, Rep.-elect Will Lawrence, whose district includes Lansing and East Lansing as well as more rural areas including in Eaton, Livingston and Shiawassee counties. “A lot of the failure that I saw from candidates was based on the fact that they came into a lot of Black spaces and saying, ‘This is what I’m going to do to fix the community, and this is what Black people need.’ And you’re not a Black member of this community,” he said. “So I saw great successes with people like Will Lawrence who walked in the room and sat down and said, ‘I’m not Black. I’m here to listen. Tell me what’s going on and how we should be trying to help this community,’ because again, the Black community is not a monolith.” Considering all of that, the lesson that Butler said she believes candidates in 2028 — including those running for president — must learn is that the results that they are able to deliver in the next two years are crucially important in convincing voters. “If you want to get reelected, you better show us and be able to show us that you have passed policy that has made life in the Black community better. We need tangible, real things that we can talk about. We don’t need anything esoteric or theoretical,” she said. “If you want to win in 2028, you better start showing us in 2026 and 2027. And I think too, it needs to be early conversations with African Americans to truly listen to what they’re saying and put into action in real time. Don’t wait until three months before the election.” Both Butler and Ramsey also noted that those tangible impacts in the next two years must be long-term positive changes in the Black community — “policies that are going to impact us generationally,” Butler described, such as promoting policies that allow small Black-owned businesses to thrive. And for any candidate seeking office in Michigan going forward, Johnson said that he believes that “the Black voter in Michigan is and has always been a game changer.” “I think it is now a much more activated base, and it has to be recognized by any politician, any political party, anyone who’s seeking office and seeking to represent this state at any level, they’re going to have to speak directly to the issues facing the community,” he said.

articles.content: It's on to the second round in the 5A Arizona high school football playoffs. The games should become much more competitive now. Who shocks? Who wins? The Arizona Republic breaks down the eight games and predicts the outcomes. All games are Friday, Nov. 13, at 7 p.m. MST. No. 16 Marana (8-3) at No. 1 Scottsdale Desert Mountain (8-1) Desert Mountain didn't get a chance to play its final regular-season game against Horizon due to weather. So it has had a few weeks to get ready for this. Expect the defending 5A champion Wolves to unleash a great deal of emotion into this game against a solid Marana team that turned back Phoenix Sunnylope in the first round last week. Desert Mountain has a tremendous defense and potent offense, led by running back Easton Conner. Prediction: Desert Mountain 31, Marana 14 No. 9 Waddell Canyon View (9-2) at No. 8 Chandler Arizona College Prep (7-3) Canyon View's losses came in close games against Desert Edge and Millennium. This is a tough, hard-nosed team that relies on a strong pass rush. Arizona College Prep, led by first-year head coach Jacob Rutter, feels well-prepared after dominating Ironwood Ridge 66-21 in the first round. This is a major test for Canyon View's defense. Expect a close game coming down to the final minute. Prediction: Canyon View 28, Arizona College Prep 24 No. 12 Phoenix Mountain Pointe (5-6) at No. 5 Goodyear Desert Edge (8-2) This might be the most intriguing 5A playoff game of the night. Can Mountain Pointe shock the Scorpions again? The Pride knocked off Desert Edge earlier in the season 34-27, behind Chris McCorkle's 192 rushing yards. Desert Edge's defense has too much talent to let that happen again. And quarterback Blake Roskopf, who threw for 300 yards in the first meeting, will be ready, along with dynamic receiver Zerek Sidney. Prediction: Desert Edge 31, Mountain Pointe 21 No. 20 Peoria Sunrise Mountain (7-4) at No. 4 ALA Gilbert North (10-0) Sunrise Mountain is playing with house money after stunning Campo Verde 31-20 last week in the first round. Can this offense continue to make big plays against one of the best defenses in the state? ALA GN linebacker McRae Skinner is one of the best in the state with 81 tackles, 7.5 for losses. His teammate, running back/safety Weston Powell, was Player of the Year in their region. Prediction: ALA Gilbert North 30, Sunrise Mountain 16 No. 19 Tempe McClintock (8-3) at No. 3 Scottsdale Notre Dame (7-2) Here comes the shocker. McClintock is playing sound football on both sides of the ball and is oozing with confidence after beating Chaparral 28-14. Aidan Whitaker of McClintock is one of the most versatile impact athletes in the state who can beat a team on offense and defense. Notre Dame has had two weeks off to get ready for this. But this is a team that was stunned by Cactus Shadows 17-7 late in the season. Prediction: McClintock 21, Notre Dame 18 No. 11 Glendale Cactus (9-2) at No. 6 Tucson Desert View (10-0) Desert View has won 21 consecutive regular-season games, continuing a streak this year without star running back Jaylee Abraham, who transferred to Peoria Centennial. It's not just smoke and mirrors. Desert View is well-coached and has great pieces on both sides of the ball. Their streak is no fluke. But Cactus has played a tough schedule and knows how to win playoff games. The Cobras beat Tucson 39-10 in the first round. Expect an upset. No. 10 Cave Creek Cactus Shadows (5-6) at No. 7 Goodyear Millennium (9-1) Much of Millennium's success will hinge on the health of star running back D'Mari Bryant, who suffered an injury in the final-regular season game, a loss to Desert Edge. If Bryant is good to go, then expect a big game from him and for the Tigers, who should bounce back from that loss two weeks ago. But this is a resilient Cactus Shadows team that came out of the meat-grinder Northeast Valley Region. Expect a close game. Prediction: Millennium, 25, Cactus Shadows 22 No. 15 Yuma Catholic (8-3) at No. 2 Phoenix Horizon (7-2) Horizon also had its final regular-season game with Chaparral canceled due to the storms. How will Horizon respond with two weeks off? Running back Dylan Brush is among the top players in the state and could have a huge game against Yuma Catholic, which started the season with a 34-17 loss to Notre Dame Prep. The Shamrocks have won their last four games, but this is their toughest opponent since losing to Cactus 25-12 on Oct. 9. Prediction: Horizon 35, Yuma Catholic 21 Richard Obert has been covering high school sports since the 1980s for The Arizona Republic.
